name: @sableui/react
description: Themeable React components, semantic tokens, layout patterns, presets, and package-owned agent skills. Default theme: Sable.

consume.stack: Sable depends on no router, data or form library; an existing app keeps its own, and links take any router's Link through render. For a blank-slate app the suggested stack is Vite + TypeScript, TanStack Router, TanStack Query, TanStack Form for forms with validation logic, and TanStack Table once a table outgrows DataTable (sable docs tables-with-tanstack).
consume.cssSources: That @source ships every component's classes (about 32 KB gzipped). Once the app is built, `sable sources --write src/sable-sources.css` lists just the modules it imports; @import that file in place of the @source. sable check fails while it is stale.

fonts.note: theme declares the stacks; the host app loads the font files

providers.required: IconProvider at the app root: import { reiconIconSet } from "@sableui/react/icons/reicon" and wrap the app in <IconProvider set={reiconIconSet}> (or pass your own IconSet). Without it every <Icon> renders nothing; development builds warn once.
providers.optional: Extend Reicon with composeIconSets(appExtras, reiconIconSet) — composeIconSets from "@sableui/react", reiconIconSet from "@sableui/react/icons/reicon". MotionProvider controls motion. SableThemeProvider supplies user-selectable color modes and themes.

consume.themeSwitching: Preferred: wrap the app in SableThemeProvider and call useSableTheme() to read mode/preference/themeId/themes and setPreference/setThemeId. The provider persists choices, toggles the `dark` class for light/dark/system, and writes data-sable-theme for non-default design themes.
consume.darkMode: Low-level contract: toggle the `dark` class on <html> (dark-by-default lives under .dark). Sable uses no `dark:` utilities, so a Tailwind `@custom-variant dark` is only needed if your own app code uses them.
consume.designTheme: Set data-sable-theme for alternate or app-owned themes; omit the attribute or use base for the default. Register portable presets with presetManifest() through SableThemeProvider customThemes, and load their scoped CSS and fonts.

cssOptional.themes.css: @import "@sableui/react/themes.css"; — all bundled alternatives. styles.css already includes the Sable theme. Alternate CSS is scoped by data-sable-theme.
cssOptional.theme/<id>.css: @import "@sableui/react/theme/prism.css"; — one bundled alternative. Prefer this when the app uses exactly one.
cssOptional.symptom: The active theme renders as the Sable theme when its stylesheet has not been imported. Load the selected theme CSS before applying its ID.

designWorkflow.skill: sable setup --agent; build, inspire, audit, polish; package-owned skills/sable/SKILL.md
designWorkflow.presets: sable docs using-presets; sable preset --check <path> --json; sable preset --css <path>
designWorkflow.visualAtlas: Optional, project-owned (.sable/atlas/atlas.json); the package ships none. sable atlas --search "<context>" --contrast --limit 3 --json; then --show <id> and view the returned evidence paths
designWorkflow.exploration: Optional when alternatives materially affect the brief: sable explore --template; build bounded rendered directions; --check <manifest.json>; --compare <manifest.json>
designWorkflow.preferences: sable prefer --search "<decision>" --scope project:<id> --json; human choices and agent observations remain distinct
designWorkflow.composition: Inspect a relevant pattern skeleton. Reuse when its information architecture fits; original compositions from layout primitives are equally valid.
designWorkflow.finish: sable check <source paths> runs doctor, lint and grade in one pass and exits 1 on any failure, then lists the review steps no tool can verify. Optional Claude Code Stop hook: sable setup --agent --target claude --hook
designWorkflow.adoption: sable check reports how much of the UI composes Sable and the app-built components Sable already ships (grade --json → adoption). Never a failure; at level none or low, ask the user before moving working screens: sable docs auditing-an-app → Adoption.
designWorkflow.localMemory: .sable/lessons/ for causal observations; .sable/preferences/ for scoped judgments; both project-owned and preserved across package upgrades
designWorkflow.qualityLimit: Source checks and evidence completeness do not independently judge visual quality. Inspect rendered desktop/mobile states and real interactions.

agentSetup.monorepo: When Sable belongs to one workspace package, run setup in that package with --root at the repository root: pnpm --filter <package> exec sable setup --agent --root <path to root>. Entries go to the root and resolve Sable through the package.
agentSetup.canonical: skills/sable/SKILL.md in the installed package; entries resolve it on every task
agentSetup.instructions: A short managed block in AGENTS.md (Codex, Cursor) and CLAUDE.md (Claude Code), between <!-- sable:begin --> and <!-- sable:end -->, that sends every UI request through the skill even when it doesn't name Sable. --no-instructions skips it.
agentSetup.upgrade: pnpm exec sable upgrade (updates the package, then runs the new version's init). From 0.17 or earlier: pnpm update @sableui/react --latest; pnpm exec sable init
agentSetup.preserves: Local edits, project instructions outside the Sable block, presets and preferences; setup only refreshes unchanged managed entries and blocks, and refuses linked destinations.

consume.distributionStatus: Public on npm as @sableui/react; install with pnpm add @sableui/react.

ios.when: Only for an explicitly requested browser iOS prototype; match components by role with sable target ios --json.
ios.css: @import "tailwindcss"; then @import "@sableui/react/ios/styles.css"; in the isolated native document.
ios.updates: Consume the shipped adapter instead of copying demo helpers. Package upgrades update the brand bridge, material, safe areas, navigation, sheets and input bindings.

init.after: Run it once the package is installed; before that `npx sable` resolves an unrelated package.
init.does: Installs missing packages with the lockfile's package manager (React, Tailwind and its build plugin), writes the css imports in order into the global stylesheet, adds bundlerDedupe and the Tailwind plugin to a Vite config (a postcss.config.mjs for Next.js), loads the fonts, wraps a Vite starter's <App /> in IconProvider, runs agentSetup (skill entries plus the AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md block; in a terminal it offers the Stop hook), then sable doctor.
init.frameworks: Vite and Next.js (App Router) get every step. Other setups get the packages and the stylesheet; the bundler and provider steps are printed.
init.manual: Each edit it cannot make safely (an unfamiliar config shape, a Next.js layout, a stylesheet split across files) is printed as the exact snippet and the file it belongs in. Apply them, then run sable doctor.
init.flags: --dry-run previews; --no-agent skips the skill; --no-install prints install commands instead of running them.
init.repair: In an app that is already wired: pnpm exec sable doctor --fix (or --dry-run) applies the same fixes to whatever doctor flags.

themes.fontsNote: fonts is the first family of each role's stack; fontStacks is the full stack the theme CSS declares. The host app loads the files (Google Fonts for every built-in primary). Generated from src/themes/*/index.ts — do not hand-edit.

semantic.name: background
semantic.intent: The page. The furthest-back surface in the page register.
semantic.whenToUse: The document body, and any surface meant to read as 'the page itself'. Never anything that floats: background is the BOTTOM of the surface stack (background < card < popover in every dark mode), so a floating panel painted with it reads as a hole beneath the cards it hovers over.
semantic.insteadOf: `popover` for anything floating, `card` for a bounded block on the page. `canvas`. `canvas` is the *work* surface in a tool — the artboard being edited — which is not the page behind the UI. Using `background` for an artboard makes the thing being edited indistinguishable from the chrome around it.

semantic.name: foreground
semantic.intent: The default ink, for `background`.
semantic.whenToUse: Body text and any content sitting directly on the page.
semantic.insteadOf: any other surface's ink. On `card`, `popover`, `panel` or a tone, use that surface's own `-foreground`.

semantic.name: card
semantic.intent: A raised content container on the page.
semantic.whenToUse: A bounded block of related content on a page: an article teaser, a settings group, a stat panel.
semantic.insteadOf: `popover`. A card sits *in* the document flow; a popover floats above it and needs its own elevation and border treatment. And never inside a docked panel — use `panel` surfaces and `PanelSection`; a card in a 240px panel spends its border and inset on nothing. Never rely on `card` as a FILL to separate something from the page: a preset's `card` can equal `background`, because a card separates by its border. A track, well or pad that must read with no border is `muted`.

semantic.name: card-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `card`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `card`. Use them as a pair — `bg-card text-card-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: popover
semantic.intent: A floating surface: menu, popover, tooltip body, select list, dialog, and any persistent floating panel (an inspector, a toolbar over a canvas).
semantic.whenToUse: Anything rendered in a layer above the page that needs its own background, dismissible or not. The test is elevation: if it floats over content (`shadow-md` or higher, fixed or absolutely positioned above the page), it is popover. Pair with `text-popover-foreground`.
semantic.insteadOf: `card` and `background`. The distinction is elevation, not shape or lifetime: a panel that stays open is still floating. `background` is the page ground and `card` sits on it; both read as sunk under a floating panel. In light mode several presets make all three equal, so a floating surface also needs its edge (ring or border) and shadow, never the fill alone.

semantic.name: popover-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `popover`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `popover`. Use them as a pair — `bg-popover text-popover-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: muted
semantic.intent: A recessed surface. Quieter than the page, not interactive.
semantic.whenToUse: An inset well: a code block background, a disabled field, a read-only region, a table's zebra stripe, a segmented-control track. On the page it always differs from `background`. Inside any OTHER surface (a card, a popover, a floating panel) use the `sable-well` utility instead: it derives the well from the surface it sits in, so it is the same visible step everywhere, whereas `muted` can land within a step of a popover in some dark modes. Never compensate with an outline on every well — that turns a panel into a stack of boxes.
semantic.insteadOf: `secondary` and `accent`. All three are near-identical in most themes, which is exactly why the rule is by ROLE: `muted` is *recessed and inert*, `secondary` is a *control fill*, `accent` is a *transient state*. Pick by what the surface does, never by which looks right — they diverge in other themes.

semantic.name: muted-foreground
semantic.intent: De-emphasised ink. The single most-used token after `foreground`.
semantic.whenToUse: Secondary text: captions, helper text, placeholder-adjacent labels, a property name next to its value, timestamps.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground` at reduced opacity. Opacity on text compounds unpredictably against whatever is behind it and can fall below the contrast floor; this token is a tuned value that does not.

semantic.name: border
semantic.intent: The default hairline. Tuned to be subtle.
semantic.whenToUse: Input outlines, badge edges, card borders — chrome that should not draw the eye.
semantic.insteadOf: `border-strong`. Reach for `border-strong` when the line carries *structure* (a grid rule, a table divider, a section separator) and for `border` when it merely bounds a control.

semantic.name: border-strong
semantic.intent: A structural divider. Visibly stronger than `border`.
semantic.whenToUse: Grid lines, table rules, separators between major sections.
semantic.insteadOf: `border`. If removing the line would make the layout ambiguous, it is structural and belongs here.

semantic.name: input
semantic.intent: The outline of a form control specifically.
semantic.whenToUse: Text inputs, textareas and selects (through `field-border`, which derives from it). Not the edge of a checkbox, radio or switch — that is `control-border`.
semantic.insteadOf: `border`. They are often the same value, but a theme is entitled to make form controls read differently from other chrome, and only this token gives it the hook.

semantic.name: control-border
semantic.intent: The resting edge of a control whose outline is the whole control. Held to 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11) on every surface.
semantic.whenToUse: An unchecked checkbox, an unselected radio, an off switch track, a selection card's check or radio mark — anywhere removing the edge would make the control disappear.
semantic.insteadOf: `input`. A text field is also found by its fill, caret and placeholder, so its outline may stay quiet; a checkbox has nothing else, and at `input`'s strength it measures about 1.4:1.

semantic.name: ring
semantic.intent: The focus indicator colour.
semantic.whenToUse: Only for `focus-visible`. Nothing else.
semantic.insteadOf: `primary`. Focus must remain distinguishable from selection; if the ring is the same colour as a selected state, a keyboard user cannot tell where focus is.

semantic.name: primary
semantic.intent: The one high-emphasis action colour.
semantic.whenToUse: The single most important action on a surface — one per view. A submit button, the primary CTA.
semantic.insteadOf: `accent`. `primary` says *do this*; `accent` says *this is the current one*. Two primary buttons on one screen means neither is primary.

semantic.name: primary-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `primary`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `primary`. Use them as a pair — `bg-primary text-primary-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: secondary
semantic.intent: A lower-emphasis control fill.
semantic.whenToUse: A secondary button, a segmented control's resting fill, a neutral chip.
semantic.insteadOf: `muted`. `secondary` is for something you can *press*; `muted` is for a surface that is inert. See the `muted` note — role, not appearance.

semantic.name: secondary-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `secondary`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `secondary`. Use them as a pair — `bg-secondary text-secondary-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: accent
semantic.intent: A transient state fill: hover, selected, current.
semantic.whenToUse: The fill behind a hovered menu item, a selected list row, the active segment of a switcher.
semantic.insteadOf: `primary` for selection, and `muted` for hover. `accent` is the state layer; the other two are emphasis and recession respectively.

semantic.name: accent-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `accent`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `accent`. Use them as a pair — `bg-accent text-accent-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: destructive
semantic.intent: Irreversible or data-losing actions.
semantic.whenToUse: Delete, revoke, remove, discard — and the error state of a form field.
semantic.insteadOf: `tone-warning`. Destructive means *this destroys something*; warning means *be careful*. A confirmation dialog's action is destructive; the banner explaining it is a warning.

semantic.name: destructive-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `destructive`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `destructive`. Use them as a pair — `bg-destructive text-destructive-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: success
semantic.intent: A confirmed, completed, healthy state.
semantic.whenToUse: A passing check, a saved indicator, a healthy status dot.
semantic.insteadOf: `tone-info`. Success asserts an outcome; info asserts a fact. 'Saved' is success, '3 items' is info.

semantic.name: success-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `success`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `success`. Use them as a pair — `bg-success text-success-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: tone-3
semantic.intent: Extra colour 3: the third, and usually the quietest, category in a classified set.
semantic.whenToUse: A third category, or the baseline one that means 'nothing special'.
semantic.insteadOf: `muted`. A tone is *semantic classification* that a reader is meant to decode; `muted` is de-emphasis. If a legend would help the user, it is a tone.

semantic.name: tone-2
semantic.intent: Extra colour 2: the second category in a classified set.
semantic.whenToUse: A second category, distinct from tone-1, in a badge, dot, card or chart.
semantic.insteadOf: `tone-1`. Distinct categories must stay visually distinct.

semantic.name: tone-1
semantic.intent: Extra colour 1, the lead of the three a theme defines beyond its status colours. The numbered tones exist so a product can classify content (categories, plans, series) without inventing colours per feature; the product decides what each one means.
semantic.whenToUse: The most prominent category in a classified set, or the first series of a chart.
semantic.insteadOf: `primary`. A tone classifies the *thing*; primary drives an *action*. A category badge is not a button.

semantic.name: tone-info
semantic.intent: Domain tone: neutral, factual information.
semantic.whenToUse: An informational note or banner, a neutral count, a 'did you know' surface.
semantic.insteadOf: `success`. Info states a fact; success states an outcome. Also not `primary` — an info banner is not an action.

semantic.name: tone-warning
semantic.intent: Domain tone: proceed with care, nothing is broken yet.
semantic.whenToUse: A caution banner, a nearing-limit indicator, a soloed/overridden state in a tool.
semantic.insteadOf: `destructive`. Warning is *advisory*; destructive is *consequential*. If nothing is lost by continuing, it is a warning.

semantic.name: highlight
semantic.intent: A marker on content the user is meant to notice — search hits, diffs, annotations.
semantic.whenToUse: Highlighting matched text, a changed line, a called-out passage.
semantic.insteadOf: `accent`. `accent` is UI state that follows the pointer or selection; `highlight` marks the *content* and persists independently of interaction.

semantic.name: tone-3-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `tone-3`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `tone-3`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-3 text-tone-3-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: tone-2-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `tone-2`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `tone-2`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-2 text-tone-2-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: tone-1-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `tone-1`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `tone-1`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-1 text-tone-1-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: tone-info-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `tone-info`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `tone-info`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-info text-tone-info-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: tone-warning-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `tone-warning`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `tone-warning`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-warning text-tone-warning-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: highlight-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `highlight`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `highlight`. Use them as a pair — `bg-highlight text-highlight-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: destructive-text
semantic.intent: `destructive` drawn on a surface: text, icons, borders and focus rings.
semantic.whenToUse: Write `text-destructive`, `border-destructive` or `ring-destructive` — they read this token; only `bg-destructive` reads the fill.
semantic.insteadOf: `destructive` itself for marks on a page. The fill is tuned to carry a label (dark mode lowers it under white ink), which can leave it too dark to read on a dark card.

semantic.name: success-text
semantic.intent: `success` drawn on a surface: text, icons, borders and focus rings.
semantic.whenToUse: Write `text-success`, `border-success` or `ring-success` — they read this token; only `bg-success` reads the fill.
semantic.insteadOf: `success` itself for marks on a page. The fill is tuned to carry a label (dark mode lowers it under white ink), which can leave it too dark to read on a dark card.

semantic.name: tone-warning-text
semantic.intent: `tone-warning` drawn on a surface: text, icons, borders and focus rings.
semantic.whenToUse: Write `text-tone-warning`, `border-tone-warning` or `ring-tone-warning` — they read this token; only `bg-tone-warning` reads the fill.
semantic.insteadOf: `tone-warning` itself for marks on a page. The fill is tuned to carry a label (dark mode lowers it under white ink), which can leave it too dark to read on a dark card.

semantic.name: tone-info-text
semantic.intent: `tone-info` drawn on a surface: text, icons, borders and focus rings.
semantic.whenToUse: Write `text-tone-info`, `border-tone-info` or `ring-tone-info` — they read this token; only `bg-tone-info` reads the fill.
semantic.insteadOf: `tone-info` itself for marks on a page. The fill is tuned to carry a label (dark mode lowers it under white ink), which can leave it too dark to read on a dark card.

semantic.name: overlay
semantic.intent: A scrim over the page behind a modal, and the wash behind media chrome.
semantic.whenToUse: Dialog and sheet backdrops, letterboxing, a pill sitting on top of an image.
semantic.insteadOf: `bg-black/50`. Pure black is never right — it crushes whatever is behind it, and a theme cannot tune it. This token is the sanctioned answer, which is why `raw-black-white` is a lint rule.

semantic.name: overlay-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `overlay`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `overlay`. Use them as a pair — `bg-overlay text-overlay-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: sidebar
semantic.intent: The app sidebar's own surface. Heads a small family (`sidebar-*`) that lets navigation chrome diverge from the page without overriding page tokens.
semantic.whenToUse: The `Sidebar` / `SideNav` background.
semantic.insteadOf: `card`. A sidebar is persistent chrome, not content — a theme frequently wants it a different tone from the cards inside the page it frames.

semantic.name: sidebar-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `sidebar`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `sidebar`. Use them as a pair — `bg-sidebar text-sidebar-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: sidebar-primary
semantic.intent: The high-emphasis colour *within* the sidebar.
semantic.whenToUse: The active nav item's fill, when the sidebar has its own tonal world.
semantic.insteadOf: `primary`. Page primary on a sidebar surface may not clear contrast; this token is tuned against `sidebar`.

semantic.name: sidebar-primary-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `sidebar-primary`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `sidebar-primary`. Use them as a pair — `bg-sidebar-primary text-sidebar-primary-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: sidebar-accent
semantic.intent: The state layer within the sidebar — hover, current.
semantic.whenToUse: Hovered or current nav items.
semantic.insteadOf: `accent`, for the same contrast reason as `sidebar-primary`.

semantic.name: sidebar-accent-foreground
semantic.intent: Ink paired with `sidebar-accent`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
semantic.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `sidebar-accent`. Use them as a pair — `bg-sidebar-accent text-sidebar-accent-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
semantic.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

semantic.name: sidebar-border
semantic.intent: Hairlines inside the sidebar.
semantic.whenToUse: Dividers between nav sections, and the sidebar's own trailing edge.
semantic.insteadOf: `border`, which is tuned against page surfaces.

semantic.name: sidebar-ring
semantic.intent: Focus indicator inside the sidebar.
semantic.whenToUse: `focus-visible` on nav items.
semantic.insteadOf: `ring`, which is tuned against page surfaces.

typography.name: display-4xl
typography.intent: The largest type: display-lg through display-4xl. Marketing-scale, one per view at most.
typography.whenToUse: A landing page hero, a section opener on a brand surface.
typography.insteadOf: `heading-1` for page titles. Display is a *statement*; headings are *structure*. A settings page titled in display-3xl looks like an advert.

typography.name: display-3xl

radii.name: none
radii.whenToUse: Edge-to-edge surfaces, table cells, anything whose corners meet another element's corners.
radii.insteadOf: omitting a radius class. Stating `none` records the intent; omitting it means the next person cannot tell square-on-purpose from square-by-accident.

radii.name: xs
radii.intent: The tightest real corner. Reads as 'crisp', not 'rounded'.
radii.whenToUse: Tool-chrome controls, tree rows, small swatches — anywhere the radius should be felt but not seen. The workspace register runs ~5px on essentially everything.
radii.insteadOf: `sm`. In a 24px-tall control an `sm` radius starts to read as a lozenge.

radii.name: sm
radii.whenToUse: Inputs, buttons in the page register, badges, small cards.

radii.name: md
radii.whenToUse: Cards, panels, popovers, menus — surfaces that hold other things.
radii.insteadOf: `sm`. A container should be softer than the controls inside it, or the nesting reads inverted.

radii.name: lg
radii.whenToUse: Dialogs, sheets, hero media, feature cards.

radii.name: xl
radii.intent: The softest rectangular corner. A styling statement.
radii.whenToUse: Marketing surfaces, large imagery, a theme that wants a soft character.
radii.insteadOf: `full`. `xl` is still a rectangle with soft corners; `full` is a capsule. Using `xl` on a small element makes it look like a failed capsule.

radii.name: full
radii.intent: A capsule or circle — radius exceeds half the height.
radii.whenToUse: Avatars, status dots, notification badges, pills, and page-register actions (the 'round action in a tight container' contrast that says *this is a control*).
radii.insteadOf: any fixed radius, for circles. And NOT in tool chrome: neither Figma nor Paper has a single pill in its chrome, which is why the compact density scope flattens `--button-radius` to ~5px.

layout.name: rhythm-unit
layout.intent: The vertical rhythm base — one baseline step (8px at the default scale). Every vertical measure is a multiple of it, and it follows the type and the density control.
layout.whenToUse: Through `Stack`/`Row`/`Grid` gap numbers, which are rhythm units rather than pixels. A gap of 2 is 16px at the default scale, and grows or tightens with density.
layout.insteadOf: arbitrary vertical spacing. The rhythm is what makes unrelated sections of a page feel like one document.

layout.name: grid-columns
layout.intent: The column count of the content grid — 12.
layout.whenToUse: `Grid`/`Columns`, WITHIN a region, for genuinely multi-column content.
layout.insteadOf: using a column span as the page's reading width. A span is not a measure — see `measure-prose`.

layout.name: grid-gutter
layout.intent: The gap between grid columns and rows — 2 baseline steps on phones, 3 on desktop, snapped to the step.

layout.name: page-inset
layout.intent: The page's outer breathing room, left and right.
layout.whenToUse: The gutter between content and the viewport edge, at every breakpoint.
layout.insteadOf: a global max-width. Sable caps width per REGION by role, never once for the whole page.

layout.name: measure-prose
layout.intent: The maximum comfortable line length for prose, in `ch`.
layout.insteadOf: a layout width. Measure and width are different things: a wide region can still hold a narrow measure, and capping the region instead makes everything else in it too narrow.

layout.name: region-form
layout.intent: The region cap for a form — narrow, because fields should not run long.
layout.whenToUse: Settings pages, auth screens, any column of inputs.
layout.insteadOf: `region-content`. A 700px-wide text input is harder to use, not more generous.

layout.name: region-feed
layout.intent: The region cap for a scrolling list of items.

layout.name: region-content
layout.intent: The default region cap for mixed page content.
layout.whenToUse: Article bodies with media, documentation, most product pages.

layout.name: region-wide
layout.intent: A wide region for dense or tabular content.
layout.whenToUse: Data tables, dashboards, galleries — content that genuinely needs the room.

layout.name: region-full
layout.whenToUse: Hero imagery, full-bleed sections, and a workspace, which is always edge-to-edge.

layout.name: region-ultrawide (legacy — prefer region-full)
layout.intent: Deprecated. Kept so existing usage keeps resolving.

typographyOverrides.name: type-base
typographyOverrides.intent: The base size the page type scale is built on, as a unitless px number — 16 by default. Every page tier keeps its ratio to it, so `14` rebuilds the whole scale at 14, and the baseline step and spacing follow the body down.
typographyOverrides.whenToUse: When the product asks for smaller or larger type everywhere: a dense technical tool at 13-14, a reading product at 17. Set it on :root, a theme scope or a preset (`tokens.shared["type-base"]: "14"`), not per component.
typographyOverrides.insteadOf: Changing the root font-size, which also moves every rem the app wrote and the control ladder; or overriding tier sizes one by one, which breaks the ratios between them. Unitless: `14`, never `14px`.

derived.name: canvas
derived.intent: The WORK surface — the artboard, the document being edited.
derived.whenToUse: Behind the thing the tool operates on. `WorkspaceCanvas` uses it.
derived.insteadOf: `background`. The thing being edited is not the page behind the UI, and collapsing the two makes the document indistinguishable from its chrome.

derived.name: canvas-foreground
derived.intent: Ink paired with `canvas`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
derived.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `canvas`. Use them as a pair — `bg-canvas text-canvas-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
derived.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

derived.name: panel
derived.intent: Docked chrome: the surface of a side panel or an inspector.
derived.whenToUse: `Panel`, `WorkspaceBar`, `StatusBar` backgrounds.
derived.insteadOf: `card`. Panels are chrome and sit in a deliberately compressed tonal band — see DESIGN.md → Registers. A card's elevation language is wrong here.

derived.name: panel-foreground
derived.intent: Ink paired with `panel`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently.
derived.whenToUse: Whenever the background is `panel`. Use them as a pair — `bg-panel text-panel-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
derived.insteadOf: `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.

derived.name: panel-raised
derived.intent: One step up from `panel`: a selected row, a hover fill, a nested well.
derived.whenToUse: Tree row selection, hovered panel rows, and the light square of a checkerboard.
derived.insteadOf: `accent`. In a workspace the tonal band is only a few units wide; `accent` is a page-register step and reads as a shout in chrome.

derived.name: panel-field
derived.intent: The inset fill of a compact control docked in a panel.
derived.whenToUse: The `size="xs"` field rung (Input, SelectTrigger, ScrubField share it) and `<Button variant="field">`. A panel control of your own that should sit among those fields.
derived.insteadOf: `canvas`. `canvas` names the work surface, and its step off the panel is too faint to read as a field in dark mode. This one is mixed from the panel itself, so it follows a theme that retunes the panel. Tune it with `--theme-panel-field`.

derived.name: panel-field-hover
derived.intent: The hover step of a `panel-field` control.
derived.whenToUse: `hover:bg-panel-field-hover` on anything filled with `panel-field`.
derived.insteadOf: `hover:bg-panel-raised`. A fixed surface token as a hover is what the surface-hover lint rejects; this one is defined against the panel field it steps from.

derived.name: hairline
derived.intent: The 1px structural line that carries all separation in tool chrome.
derived.whenToUse: Between panel sections, under a toolbar, above a status bar.
derived.insteadOf: a bigger tonal step. This is one of the two rules the workspace register deliberately reverses: on a page prefer space or tone over a line, in chrome the hairline *is* the structure.

derived.name: hairline-strong
derived.intent: A hairline that must be seen — an input edge, a swatch ring.
derived.whenToUse: Bounding a control whose fill is arbitrary (a colour swatch) or user content.
derived.insteadOf: `hairline`, when the line would otherwise disappear against what it bounds.

derived.name: border-floating
derived.intent: The edge of a floating surface. Fainter than `border`: the shadow carries the elevation.
derived.whenToUse: Every floating surface — popover, menu, select, tooltip, dialog, sheet, toast, a floating panel — as `border-border-floating` or `ring-border-floating`, together with `bg-popover` and a `shadow-md`+ shadow. Derived for every theme (a faint alpha of the foreground); a theme may tune it with `--theme-border-floating`.
derived.insteadOf: `border`. A full hairline plus a shadow stacks into a heavy outline around anything that floats. `border` is for resting edges: inputs, cards, badges.

derived.name: field
derived.intent: The fill of a text field: Input, Textarea, Select, Combobox, SearchInput, InputGroup, ChatComposer.
derived.whenToUse: Read by every field through its shell, so you rarely name it. Derived for every theme (`card`, an outlined field on the card); a theme fills its fields instead with `--theme-field: var(--muted)` and `--theme-field-border: transparent`, and every field changes at once. Name it only for a field-shaped surface of your own that must match.
derived.insteadOf: `card` or `muted` on a hand-built field. A field that paints `card` keeps its outline when the theme fills the rest, and one that paints `muted` stays filled when the theme outlines them.

derived.name: field-border
derived.intent: The outline of a text field. Derived from `input`; `transparent` in a theme with filled fields.
derived.whenToUse: With `field`, on the same field-shaped surfaces. Tune it with `--theme-field-border`.
derived.insteadOf: `input` on a text field. `input` stays the theme's outline colour for form chrome; this is the field's outline, which a filled theme turns off.

derived.name: shell-ground
derived.intent: The ground of an inset app frame: the rail and the gap around the raised main panel.
derived.whenToUse: Painted by `<AppShell frame="inset">` and the Sidebar in its slot; you rarely name it. Derived for every theme as one step off `sidebar` toward its ink, so the panel reads as lifted even where the rail is the page colour. Tune it with `--theme-shell-ground`.
derived.insteadOf: `sidebar` or `canvas` behind an inset panel. `sidebar` is the page colour in most themes, so the panel would sit on itself; `canvas` is a workspace's artboard, not app chrome.

derived.name: destructive-mark
derived.intent: `destructive` at graphic strength: the same hue lifted and saturated, for a mark that carries no text.
derived.whenToUse: A meter's or progress fill, a segmented bar, a status dot, a chart series, and the soft tint behind a badge or note (`bg-destructive-mark/15`). Held to 2:1 on the page — visibility, not a text ratio — because each of these sits beside text that says the same thing. Every bundled theme tunes its own; a preset sets `--theme-destructive-mark` or gets one derived from `destructive`.
derived.insteadOf: `bg-destructive` on a mark. The fill is pinned dark enough to carry a white label, so a meter or dot painted with it reads brown, forest or plum. And not for text — that is `text-destructive` — nor for a graphic that is the only carrier of its meaning, which owes 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11): use the fill or add the text.

palette.about: More colour for apps, generated from the active theme: neutral and eight hue families, plus a 50–950 scale under every tone. Each family keeps its hue and leans toward the brand (half the gap, at most 15°; --theme-palette-harmony scales it, 0 = own hues). Neutral is the theme's --background mixed toward its --foreground. Steps follow the mode: low steps sit near the page and high ones far from it in light and dark alike, so a pair needs no dark: variant. For decorative and categorical colour (tags, avatars, labels, legends, illustration); surfaces, text and actions take roles. Components never name a step.
palette.utilities: bg-blue-100, text-blue-800, border-neutral-200, bg-tone-1-100 — or var(--teal-500). Tailwind's other families (slate, gray, zinc, stone, amber, lime, emerald, cyan, sky, indigo, violet, fuchsia, rose) are switched off.

pairs.tag / label: bg-<family>-100 text-<family>-800 (held to 4.5:1 in every theme and mode)

palette.components: Badge, Pill and StatusDot take a family as tone (tone="blue"): a category with no meaning attached.

slots.about: data-palette="<family>" on an element fills these from that family, so one set of classes paints any family: bg-palette-wash text-palette-text.

enforcement.note: The design-system hard rules are enforced in CI, not just documented. design-lint is a zero-dependency lexical linter over the package's own src/ (excludes themes/ and *.meta.ts).
enforcement.ci: .github/workflows/ci.yml (also runs typecheck, package build, docs build)

rules.fails-on: inline oklch()/hex literals
raw palette-step refs (--zinc-950, text-(--purple-heart-700))
bg-black/text-white etc.; use overlay/overlay-foreground or a semantic token
bare transition-colors; use the motion-interactive recipe
transition-all / transition: all; it animates properties you never named. Use motion-interactive, or list the properties
Tailwind animate-{spin,pulse,bounce,ping} (bypass --motion-scale)
raw duration-<n>; use duration-(--motion-duration-*)
bare text-{size} + font-{weight}; use a paired type utility
a raw z-index utility that joins the global layer order (z-50, z-[9999]); name a step on the layering scale instead — z-(--z-sticky|nav|overlay|toast|skip-link)
rules.exceptions: z-0 through z-20 are local stacking inside one component's own box and are not flagged; the scale starts at 30 so the two ranges never overlap

rules.fails-on: typo'd tone/overlay/highlight token (validated against _contract.ts)
typo'd motion duration var / easing (validated against _contract.ts)
an element styled for pointer states (hover:/active:/focus-visible:) carrying no motion recipe
rules.note: The only PRESCRIPTIVE rule. Every other motion rule fires on motion that is present and wrong; none can fire on motion that is absent, so an interface that simply snaps between states used to clear the whole contract. Fix with motion-interactive, or motion-press when it should also move under the press.

rules.fails-on: importing the package's own barrel (@sableui/react) from inside src/; deep-import a relative module instead
a hard-coded <Icon name>/icon: literal that is missing from iconContract.names (keeps the machine-readable icon contract complete)
SABLE_UI_VERSION in src/index.ts OR registry.json version not matching package.json version
a <name>.meta.ts tokensUsed entry that is not a real SEMANTIC_TOKEN (validated against _contract.ts) — so component meta can't advertise a token that doesn't exist
an overflow-*-auto|scroll utility with no scrollbar policy; pair with `scrollbar-quiet` or `scrollbar-hidden`
a hardcoded control height (h-[40px]); read the density ladder (h-(--control-md)) so a data-density scope can retune it
var(--color-*) — Tailwind's generated alias, frozen to the DEFAULT theme. Read the semantic token (var(--primary)) or a themed subtree silently paints the wrong theme

a physical direction utility (ml-*, pr-*, text-left, left-*) where a logical property belongs, so RTL mirrors for free. A per-file ratchet: existing occurrences are grandfathered in scripts/lint-baseline.json and only an increase fails
Opacity on semantic focus ink weakens the theme's tested contrast. Use ring-ring or ring-sidebar-ring at full opacity; tune the semantic token in the theme instead.

Opacity on a surface text ink (text-foreground/60). An alpha step over an unknown surface has unknown contrast and shifts per theme. Use text-muted-foreground — it is contrast-tested on every surface. See `sable docs typography`.

`highlight` is a SURFACE, always paired with `highlight-foreground` (bg-highlight text-highlight-foreground). Presets disagree on what it looks like (a vivid accent in some, a pale wash in Atelier, Inkwell and Verdant), so as a bare text or icon ink it vanishes in half of them. For an accented mark put the icon in a bg-highlight chip; for links and hovers use text-foreground.

A hand-built control where Sable ships the component. Sable's version carries the keyboard model, focus handling, ARIA wiring and theming (it is built on Base UI); a hand-rolled one usually misses some of it — a role="radio" button row without arrow keys is the common case. Use the named component. If none genuinely fits (a 2D pad, a bespoke strip), keep it keyboard-complete and add the escape hatch with the reason.

A floating surface painted with the page ground. `shadow-md` and above mean the element floats (menus, popovers, floating panels, toolbars over a canvas, dialogs), and every floating surface is `bg-popover`. `background` is the BOTTOM of the stack — background < card < popover in every theme's dark mode — so a floating panel on `bg-background` reads as a hole beneath the cards it hovers over (Sable's own Customize inspector shipped that way). Use `bg-popover text-popover-foreground`. A device screen or other genuine page ground that happens to carry a shadow takes the escape hatch with the reason.

A floating surface with a resting surface's fill or edge. `shadow-md` and above mean the element floats (menus, popovers, selects, tooltips, dialogs, sheets, toasts, a floating panel), and a floating surface is `bg-popover text-popover-foreground` with `border-border-floating` (or `ring-border-floating`). FILL: `background` is the bottom of the stack and `card` sits on it — background < card < popover in every dark mode — so a floating panel on either reads as sunk beneath what it hovers over (Sable's Customize inspector shipped on `bg-background`; Dialog, Sheet and Toast shipped on `bg-card`). EDGE: the shadow carries the elevation; a full `border-border` hairline on top of it stacks into a heavy outline. `border-floating` is the lighter, alpha edge made for this. A device screen or other genuine page ground that carries a shadow takes the escape hatch with the reason.

A raw element dressed as a Sable component. `border-input` is the field shell (Input, Textarea, SearchInput, Select…); a `bg-primary` / `bg-secondary` / `bg-destructive` fill or a `--control-*` height on a <button> or <a> is a Button. Hand-built, they drift from the component — no density, no loading or disabled states, no focus contract — and every token on them still passes lint. Use the component: Button (a link takes `render={<a href=… />}`), Input / SearchInput, or CommandMenuTrigger for a search-shaped button that opens a palette. If none fits, that is a library gap: say so, then take the escape hatch with the reason.

A colour hand-mixed from the foreground ink — `color-mix(… var(--foreground) …)`. Sable already derives these from the surface underneath, in every theme and mode: `sable-well` (a recessed track, pad or well), `sable-surface` + `sable-surface-interactive` (hover and selected fills on any surface), `bg-hairline` / `border-hairline` (a faint ink edge or fill). `npx sable search` finds them; `registry.json → utilities` explains each. If none fits, it is a gap — report it, then take the escape hatch with the reason.

A hover, highlight or selected state painted with a fixed token (hover:bg-muted, hover:bg-accent, hover:bg-popover, data-[selected]:bg-card…). It only reads on the surface it was designed for: on a well, a muted row or a popover it can match the parent, and the state turns into a hole. Use `sable-surface-interactive`, which steps hover and selected off whatever surface the element sits on — or a Sable component whose states are built in. Exempt: an opacity step on the element's own surface (bg-popover/90 hover:bg-popover, bg-card hover:bg-card/85), which is not a surface swap.

A component renders a raw <button> instead of composing Sable's Button. A hand-built button picks its own height, padding, icon size, radius, hover and focus ring, so it drifts from every other button (CopyButton was 28px with a 14px glyph beside 32px icon buttons).

A control-height class passed to a sized component (h-(--control-*) on Input, Button, SelectTrigger or ComboboxInput). These components take their height from `size` — Button: xs | sm | md | cta | icon-*; Input, SelectTrigger, ComboboxInput: md | xs. Use the size prop; if no size fits, that is a gap in the component, not a className.

An `onClick` on a non-interactive element (div, span, li, img, td, tr, section, article, p). It reaches mouse users only: no focus, no Enter/Space, no role. Use Button (variant="ghost" for a quiet hit area; `render={<a href=… />}` for a link), or a Sable component whose rows are interactive (Entity, TreeRow, a Menu/Select item). A handler that only stops propagation, or a backdrop whose keyboard path is elsewhere, takes the escape hatch with the reason.

A hand-written `mask-image` gradient. For a scroll region, Scroller draws the edge fade — only on the side that has more, following the scroll. For streaming text, StreamingText. For clamped text that expands, ShowMore. If none of these fit, take the escape hatch with the reason.

A menu row coloured by className (text-destructive, a tone ink, or a destructive highlight). MenuItem and ContextMenuItem take `variant="destructive"`, which keeps the ink while highlighted and tints the highlight to match; a class override loses it on hover. Use the variant.

A look-changing class on a Sable component (border*, bg-*, rounded*, ring-*, shadow-* on Button, Pill or Badge). Their appearance is set by variants — Button `variant` (floating for a control over content), Pill `appearance`/`size`, Badge `appearance`/`tone` — and an override fights the variant's own hover, selected and focus states. Use a real variant, or add one to the component. Layout classes (width, margin, flex, position) are fine.

Inline-edge padding hand-set on a TableHead or TableCell (pl-*, pr-*, ps-*, pe-*). Table insets its first and last columns by `--table-edge-px`; put the table in `<CardContent flush>`, which sets it to the card's padding at every density — or set `[--table-edge-px:…]` on a wrapper. Never pad the cells by hand.

A separator bled to the popup edge with a fixed negative margin (-mx-1, -mx-[…]). Popup padding is `popup-inset`, which follows the radius and the density; use `popup-bleed`, which bleeds by exactly that amount, or the popup's own *Separator part (MenuSeparator, ContextMenuSeparator, SelectSeparator) which already does.

A fixed rem/px padding, margin, gap or inset in a component (p-[1.5rem], px-[12px], gap-[0.5rem], padding: "12px", "--card-p": "1.5rem"). Spacing goes on the scale — a step (p-3, gap-2) or `--spacing(n)` / `calc(var(--spacing) * n)` in an arbitrary value — so the density control moves it. Keep fixed units only for what must not scale (a 1px hairline, a ring width), and disable the rule at the site with that reason.

A direct import from konsta. In an iOS prototype, Sable components build every screen; Konsta supplies only system chrome, and that comes through @sableui/react/ios (NativeApp, IosPage, IosNavbar, IosBackLink, IosTabbar, IosTab, IosSheet, IosIconButton, NavigationStack). For a row, input, switch, slider, search, button, list or toast, use the Sable component — `sable target ios --component <Name>` says which.

A label on a brand fill (`--primary`, `--sidebar-primary`, `--highlight`, each with its `-foreground`) should clear 4.5:1 AND APCA Lc 60 — a pair can pass the ratio and still read muddy (dark ink on a bright red-orange, Lc 42). The finding names the nearest pair that reads: the ink the colour takes as picked, with the fill's lightness moved to meet it, hue kept. If the pair is your brand's deliberate choice, keep it on the record: `/* design-lint-disable-next-line label-contrast -- <reason> */` above the declaration.

A status colour has two tokens: the fill (`--destructive`, `--success`, `--tone-warning`, `--tone-info`), which `bg-*` paints, and its `-text` (`--destructive-text` …), which `text-*`, `border-*`, `ring-*`, `outline-*`, `fill-*` and `stroke-*` read. Setting the fill alone leaves the text on the theme's colour, so a retuned red button sits beside the theme's red error message. Set the `-text` in the same theme and mode: the fill itself where it already reads on your surfaces, or a step of it moved away from them (lighter in dark mode) so it clears 4.5:1 on a card.

A raw CSS grid laid over a collection — `grid` with an auto-fill/auto-fit `minmax()` track, or uniform `grid-cols-N` columns over mapped or repeated items. That is Sable's `Grid`: `cols` takes the same counts per breakpoint (`{ base: 2, md: 4 }`), `minItemWidth` is the auto-fit track with a `min(…, 100%)` guard so a cell never overflows a narrow container (a bare `minmax(12rem,1fr)` does), every track is `minmax(0, 1fr)` so one long string cannot blow a column out, and the gap defaults to the theme's `--grid-gutter` or takes rhythm units (`gap={2}` = `gap-4`). Not flagged: a grid with no columns, a form layout (field children, no mapping), a non-uniform track (`grid-cols-[auto_1fr]`), a `ul`/`ol`/`dl` (Grid renders a div), or an element with a widget role.

A link or button dressed as a card — a radius, a surface (`bg-card` / `bg-popover`, or a border) and card padding on an <a>, <button> or router <Link>. That is `<Card render={<Link to=… />}>` (or `<a href>` / `<button>`): rendered as a link or button, Card adds the hover (a stronger edge and shadow), a full-card focus-visible ring and motion-interactive easing; its padding follows the density control (`--card-p`) and its corner follows the theme radius; children answer the hover with `group-hover/card:`. Hand-built, a tile keeps none of that when the theme or density moves. Not flagged: a text link, a nav row (no surface), a pill (`rounded-full`), a button fill (lookalike-control's), or an element inside a `render` prop.

A round, fixed-size box holding a person's or artist's picture — `rounded-full` + `size-*` (or equal `h-*`/`w-*`) around an , GradientArt or initials, or a round fixed-size itself. That is `Avatar`: `src`/`alt` with a fallback that shows while the image loads or when it fails, `variant="art"` for initials over GradientArt seeded by the person (a stable colour each, from the theme), a `size` ladder, an accessible name (role=img), a `status` slot that clears the circle, and AvatarGroup for an overlapping stack. Not flagged: a dot or an icon in a circle (no picture or initials), a round box without a fixed size, or AvatarRoot and its parts.
A cover or media frame built by hand — an `aspect-*` ratio + `overflow-hidden` wrapped around an ,

A `required` Field with an `error` prop, inside a `Form` that validates for you. On submit Form checks every Field first, so an empty required one stops the submit with the browser's message ("Please fill out this field.") and your onSubmit, which would set `error`, never runs. Either let your code own validation, `<Form noValidate>` (onSubmit always runs and the Field shows your `error`), or let Form validate and word the message on the Field: `messages={{ valueMissing: "Enter a subject." }}`.

Leftover shadcn/ui or Radix code. Sable replaces the stack: `asChild` → `render`, `@radix-ui/*` and `@/components/ui/*` → the Sable component (`sable search "<name>"`), `lucide-react` → <Icon name> under IconProvider, `sonner` → ToastProvider + toast, `vaul` → Sheet, `cmdk` → CommandMenu, `input-otp` → OtpField, `next-themes` → SableThemeProvider. `sable docs migrating-from-shadcn` has the full map.

escapeHatch.note: A disable directive with no reason is itself a lint error — every exception is auditable.

iconContract.note: Components reference semantic names through <Icon>, rendered by the app's IconProvider set. Reicon is opt-in from @sableui/react/icons/reicon; there is no fallback, so an app that supplies its own set ships no Reicon code.

doctrine: A page's width is a Region — a centered, opt-in, purpose-named cap (prose/form/feed/content/wide/full). Pick by ROLE, not size. Never a global page max-width.
The 12-column grid (Grid/Columns) is used WITHIN a region, for genuinely multi-column content. Never use a column span as the page's reading width.
App chrome is not on the grid: Sidebar and rails are fixed-width chrome outside the content grid.
Measure ≠ width: cap text line-length (prose, in ch) independently of a region's layout width.
One direction is flex (Stack, Row); content that must line up across rows AND columns is Grid/Columns; width is a Region. A card's single column stacks with Stack, not a one-track grid.

Vertical space is set in lines: the baseline is one line of body text, split into steps (thirds by default, 8px at 15/24). Line heights round to the step, Stack/Row/Grid gap numbers are steps, and even Tailwind spacing steps (p-4 = two steps) stay on it. A rhythm to keep, not a grid to force: components are as tall as their content.

primitives.name: Region
primitives.summary: The page region: fluid, edge-to-edge with the fluid page inset (--page-inset). Opt-in centered max cap picked by ROLE (prose/form/feed/content/wide/full), never a global page max-width. The root of nearly every route. The inset and cap are classes (px-(--page-inset), max-w-…), so className overrides them at a breakpoint (max-sm:px-0); only safeArea padding is inline.

usage.description: Use Region as the page-width primitive that applies fluid page inset and an optional purpose-named max width.

bestPractices.description: Choose the max value by what the person does on the page: read (prose), fill in a form (form), scroll one stream (feed), review one record or settings (content), scan and compare rows or cards (wide).
Omit max (fluid) for work across panes, a board, an editor or a map, where a flexible part uses the extra width; cap text inside it with --measure-prose.
Give sibling routes in one nav the same width so the header does not jump between them.
Review a capped or fluid route at 1920px and 2560px: a cap is a ceiling, so below the cap plus app chrome every choice looks the same.
Use Region near the route or section boundary so inner layout stays intentional.
Do not use Region as a global wrapper that forces every page into the same max width.
Do not go fluid when the extra width only widens the gaps between fixed columns; cap it.
Do not read full as edge to edge: it is the largest cap and keeps the page inset. Use bleed for edge to edge.

props.name: as
props.description: Semantic element to render (e.g. "main", "section", "nav").

props.name: inset
props.description: Apply the fluid horizontal page inset (--page-inset).

props.name: max
props.description: Opt-in centered max-width cap, purpose-named: prose 65ch (long-form reading) · form 480px (auth, narrow single-column forms) · feed 640px (single-column timeline) · content 896px (settings/admin panes) · wide 1280px (dashboards, tables, card grids) · full 1536px (the largest cap; keeps the inset, so not edge to edge — that is bleed). Omit for fluid: work views whose panes, board or canvas use the extra width. A cap is a ceiling: it applies only once the viewport minus app chrome exceeds it, so judge it at 1920px and up.

props.name: bleed
props.description: Full-bleed: edge to edge with no inset. Overrides inset.

props.name: safeArea
props.description: env(safe-area-inset-*) padding for fixed or native-shell surfaces. true pads top+bottom; pass an edge array to target edges.

primitives.name: Page
primitives.summary: A route shell: Region (inset + opt-in max cap) whose children flow as a vertically-rhythmic Stack. Use as the top-level wrapper of a route's content — distinct from AppShell (the frame around routes) and PageHeader (the heading block inside).

usage.description: Use Page as a route content shell that combines Region sizing with vertical rhythm.

bestPractices.description: Use it as the top-level wrapper for route content after application chrome.
Set max by the page's content role rather than by the current viewport.
Do not confuse Page with AppShell; Page is content, AppShell is the frame around routes.

props.name: gap
props.description: Vertical gap between stacked page sections. Number = rhythm units (×8px, so 4 = 32px); string = raw CSS.

primitives.name: Grid
primitives.summary: CSS Grid within a region. Two modes: fixed/responsive cols count, or minItemWidth so cells breathe with NO breakpoints (the default choice for card grids). A minItemWidth grid keeps its empty columns (track="fill"), so one result stays one cell wide; track="fit" stretches a fixed set across the row. display is the grid class and the gap a CSS variable, so className utilities win at any breakpoint (hidden md:grid, md:gap-6, lg:grid-cols-3).

usage.description: Use Grid for uniform grid layouts inside a Region, especially card grids that can breathe responsively.

bestPractices.description: Prefer minItemWidth for responsive card grids that do not need breakpoint-specific spans.
Keep the default track="fill" for collections whose count is data (search results, shelves, galleries): sparse rows keep their empty columns, so one result stays one cell wide.
Use track="fit" only for a fixed set designed to span the row, such as three KPI cards.
Use explicit columns only when the design truly needs a fixed track count.
Do not use Grid to set a page's reading width; use Region or Center.

Do not use track="fit" for results or other data-driven collections: with one or two items the empty columns collapse and each item stretches across the row (a single result rendered as a full-width cover).

props.name: cols
props.type: number | { base?, sm?, md?, lg?, xl?, "2xl"? }
props.description: Fixed column count or a mobile-first breakpoint map ({ base: 2, md: 4 }). Ignored when minItemWidth is set.

props.name: minItemWidth
props.description: Breathing mode: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(minItemWidth, 1fr)) — as many columns of at least minItemWidth as fit, wrapping without breakpoints. e.g. "16rem".

props.name: track
props.description: What a minItemWidth grid does with columns it has no items for (only visible when fewer items than fit one row). "fill" (auto-fill) keeps them, so items keep their size whatever their count — one search result is one cover wide, not a banner. Use it for collections whose count is data: results, shelves, galleries. "fit" (auto-fit) collapses them and stretches the items to share the row — only for a fixed set designed to span it (three KPI cards, plan tiers).

props.name: gap
props.description: Gap between cells. Number = rhythm units (×8px); [row, column] = two rhythm counts, for a gallery whose rows want more air than its columns; string = raw CSS.

primitives.name: Columns
primitives.summary: An explicit N-column track (default 12) for proportioned layouts — pair with Col spans (list-detail, asymmetric editorial layouts). For uniform card grids prefer Grid minItemWidth. display is the grid class, so hidden md:grid works; a gap-* utility replaces both gaps and the column-gap cap.

usage.description: Use Columns and Col for proportioned layouts that need explicit spans, such as list-detail or asymmetric panes.

bestPractices.description: Use breakpoint span maps when the same layout needs to collapse cleanly on smaller screens.
Use Columns for proportional composition, not for uniform card wrapping.
Do not use column spans as a replacement for Region width or text measure.

anatomy.name: Columns
anatomy.description: The explicit column track container.

anatomy.name: Col
anatomy.description: A child cell with span and optional start placement.

props.name: count
props.description: Columns in the track; a breakpoint map ({ base: 2, md: 6, lg: 12 }) thins the track on small screens.

props.name: gap
props.description: Gap between columns and rows. Number = rhythm units (×8px); string = raw CSS. The column gap is capped so all gaps together never take more than 75% of the track's width — a large gap can't push a narrow screen into horizontal scroll, and at normal desktop widths it renders exactly as given. The row gap is never capped.

subcomponents.name: Col
subcomponents.type: span?: number | breakpoint map · start?: number | breakpoint map
subcomponents.description: A cell in the track: columns to span (default 1) and optional 1-based start column. Both accept breakpoint maps ({ base: 12, lg: 8 }).

primitives.name: Stack
primitives.summary: Vertical flow on the 8px rhythm — the default container for stacked content. Gap by role: tight within a group (1.5–2), looser between groups (3–4), generous between sections (6+). Layout lives in classes (flex flex-col items-* justify-*) and the gap in a CSS variable, never inline style, so className utilities override any prop at a breakpoint (max-lg:hidden, md:flex-row, md:gap-8).

usage.description: Use Stack for vertical flow where child spacing should follow the Sable rhythm scale.

bestPractices.description: Use smaller gaps within a group and larger gaps between sections.
Use Stack instead of ad hoc margins when siblings form a vertical composition.
Do not use Stack to create page width or grid structure; pair it with Region, Grid, or Columns.

props.name: gap
props.description: Vertical gap. Number = rhythm units (×8px, fractions ok — 2 = 16px); string = raw CSS.

props.name: align
props.description: Cross-axis alignment.

primitives.name: Row
primitives.summary: Horizontal flex flow — inline rows of controls, toolbars, action clusters. Defaults to center-aligned, no wrap. Layout lives in classes (flex flex-row items-* justify-*) and the gap in a CSS variable, never inline style, so className utilities override any prop at a breakpoint (hidden md:flex, max-md:flex-col, md:gap-6).

usage.description: Use Row for horizontal clusters such as action groups, toolbars, metadata, and inline controls.

bestPractices.description: Use wrap when controls may not fit on smaller screens.
Use justify and align intentionally so clusters scan as one unit.
Do not use Row for navigation menus or dense tabular structure.

components.name: Accordion
components.summary: Stacked, collapsible disclosure sections over Base UI Accordion — roving focus, arrow-key navigation, ARIA region/heading/button wiring, and an animated height transition. Each item pairs a full-width trigger (with a rotating chevron) and a panel.

usage.description: Use Accordion to reveal a vertical set of related sections while keeping the surrounding page scannable.

bestPractices.description: Use concise trigger text that describes the content revealed below it.
Keep section content focused so expanding one item does not feel like navigating to a new page.
Do not hide required fields, primary actions, or critical errors inside collapsed sections.
Do not nest an Accordion inside an Accordion. Two layers of roving focus fight each other, and the arrow keys become ambiguous — flatten the hierarchy or use a Tree.

anatomy.name: AccordionItem
anatomy.description: One expandable section in the group.

anatomy.name: AccordionTrigger
anatomy.description: The button-like control that opens the section.

anatomy.name: AccordionPanel
anatomy.description: The content revealed by the trigger.

props.name: Accordion (Root)
props.type: Base UI Accordion.Root props (value, defaultValue, multiple, disabled, onValueChange, orientation, loopFocus, keepMounted, hiddenUntilFound)
props.description: Groups all items and owns the open value(s). Uncontrolled via defaultValue, controlled via value.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Uncontrolled set of item values that start expanded (e.g. ['faq-1']).

props.name: value
props.description: Controlled set of expanded item values; pair with onValueChange.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called with the new set of expanded item values when an item opens or closes.

props.name: multiple
props.description: Whether more than one item can be open at the same time. When false, opening one closes the others.

subcomponents.name: AccordionItem
subcomponents.type: Base UI Accordion.Item props + className (value, disabled, onOpenChange)
subcomponents.description: Pairs a header with its panel. Give each a stable `value` to control or set initial open state.

subcomponents.name: AccordionTrigger
subcomponents.type: Base UI Accordion.Trigger props + className + indicator?: ReactNode
subcomponents.description: The header button (Header + Trigger composed). Renders children plus a chevron that rotates via data-[panel-open] by default; pass `indicator` to replace the icon and its open-state behavior entirely (e.g. a plus that becomes an × for a FAQ-style toggle).

subcomponents.name: AccordionPanel
subcomponents.type: Base UI Accordion.Panel props + className (keepMounted, hiddenUntilFound)
subcomponents.description: The collapsible body. Animates height using the --accordion-panel-height CSS var; fades on data-[starting-style]/data-[ending-style].

motion.why: An accordion is page furniture that is present from first paint. Animating it in would stage content the reader is already scanning past.
The whole header row is the hit target, and it looks like a heading rather than a control. The hover shift is what tells the reader it can be clicked before they click it.

Panel height is the only cue that content came from THIS header rather than appearing at the bottom of the page. Snapping it open moves everything below by a screenful with nothing connecting cause to effect.

The chevron turning is the header's half of the same event as the panel opening. motion-interactive lists `rotate` (what Tailwind's rotate-* writes), so it turns with the panel instead of flipping 180° in one frame beside an easing panel. A custom `indicator` that rotates should carry motion-interactive itself.
Nothing here is indeterminate — the panel content is already resident. A panel that loads on expand should put its own loader inside the panel.

a11y: Base UI renders the trigger inside an <h3> heading and wires aria-expanded / aria-controls to the panel region.
Arrow keys move roving focus between triggers; Home/End jump to the first/last; loopFocus wraps by default.
Each trigger toggles its panel with Enter/Space; the panel is announced as a labelled region.
A disabled AccordionItem dims and is skipped by keyboard focus while neighbouring items stay interactive.
The chevron rotation is driven by data-[panel-open] and the focus ring by focus-visible; both ride motion-interactive, so reduced motion stills them with everything else.
