components.name: ActivityHeatmap
components.summary: A calendar heatmap: one value per day as a grid of weeks by weekdays — the GitHub contribution graph, for any daily measure. Levels by quartile, categories by source, a real ARIA grid with one tab stop, and a sideways scroll on narrow screens that opens on the latest week.

usage.description: Use ActivityHeatmap to show how often something happened day by day over weeks or months: commits, habits kept, orders, uptime. Pass days as ISO dates with a value; levels, colours, labels, keyboard and tooltips work with no further props. Put it inside a Card and compose any totals beside it (NumberTicker, StatRowBlock). For a value over time that a reader needs to compare precisely, use AreaChart or BarChart; for a month calendar with marked days (a streak calendar), use Calendar.

bestPractices.description: Pass dates as "YYYY-MM-DD" strings. The grid reads them as calendar days, so no time zone can shift a day — never build them with `new Date(...).toISOString()` from a local date.
Give it a `unit` ("contribution" / "contributions") so the tooltip and every cell's name say what the number counts.
Let the default quantile scale pick levels — one exceptional day then does not wash every other day out. Pass a day's own `level` when the source already has one (GitHub's API).
Use it for a handful of values or for values a reader must compare exactly; a heatmap shows rhythm, not amounts. Use BarChart.
Use it for a single month of marked days with a streak; that is Calendar with modifiers.
Fetch inside the component or call GitHub from the browser with a token. Fetch on your server and pass days in; `@sableui/react/adapters/github` converts GitHub's response.

anatomy.name: Weekday labels
anatomy.description: Short weekday names beside the rows, outside the scroller so the weeks never slide under them.

anatomy.name: Month labels
anatomy.description: Short month names over each month's first week; they scroll with their weeks.

anatomy.name: Cell grid
anatomy.description: A role=grid table, one gridcell per day, inside a horizontal Scroller that opens on the latest week.

anatomy.name: Tooltip
anatomy.description: The chart tooltip card, anchored to the hovered, focused or tapped day.

anatomy.name: Legend
anatomy.description: A Less–More ramp for intensity, or swatches for categories.

props.name: label
props.description: What the grid shows ("Contributions in 2026") — its caption and accessible name.

props.name: data
props.description: The days: `{ date: "YYYY-MM-DD", value, level?, category? }[]`, or a map of date to value. Sparse is fine — a missing day is 0; duplicates sum.

props.name: start
props.description: First day drawn, "YYYY-MM-DD". The default starts at the beginning of that week, as GitHub's does.

props.name: end
props.description: Last day drawn. Days after today inside the range are drawn hollow and skipped by the keyboard.

props.name: year
props.description: Draw Jan 1 – Dec 31 of this year. Wins over start / end.

props.name: weekStart
props.description: 0 puts Sunday on the top row, 1 Monday.

props.name: levels
props.description: How many levels, including the empty level 0.

props.name: levelScale
props.description: How a value becomes a level. Quantile splits the positive values evenly, as GitHub does; an array gives each level's lower bound from 1 up; a function decides. A day's own `level` always wins.

props.name: tone
props.description: The hue of the intensity ramp. Decorative tones lead, as on every chart; "success" gives the GitHub look.

props.name: categories
props.description: Colour days by `day.category` (label, tone or colour per key). Pair with `levels={2}` for flat category colours.

props.name: unit
props.description: Names the value in the tooltip and each cell's accessible name, pluralised with Intl.PluralRules.

props.name: formatValue
props.description: Formats a value wherever it is shown or read.

props.name: tooltip
props.description: Show the tooltip on hover, focus and tap; a function replaces its content on the same card.

props.name: legend
props.description: The Less–More ramp for intensity, swatches for categories.

props.name: legendLabels
props.description: The ramp's end words.

props.name: monthLabels
props.description: Short month names over each month's first week.

props.name: weekdayLabels
props.description: Which weekday names to show beside the rows; alternate is Mon, Wed, Fri.

props.name: size
props.description: The smallest a cell may get (10, 12, 14 px) before the grid scrolls instead of shrinking.

props.name: stretch
props.description: Grow cells to fill the width, up to 20 px. false keeps them at `size`.

props.name: activeDate
props.description: The hovered or focused day, controlled. Pair with defaultActiveDate / onActiveDateChange.

props.name: selectedDate
props.description: The selected day, controlled. Selection is on only when onSelectDate is set.

props.name: onSelectDate
props.description: Called when a day is clicked or chosen with Enter / Space — to filter a feed below, as GitHub does.

props.name: renderCell
props.description: Draw something over a cell's fill — an icon for a milestone, a reward, an outage.

props.name: loading
props.description: Draw the empty grid, shimmering, while data loads.

props.name: motion
props.description: Turns the arrival down; `subtle` shows the finished grid at once.

props.name: locale
props.description: Month and weekday names, numbers and plurals.

motion.why: Weeks fade in left to right as the grid first scrolls into view, staggered on the chart motion helpers; expressive, so subtle shows the finished grid.
The active day takes a ring outline at once and the tooltip glides to it; the other cells stay still — dimming hundreds of cells reads as a flash.
When data or the range changes, each cell's fill cross-fades on the base duration token, so the reader sees which days changed.
`loading` shimmers the empty grid until days arrive.

a11y: The grid is a role=grid table, as GitHub's is: weekday row headers and month column headers carry full names for screen readers, and the caption is `label`.

One tab stop. Arrows move a day or a week; Home / End go to the ends of the row, Page Up / Page Down to the ends of the column, Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End to the first and last day. Enter or Space selects when onSelectDate is set; Escape hides the tooltip.
Each cell is named with its date and value ("Tuesday, October 14, 2026: 12 contributions") and described by its level's words, which the legend repeats visually.
Levels rise in lightness, so they read without colour; under forced colours each level draws as a larger inner square.

examples.label: Contributions, last year
examples.code:
const days = [
	{ date: "2026-10-12", value: 4 },
	{ date: "2026-10-13", value: 11 },
	{ date: "2026-10-14", value: 2 },
]

<ActivityHeatmap label="Contributions in the last year" data={days} tone="success" unit={{ one: "contribution", other: "contributions" }} />

examples.label: Two sources, in a card
examples.code:
const github = [{ date: "2026-10-13", value: 6 }]
const codex = [{ date: "2026-10-13", value: 1 }, { date: "2026-10-14", value: 3 }]

<Card>
	<CardHeader>
		<CardTitle>Building, day by day</CardTitle>
	</CardHeader>
	<CardContent>
		<ActivityHeatmap
			label="GitHub and Codex activity in 2026"
			year={2026}
			levels={2}
			data={mergeActivity({ github, codex })}
			categories={{ github: { label: "GitHub", tone: "success" }, codex: { label: "Codex", tone: "info" }, both: { label: "Both", tone: "2" } }}
		/>
	</CardContent>
</Card>

components.name: AppHeader
components.summary: Mobile top bar (sticky, hidden at lg) with leading / title / actions slots on a 3-column grid that keeps the title optically centered. Grows into the top safe-area.

usage.description: Use AppHeader for compact application chrome at the top of a screen, usually with navigation, identity, and a small action set. Pass it to AppShell's `header` slot so screen content clears it on mobile (it is sticky and hides itself at lg).

bestPractices.description: Keep the header actions narrow and predictable so the page title remains legible.
Use it once per app view as chrome, not as repeated content inside page sections.
Do not overload it with filters, forms, or page-specific controls that belong in the content area.
Do not render more than one per app, or put a second one inside a route. It is sticky chrome, so two of them stack and permanently eat the top of the viewport.

props.name: leading
props.description: Leading slot — back button, create action, or menu trigger.

props.name: title
props.description: Center slot — brand wordmark or contextual page title.

props.name: actions
props.description: Trailing slot — account menu, action buttons.

a11y: Renders a <header> landmark.
Pair with a leading control that has an accessible label (e.g. a BackButton).

components.name: AppShell
components.summary: The application frame: slots for status banners, a mobile header, a desktop sidebar, main content, a mobile bottom nav, a persistent dock (a now-playing or call bar), and floating overlays — plus a built-in skip link and #main-content target.

usage.description: Use AppShell as the outer product frame for authenticated or app-like experiences. It coordinates responsive chrome slots and guarantees a skip link plus main landmark; put route content inside the children and let AppHeader, Sidebar, BottomNav, and Banner own their own semantics.

bestPractices.description: Use AppShell once around the route tree or major app area so the skip link and main landmark stay stable.
Pass app-wide outage or status messages through banners so they remain above the frame.
Use Region inside the main content to choose each route's reading width.

Wrap EVERY return of a route in its own Page or Region — including early returns for loading, empty and error states. AppShell's <main> deliberately carries no padding (it is a frame, and padding belongs to the region that chose the width), so a route that returns a bare spinner or error renders flush against the chrome. This is the most common conversion bug: the happy path gets a Page, the three early returns do not.

Use frame="inset" for dense, multi-pane product apps — a CRM, an issue tracker, an AI workspace — where framing the content as one raised panel on the rail's ground helps it read as the workspace and the rail as chrome. Keep the Sidebar on surface="rail" so its tint is the ground. Inset moves the page scroll from the window to <main id="main-content"> on desktop: point scroll listeners, scroll restoration and scroll-to-top at that element, not window.
Nest AppShell inside route cards or panels. It is page chrome, not local content.

Wrap a route in its own h-full overflow-y-auto box inside an inset shell. main is already the page's scroll container; a second one traps the scrollbar inside a smaller box and breaks sticky headers and the skip link's scroll target. Scroll a genuinely separate pane (a list beside a detail view) with Scroller.

Combine frame="inset" with a full-width header bar above the rail. The inset ground is the rail running the full height of the window; a bar across the top cuts it off. Use the flush frame with Sidebar surface="page" for that layout.
Put desktop-only navigation in the mobile header slot or mobile-only controls in the sidebar slot.

anatomy.name: Banners
anatomy.description: Full-width app status messages rendered above the shell.

anatomy.name: Header
anatomy.description: Mobile top chrome, usually AppHeader.

anatomy.name: Sidebar
anatomy.description: Desktop navigation chrome, usually Sidebar.

anatomy.name: Main
anatomy.description: The route content landmark with id main-content. With frame="inset", from lg it is a rounded, bordered panel that scrolls inside itself.

anatomy.name: Bottom nav
anatomy.description: Mobile fixed navigation with reserved bottom space.

anatomy.name: Dock
anatomy.description: Persistent bottom chrome that outlives routes — a now-playing bar, a call bar. Sticky above the bottom nav; the desktop Sidebar shortens to clear it.

props.name: banners
props.description: Full-width status banners pinned in flow above the frame (offline / chain-down).

props.name: header
props.description: Mobile top header (e.g. AppHeader); expected to hide itself at lg.

props.name: sidebar
props.description: Desktop side navigation (e.g. Sidebar); expected to hide itself below lg. Leading column of the body row.

props.name: bottomNav
props.description: Mobile bottom navigation (e.g. BottomNav); fixed to the bottom edge. main reserves space for it.

props.name: dock
props.description: Persistent chrome kept on screen across routes (a now-playing bar, an active-call bar, an upload tray). Full width, sticky to the bottom edge and above bottomNav on mobile; its height is published as --dock-height and the app Sidebar subtracts it. In flow, so main needs no reserved space. The contents paint their own surface and top border, and name themselves (e.g. <section aria-label="Player">). Mount AppShell in a layout that survives navigation, or the playback restarts.

props.name: overlays
props.description: Floating overlays — a message launcher, FAB, or modal mount points.

props.name: frame
props.description: How the desktop frame (lg and up) holds the content; below lg both are the same mobile layout with page scroll. "flush": main sits on the page beside the rail and the document scrolls. "inset": the shell fills the viewport and paints the shell-ground token (one step off the rail's surface, tunable with --theme-shell-ground) behind the rail and around the panel; main becomes a rounded-lg panel with a hairline border and shadow-sm, inset by a spacing step from the window edges, that scrolls inside itself (scrollbar-quiet) while the rail stays put. The Sidebar in the sidebar slot drops its right border and fills the row. main stays the #main-content target (tabIndex -1, so the skip link lands focus in the scroller) and the inline-size query container; sticky children stick to the panel's top; banners and the dock stay in flow, so the panel's bottom gap sits above a dock. With Sidebar surface="page" the ground is the page colour and the panel's border alone lifts it.

subcomponents.name: SkipLink
subcomponents.description: AppShell's skip link on its own, for a layout that is not an AppShell (a storefront with a top header). Put it first in the body and give the page's <main> the matching id: `<SkipLink />` then `<main id="main-content" tabIndex={-1}>`. `href` defaults to #main-content, the label to "Skip to content".

a11y: Renders a skip link to #main-content as the first focusable element.
Wraps content in a <main id="main-content"> landmark.
Slot components own their own ARIA (nav landmarks, labels).
The dock follows <main> in DOM order, so keyboard and screen-reader users reach the player after the page content, not before it.
With frame="inset", <main> is the desktop scroll container and takes tabIndex -1: the skip link moves focus into it, so PageDown and the arrow keys scroll the content, without adding a tab stop.

components.name: AreaChart
components.summary: A trend over a sequence, filled to the baseline: overlapping translucent series, stacked, or stacked to 100%, with smooth, linear or step curves and optional gradient fills. The line draws on and the fill rises as it scrolls into view.

usage.description: Use AreaChart for volume over time — visitors, revenue, usage — where the filled shape helps the eye read the size of the total. Stack the series to show a total and its parts; `stacked="expand"` shows each category as 100%. For comparing how measures move relative to each other, LineChart is cleaner; for amounts per category, BarChart.

bestPractices.description: Keep to one to three series; past that the tints muddy — stack them or switch to LineChart.
Set a height on className (h-72, aspect-video h-auto); the chart fills the box it is given.
Overlap more than two unstacked series — the translucent tints blend into a colour no series has.

Use it for data-heavy views — streaming or real-time data, thousands of points, zoom and brushing, trading charts. Those belong on a charting library (Recharts, visx, ECharts); Sable's charts are for dashboards, landing pages and decks.

props.name: data
props.description: The rows, in order along the category axis.

props.name: index
props.description: The datum field naming each row's category (a month, a day, a channel).

props.name: series
props.type: { key: string; label: string; tone?: ChartTone; color?: string; icon?: string }[]
props.description: The measures to plot: the datum field, its name in the legend/tooltip/table, and its colour (a tone by role, or any CSS colour). Omitted, series take the chart palette in order: --chart-1 … --chart-8, validated for colour-blind separation in light and dark; a theme may override the set.

props.name: label
props.description: What the chart shows. Its accessible name and the caption of the data table assistive tech reads.

props.name: className
props.description: Sizes the chart (plot + legend). Set a height: `h-72`, `aspect-video h-auto`.

props.name: valueFormatter
props.description: Format values everywhere (axis, labels, tooltip, table) — units like "$12,480". Default: compact on the axis, full elsewhere.

props.name: indexFormatter
props.description: Shorten category labels on the axis ("January" → "Jan"); the tooltip keeps the full value.

props.name: locale
props.description: BCP 47 locale for default number and date formatting.

props.name: tooltip
props.type: boolean | { indicator?: "dot" | "line" | "dashed" | "none"; hideLabel?: boolean; labelFormatter?: (label, datum) => ReactNode; showTotal?: boolean }
props.description: Show a tooltip on hover and keyboard focus, or configure it: the row marker, hiding the heading, rewriting it, adding a Total row.

props.name: legend
props.default: true when there is more than one series
props.description: Show the legend under the chart.

props.name: grid
props.description: Hairline gridlines along the value axis.

props.name: xAxis
props.default: true for columns; false for horizontal bars
props.description: The horizontal axis.

props.name: yAxis
props.default: false for columns; true for horizontal bars
props.description: The vertical axis.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. The arrival (draw-on, rising fill) and the data-change morph are the flourish; the gliding cursor and tooltip are the feedback `subtle` keeps.

props.name: animate
props.description: Play the arrival once the chart scrolls into view. Reduced motion shows the finished chart. `animate={false}` is `motion="subtle"`.
props.deprecated: motion="subtle" (what animate={false} now maps to: no arrival, hover kept) or motion="off"

props.name: activeIndex
props.description: The highlighted row (controlled); `null` for none.

props.name: defaultActiveIndex
props.description: The row highlighted at first — a tooltip already open before anyone hovers.

props.name: onActiveIndexChange
props.description: Called as the pointer or keyboard moves between rows.

props.name: curve
props.description: How the line runs between points. `smooth` is monotone: it never overshoots a value the data does not contain.

props.name: stacked
props.description: Stack the series, or `"expand"` to show each category as 100%.

props.name: gradient
props.description: Fill each area with a fade from its colour to transparent instead of a flat tint.

motion.why: Once on screen, each line draws on (stroke-dashoffset) and its fill rises from the baseline, series staggered — the trend is read as it is drawn. On the motion tokens; reduced motion shows the finished chart. The arrival is expressive: it plays at the full motion level only, so `motion="subtle"` (or a subtle app policy) shows the finished chart while hover feedback stays.
Hover and focus move the cursor and tooltip instantly — a lagging cursor reads as a slow chart.

Geometry eases from the old shape to the new one through a CSS `d` transition on the motion tokens (no recipe animates path geometry); browsers without `d` transitions update in place. Expressive, like the arrival: under `subtle` new data swaps in place.
A chart has no indeterminate state; show a Skeleton while the data loads.

a11y: The drawing is aria-hidden; the same numbers are in a visually hidden data table (captioned by `label`) that the chart is aria-describedby, so assistive tech reads values, not shapes.

With a tooltip, the chart is one tab stop (role=group, aria-roledescription="chart"): arrow keys, Home and End step through the data, Escape clears, and each step is announced in a polite live region.
Colour is never the only key: series are named in the legend, tooltip and table.

const visitors = [
	{ month: "January", desktop: 186, mobile: 80 },
	{ month: "February", desktop: 305, mobile: 200 },
	{ month: "March", desktop: 237, mobile: 120 },
	{ month: "April", desktop: 73, mobile: 190 },
	{ month: "May", desktop: 209, mobile: 130 },
	{ month: "June", desktop: 214, mobile: 140 },
]

<AreaChart
	label="Visitors, January to June"
	data={visitors}
	index="month"
	series={[
		{ key: "desktop", label: "Desktop" },
		{ key: "mobile", label: "Mobile" },
	]}
	indexFormatter={(m) => m.slice(0, 3)}
	gradient
/>

	data={visitors}
	index="month"
	series={[
		{ key: "desktop", label: "Desktop" },
		{ key: "mobile", label: "Mobile" },
	]}
	stacked="expand"
	yAxis
	tooltip={{ indicator: "line", showTotal: true }}
/>

components.name: Attachment
components.summary: A file or image attached to a message: media or icon lead, name and metadata, upload and error states, an actions slot, and a full-card trigger that keeps those actions separately clickable.

usage.description: The card a file takes in a conversation — in the composer while it uploads, and in the transcript once it has. It renders all four states an attachment actually moves through (queued, uploading, failed, delivered) rather than only the delivered one, because the other three are the states that are hard to get right and would otherwise fall back on every caller.

bestPractices.description: Use `variant="media"` for images and `variant="card"` for documents. A filename tells you nothing about a photo, and a thumbnail tells you nothing about a contract.

Pass `onOpen` rather than wrapping the card in your own button. It renders a stretched trigger underneath the actions, so the card is one tab stop, each action is its own, and clicking "remove" never opens the file.
Give `status="uploading"` a numeric `progress` when you have one and omit it when you do not — the bar goes indeterminate rather than lying about 0%.
Put the reason in `meta` when `status="error"`. The card re-colors but keeps its shape, so a failed upload stays recognisable as the file it was — the text is what says why.
Do not nest interactive controls inside a card you have wrapped in a link or button yourself. That is invalid HTML and unreachable in the order it looks like; `onOpen` exists to avoid it.
Do not use it as a generic file-list row. `Tree` is the file listing; this one is shaped for a conversation, where an attachment is a message payload.
Do not rely on the error colour alone to signal failure. Colour is not a status for anyone who cannot see it — say what happened in `meta`.

anatomy.name: Media
anatomy.description: Thumbnail crop or file glyph. Fills the tile in `media`, a lead square in `card`.

anatomy.name: Label
anatomy.description: Name and metadata. A row beside the media in `card`; a scrim strip over the picture in `media`, shown only when there is something to say.

anatomy.name: Actions
anatomy.description: Remove / retry / download controls, stacked above the stretched trigger so they stay separately clickable.

anatomy.name: Progress
anatomy.description: A hairline bar along the bottom edge while `status="uploading"`; determinate with `progress`, indeterminate without.

props.name: name
props.description: File name. Truncated rather than wrapped — the stem truncates and a short extension stays visible — and used as the default label for the stretched trigger and the media tile's alt text.

props.name: meta
props.description: Size, type, upload progress, or the failure reason — the quiet second line.

props.name: thumbnail
props.description: Image preview URL. Present means the card shows a crop of the file instead of a glyph.

props.name: icon
props.description: Semantic icon name for a non-image file (resolved through IconProvider). Defaults to "image-stack" when a thumbnail is set.

props.name: variant
props.description: `card` is a name-led horizontal row for documents; `media` is a square tile that is mostly picture.

props.name: status
props.description: Transfer state. `uploading` adds a progress bar; `error` re-colors the card without changing its shape.

props.name: progress
props.description: Percentage 0–100 while uploading. Omit for an indeterminate bar.

props.name: actions
props.description: Remove / retry / download controls. Stay clickable when `onOpen` makes the card a trigger. On a `media` tile they float on the top-end corner over the picture, so pass `variant="floating"` buttons there.

props.name: onOpen
props.description: Makes the whole card activate, via a stretched button rendered beneath the actions rather than by wrapping the card.

props.name: openLabel
props.description: Accessible label for that stretched trigger.

props.name: ...div props
props.description: Spread onto the card. Use `onOpen` rather than `onClick` — a click handler on a div is not a control.

motion.why: An attachment lands as part of a composer or a message, and that surface owns the entrance. A card that animated in on its own would read as a second, separate event — as if another file had been added.

With `onOpen`, the edge steps up under the pointer; it is the only cue that the card itself opens the file, not just its actions. Eased, it reads as the card answering the cursor rather than a border flickering as the pointer crosses a busy composer.

Uploading to failed re-colours the edge and fill without changing the shape. The ease keeps it legible as the same file turning red; snapped, a failed card looks like a different card replaced the one that was sent.

While uploading with no known `progress`, the bar is indeterminate and pulses (Progress's own recipe); with a number, the fill eases toward each new value. A still bar at a fixed width is indistinguishable from an upload that has stalled.

a11y: The full-card trigger is a real stretched `<button>` with an accessible label, not a click handler on a div — so it is one tab stop, keyboard-activatable, and focus-ringed.

Actions sit above that trigger in the stacking order, which keeps them individually focusable and stops a click on `remove` from also opening the file. Text is only made click-through when a trigger is present, so a filename stays selectable otherwise.

A thumbnail is described as the attachment in `media` (where the picture is the only label) and left decorative in `card` (where the filename is right beside it), so AT never reads the same name twice.
The upload bar carries an accessible name via Progress; the error state is carried by text in `meta` as well as colour.
Label text on a media tile sits on `overlay` / `overlay-foreground` — a fixed pairing that stays legible over arbitrary imagery, where a theme surface token would not.

examples.label: Document with a remove action
examples.code: <Attachment name="proposal.pdf" meta="2.4 MB · PDF" onOpen={() => open(file)} actions={<Button variant="ghost" size="icon-xs" aria-label="Remove"><Icon name="xmark" /></Button>} />

examples.label: Image tile, uploading
examples.code: <Attachment variant="media" name="cover.png" thumbnail={previewUrl} status="uploading" progress={62} meta="Uploading… 62%" />

examples.label: Failed upload with a retry
examples.code: <Attachment name="recording.mov" meta="Upload failed — file is over the 50 MB limit" status="error" icon="warning" actions={<Button variant="ghost" size="xs" onClick={retry}>Retry</Button>} />

components.name: Avatar
components.summary: Circular (or square) profile image over Base UI Avatar — automatic image-load tracking with an initials/glyph fallback. Ergonomic Avatar plus low-level AvatarRoot/AvatarImage/AvatarFallback parts, and AvatarGroup for an overlapping stack with a "+N" overflow count.

usage.description: Use Avatar to represent a person, team, or account with a compact visual identity. Wrap several in AvatarGroup for collaborators, assignees, or attendees — it overlaps them, rings each in the surface colour, and collapses the rest into a "+N" count; use the low-level parts only when you need custom image/fallback layout.

bestPractices.description: Use `variant="art"` where people without photos sit side by side — a member list, an activity feed, a chat. Seeded by the person, each gets their own colour, so faces stay tellable apart at a glance; the neutral fallback makes everyone the same grey circle.
Provide meaningful alt text for profile images, or an empty alt when the adjacent text already names the person.
Use initials or a simple glyph fallback so missing images still communicate identity.

Pick the size by the job: 2xs (20px) or xs (24px) in a compact workspace row (an assignee in an issue list, a project mark in a nav item), sm in dense rows and tables, md (the default) beside one line of text, lg in a row with a title and subtitle, xl (96px) for a profile header beside the person's name, 2xl (160px) for an artist or profile hero and roster portraits. Keep one size within a list or group.

Use AvatarGroup for a stack of people, and give it an aria-label with the real count ("12 collaborators"). Set `surface` (or `--avatar-group-ring`) to whatever the group sits on, so the separating ring matches a card or popover, not the page. When it shares a row with actions, set `fit` so it gives up avatars to the "+N" count before the row has to wrap.

Use `shape="square"` for what is not a person (a workspace, a project, an org, a team), with `tone` set to a palette family so each one keeps its own colour: `<Avatar shape="square" tone="teal" fallback="N" alt="Northwind storefront" size="xs" />`. Circles mean people; keep that distinction across the app.

Hand-build a stack with negative margins and per-avatar ring classes, or fake the overflow as an Avatar with "+4" initials — screen readers hear "plus 4" with no context. Use AvatarGroup's `max`/`total`, or AvatarGroupCount.
Use avatars as decoration without nearby identity context. They should help users recognize a person or account.
Overload a dense table with large avatars; use sm or omit images when scanning data is more important.

Resize an Avatar with size classes (`className="size-5"`, `className="size-40"`) — the initials, the status indicator and the image fade stay at the size they were drawn for. Use size="2xs"/"xs" for dense rows and size="xl"/"2xl" for portraits, which scale all three. Don't hand-build a tinted initials tile for a project or workspace mark either: that is Avatar shape="square" with a tone. Past 160px, or for a cover, it is media: an AspectBox, not an avatar.

anatomy.name: Root
anatomy.description: The circular frame that clips the image, owns size, and contains image plus fallback.

anatomy.name: Image
anatomy.description: The loaded profile image, cropped to fill the root.

anatomy.name: Fallback
anatomy.description: Initials, a glyph, or short text shown while loading, on error, or when no image exists.

anatomy.name: Group
anatomy.description: AvatarGroup: the overlapping stack. Sets one size for every avatar and rings each in the surface colour.

anatomy.name: Count
anatomy.description: AvatarGroupCount: the "+N" avatar ending a group, read as "and N more". Rendered automatically by `max`/`total`.

props.name: src
props.description: Image source. When omitted, still loading, or failed, the fallback shows.

props.name: alt
props.description: Alt text for the image. Without an image it becomes the avatar's accessible name (role=img), so the initials are never read out as the name.

props.name: fallback
props.description: Initials or a glyph rendered when no image is displayed.

props.name: fallbackDelay
props.description: Delay before showing the fallback, in ms — avoids a flash on fast loads.

props.name: status
props.description: A presence indicator pinned to the bottom-end edge, usually <StatusDot tone="success" />. It sits outside the clipped circle and wears a ring in the surface colour (--avatar-group-ring, else the page background). Use this instead of absolutely positioning a dot over an Avatar.

props.name: size
props.description: Square footprint: 20px / 24px for compact workspace rows; 32px / 40px / 48px for rows; 96px / 160px for portraits (a profile header, an artist hero, a roster tile). The initials, a status indicator and its cut-out ring scale with it, and at the portrait sizes the photo fades in over the resting surface.

props.name: shape
props.description: The frame's corner. circle is a person. square is what is not a face — a workspace, a project, an org, a team — with a radius from the theme's steps that grows with the size (4px at 20–24px to 20px at 160px), so a square theme stays square. A status indicator sits on the square's corner.

props.name: tone
props.description: The fallback's colour. neutral is the muted surface; a palette family paints its wash behind the initials and its deep ink on them (a soft Badge's pair, held to contrast in every theme), for a category colour such as one per project. Ignored by variant="art", which colours by seed.

props.name: variant
props.description: What the fallback looks like. neutral: initials on the muted surface. art: initials over GradientArt seeded by the person, so each person without a photo gets their own stable colour from the theme.

props.name: seed
props.description: The art variant's seed. Defaults to the fallback text, then `alt`, so a person keeps one colour wherever they appear; pass a user id to tell apart two people who share initials.

subcomponents.name: AvatarRoot
subcomponents.type: Base UI Avatar.Root props + size + shape + tone + className
subcomponents.description: Low-level circular frame for full composition control — clips the image and holds the `size` axis. Wraps AvatarImage and AvatarFallback.

subcomponents.name: AvatarImage
subcomponents.description: The profile image. Fills and crops the frame; hidden by Base UI until it loads.

subcomponents.name: AvatarFallback
subcomponents.description: Shown when no image is available — typically initials or a glyph. Accepts a delay prop.

subcomponents.name: AvatarGroup
subcomponents.type: { size?: "2xs" | "xs" | "sm" | "md" | "lg"; surface?: "background" | "card" | "popover" | "muted"; max?: number; fit?: boolean; total?: number; countLabel?: (count: number) => string; "aria-label"?: string; className?: string; children: ReactNode }
subcomponents.description: Overlapping stack (role=group) — name it with aria-label ("12 collaborators"). `size` applies to every avatar inside. `max` shows that many and collapses the rest into a "+N" count; `total` is the real head-count when you only pass some people. `fit` shows only as many avatars as fit the width the group is given (it fills the space left in a flex row) and folds the rest into the count, so a tight row reads "MO SR +5" instead of wrapping. The separating ring reads the inherited `--avatar-group-ring` (default: the page background); `surface` sets it to card, popover, or muted.

subcomponents.name: AvatarGroupCount
subcomponents.type: { count: number; label?: string; size?: "2xs" | "xs" | "sm" | "md" | "lg"; className?: string }
subcomponents.description: The "+N" avatar. Shows "+4" and reads "and 4 more" (override with label). AvatarGroup renders it for you from max/total; use it directly only when composing the stack yourself.

motion.why: At the portrait sizes (xl, 2xl) the photo replacing the initials is a visible pop across one of the page's largest elements; fading it in reads as the picture arriving, not the layout glitching. Row sizes swap instantly — too small to register, and a list of fading faces would shimmer.
An avatar is not interactive itself; a link or button wrapping it owns the response.
It has no states of its own to move between beyond the image arriving.
Loading shows the fallback, which is already a finished resting state rather than a spinner.

a11y: Base UI tracks the image loading status and swaps to the fallback on missing/loading/error — no manual onError wiring.
Provide meaningful alt text via the alt prop; pass an empty alt for decorative avatars.
The fallback (initials/glyph) gives a non-image identity cue for screen readers and slow connections.
AvatarGroup renders role=group; give it an aria-label naming the whole set ("12 collaborators"), since the visible stack only shows some of them.
The "+N" count is hidden from screen readers and replaced by "and N more" (AvatarGroupCount `label`, or AvatarGroup `countLabel`).

components.name: Badge
components.summary: Compact static label, set on two axes: appearance (soft, outline, solid, overlay on media, plain text) and tone (neutral, a semantic tone, or a palette family like blue for a category with no meaning attached). An optional leading icon, or a status dot (with pulse) for state.

usage.description: Use Badge for any short static label: metadata, categories, tone-coded labels, a label on artwork (appearance="overlay"), or a status line (appearance="plain" with dot). Use Pill for a chip someone clicks, NotificationBadge for an unread count on an icon, and Banner or Toast for messages that need attention.

bestPractices.description: Keep badge text short: one to three words or a compact count.
Use tone variants when the badge carries meaning, such as success, warning or destructive, or a decorative tone for a category or plan.
Pair icons with text; the icon reinforces meaning but should not be the only cue.
Use a Badge as a button. If it triggers an action, use Button, Toggle, or a menu item.
Choose appearance and tone separately: appearance is how loud it is (soft by default, solid for emphasis, overlay on images, plain for a status line); tone is what it means.
Stack many loud tone badges in one row; too many semantic colors compete with the actual content.

anatomy.name: Container
anatomy.description: The compact pill surface carrying the tone or neutral treatment.

anatomy.name: Label
anatomy.description: Short visible text that names the category, state, role, or metadata value.

anatomy.name: Icon
anatomy.description: Optional leading Icon used to reinforce the label.

props.name: appearance
props.description: How it is drawn. soft: a tinted fill (neutral is the secondary surface). outline: a hairline. solid: the tone at full strength (neutral is the inverted chip). overlay: legible on images — a dark scrim, or the solid tone. plain: no fill or padding, a status line.

props.name: tone
props.description: What it means. Every appearance takes every tone. The palette families (red … pink) are categories with no meaning attached — tags, labels, project colours — painted from the theme's generated palette, so they lean toward the brand and read in both modes.

props.name: size
props.description: "sm" uses tighter padding + text-label-sm; "md" is the default look.

props.name: icon
props.description: Optional leading glyph (e.g. <Icon name="lock" />), rendered before the children with the base gap. Ignored when dot is set.

props.name: dot
props.description: A leading status dot in the badge's tone. With appearance="plain" it is a status line (● Ready).

props.name: pulse
props.description: Pulse the dot, for a state in progress. Needs dot.

a11y: Badges are static text by default; do not rely on color alone for meaning.
Use clear label text for semantic tones so assistive tech receives the same status information sighted users see.

examples.label: Tones
examples.code: <Row gap={1}><Badge tone="1">Business</Badge><Badge tone="2">Studio</Badge><Badge tone="3">Starter</Badge></Row>

examples.label: Palette colours (categories)
examples.code: <Row gap={1}><Badge tone="blue">Design</Badge><Badge tone="teal">Research</Badge><Badge tone="orange">Marketing</Badge><Badge tone="pink" appearance="outline">Ops</Badge><Badge tone="purple" appearance="solid">Launch</Badge></Row>

examples.code: <Badge appearance="solid" size="sm">Admin</Badge>

examples.code: <Badge tone="success">Resolved</Badge>

examples.label: With icon

examples.code: <Row gap={1}><Badge tone="success">Synced</Badge><Badge tone="warning">Review</Badge><Badge tone="destructive">Blocked</Badge></Row>

components.name: Banner
components.summary: Full-width, page-level announcement bar. A tone (neutral, info, success, warning, the decorative 1, destructive) × an appearance (soft tint or loud solid fill), and an optional leading scope label. Centers its message, or — with a trailing action — switches to a leading-text + trailing-button layout. Optionally sticky and dismissible.

usage.description: Use Banner for page-level or app-level messages that affect the current experience: outages, maintenance, success confirmations, policy notices, or major warnings. Prefer Toast for transient feedback from a specific action, and prefer InlineStatus for local row or form state.

bestPractices.description: Use soft appearance for contextual notices and solid appearance for urgent, blocking, or system-wide states.
Set live='polite' or live='assertive' only when the banner appears or changes dynamically.
Include one clear action when the user can resolve or inspect the state.
Use multiple stacked solid banners unless the page is genuinely blocked by multiple independent states.
Use Banner for field-level validation, row status, or small local hints; use Field, InlineStatus, or Badge instead.

Use Banner inside a dialog, a form, or a section to qualify the content around it — that is Note. Banner is a full-width announcement strip for page- or app-level state, so in a modal it reads as a slab heavier than the fields it warns about, and its soft appearance has no border and no tone-colored icon: the severity survives only as a faint wash.

anatomy.name: Message
anatomy.description: The short announcement text. It should explain the state in plain language.

anatomy.name: Action
anatomy.description: Optional trailing action that changes the layout from centered copy to text plus action.

anatomy.name: Dismiss
anatomy.description: Optional close control for notices the user can safely hide.

props.name: tone
props.description: Neutral surface or a tone that encodes the announcement's intent (info / success / warning / the decorative 1 / destructive).

props.name: appearance
props.description: "soft" is a quiet tinted fill; "solid" is the full tone with its paired ink — for loud, can't-miss states (offline, chain-down, RPC errors).

props.name: label
props.description: A short scope label ("Preview", "Staging", a project name) in a leading chip — a Badge that reads on soft and solid fills.

props.name: action
props.description: A trailing action (e.g. a Button). Switches the bar to leading text + trailing action instead of centered text.

props.name: sticky
props.description: Stick the banner to the top of its scroll container (sticky top-0, z-30).

props.name: live
props.description: ARIA live-region politeness for banners shown/updated at runtime (offline, RPC-down, "N new posts"). "polite" → role=status; "assertive" → role=alert. "off" keeps a static labelled region.

props.name: dismissible
props.description: Render a trailing close button that hides the banner when clicked.

props.name: onDismiss
props.description: Called after the banner is dismissed.

a11y: Static banners render as a labelled region (role=region); set `live` to announce dynamic status bars (role=status / role=alert) when they appear or change.
The dismiss control is Button (on-color-ghost, icon-xs) with an aria-label; it takes the bar's own ink, so its glyph and focus ring stay legible on soft and solid fills alike.
Solid fills pair each tone with its theme-adaptive ink token, so text stays legible in light and dark.

components.name: BarChart
components.summary: Bars comparing amounts across categories: grouped, stacked or stacked to 100%, vertical columns or horizontal bars, with value labels, per-category colours and a separate tone for negative values. Bars rise from the baseline in sequence as the chart scrolls into view.

usage.description: Use BarChart to compare amounts across categories — the default chart for "how much of each". Go horizontal (`orientation="horizontal"`) when category names are long or there are many of them; group series side by side to compare them, stack them to show a total. For parts of one whole, a stacked bar or PieChart; for a trend, AreaChart or LineChart.

bestPractices.description: Sort categories by value unless they have a natural order (months, steps).
Use negativeTone for diverging data (profit and loss), so a loss reads apart from a gain.
Group more than three series side by side — the bars get too thin to compare; stack them or split the chart.

Use it for data-heavy views — streaming or real-time data, thousands of points, zoom and brushing, trading charts. Those belong on a charting library (Recharts, visx, ECharts); Sable's charts are for dashboards, landing pages and decks.

props.name: data
props.description: The rows, in order along the category axis.

props.name: index
props.description: The datum field naming each row's category (a month, a day, a channel).

props.name: series
props.type: { key: string; label: string; tone?: ChartTone; color?: string; icon?: string }[]
props.description: The measures to plot: the datum field, its name in the legend/tooltip/table, and its colour (a tone by role, or any CSS colour). Omitted, series take the chart palette in order: --chart-1 … --chart-8, validated for colour-blind separation in light and dark; a theme may override the set.

props.name: label
props.description: What the chart shows. Its accessible name and the caption of the data table assistive tech reads.

props.name: className
props.description: Sizes the chart (plot + legend). Set a height: `h-72`, `aspect-video h-auto`.

props.name: valueFormatter
props.description: Format values everywhere (axis, labels, tooltip, table) — units like "$12,480". Default: compact on the axis, full elsewhere.

props.name: indexFormatter
props.description: Shorten category labels on the axis ("January" → "Jan"); the tooltip keeps the full value.

props.name: locale
props.description: BCP 47 locale for default number and date formatting.

props.name: tooltip
props.type: boolean | { indicator?: "dot" | "line" | "dashed" | "none"; hideLabel?: boolean; labelFormatter?: (label, datum) => ReactNode; showTotal?: boolean }
props.description: Show a tooltip on hover and keyboard focus, or configure it: the row marker, hiding the heading, rewriting it, adding a Total row.

props.name: legend
props.default: true when there is more than one series
props.description: Show the legend under the chart.

props.name: grid
props.description: Hairline gridlines along the value axis.

props.name: xAxis
props.default: true for columns; false for horizontal bars
props.description: The horizontal axis.

props.name: yAxis
props.default: false for columns; true for horizontal bars
props.description: The vertical axis.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. The arrival (bars rising in sequence) and the data-change morph are the flourish; the hover dim and gliding cursor are the feedback `subtle` keeps.

props.name: animate
props.description: Play the arrival once the chart scrolls into view. Reduced motion shows the finished chart. `animate={false}` is `motion="subtle"`.
props.deprecated: motion="subtle" (what animate={false} now maps to: no arrival, hover kept) or motion="off"

props.name: activeIndex
props.description: The highlighted row (controlled); `null` for none.

props.name: defaultActiveIndex
props.description: The row highlighted at first — a tooltip already open before anyone hovers.

props.name: onActiveIndexChange
props.description: Called as the pointer or keyboard moves between rows.

props.name: orientation
props.description: `vertical` columns rise from the bottom; `horizontal` bars run from the left, for long category names.

props.name: stacked
props.description: Stack the series in one bar, or `"expand"` to show each category as 100%. Unstacked series sit side by side.

props.name: labels
props.description: Print each bar's value at its end, or (`"inside"`, horizontal) the category name inside the bar as well.

props.name: colorBy
props.description: Colour by series, or give each category its own tone (one series).

props.name: negativeTone
props.description: Colour negative values with this tone.

props.name: radius
props.description: Corner radius of each bar's far end, in px. Stacks round only the outer segment.

props.name: barWidth
props.description: Maximum thickness of a bar, in px: the band's leftover is air, not a fatter bar. Raise it for a bolder presentation look.

motion.why: Once on screen, bars rise from the baseline in sequence on the emphasized easing (scale from the zero line) and their labels fade in. On the motion tokens; reduced motion shows the finished chart. The arrival is expressive: it plays at the full motion level only, so `motion="subtle"` (or a subtle app policy) shows the finished chart while hover feedback stays.

The hovered category gets a band behind it and the other bars dim at once — a lagging highlight reads as a slow chart. The dim mixes each bar toward the surface instead of fading it, so gridlines never strike through a dimmed column and stacked segments stay solid. Essential: `subtle` keeps it.

Geometry eases from the old shape to the new one through a CSS `d` transition on the motion tokens (no recipe animates path geometry); browsers without `d` transitions update in place. Expressive, like the arrival: under `subtle` new data swaps in place.
A chart has no indeterminate state; show a Skeleton while the data loads.

a11y: The drawing is aria-hidden; the same numbers are in a visually hidden data table (captioned by `label`) that the chart is aria-describedby, so assistive tech reads values, not shapes.

With a tooltip, the chart is one tab stop (role=group, aria-roledescription="chart"): arrow keys, Home and End step through the data, Escape clears, and each step is announced in a polite live region.
Colour is never the only key: series are named in the legend, tooltip and table.

examples.label: Grouped series
examples.code:
<BarChart
	label="Visitors by device"
	data={visitors}
	index="month"
	series={[
		{ key: "desktop", label: "Desktop" },
		{ key: "mobile", label: "Mobile" },
	]}
	indexFormatter={(m) => m.slice(0, 3)}
/>

examples.label: Horizontal, labelled inside
Profit and loss
examples.code:
<BarChart
	label="Net revenue by month"
	data={[
		{ month: "Jan", net: 186 },
		{ month: "Feb", net: -95 },
		{ month: "Mar", net: 137 },
		{ month: "Apr", net: -60 },
	]}
	index="month"
	series={[{ key: "net", label: "Net", tone: "success" }]}
	negativeTone="destructive"
	labels
/>

components.name: BottomNav
components.summary: Mobile bottom tab bar (fixed, hidden at lg), with home-indicator safe-area padding and evenly distributed BottomNavItem tabs. Items are router-agnostic via `render`.

usage.description: Use BottomNav for a small set of top-level mobile destinations that should remain reachable with one thumb. Mount it through `<AppShell bottomNav={…}>` so the content area reserves matching bottom space; it hides at lg, where the Sidebar takes over.

bestPractices.description: Limit the nav to the primary destinations users switch between often.
Give every item a clear label (it is the accessible name), and turn on showLabel when the icons alone are not obvious.
Do not use BottomNav for desktop navigation, dense menus, or page-local actions.
Do not omit the safe-area padding by overriding its padding-bottom. On a device with a home indicator the last row of targets ends up under the gesture area, where taps dismiss the app instead.

anatomy.name: BottomNav
anatomy.description: The fixed or anchored navigation container.

anatomy.name: BottomNavItem
anatomy.description: One destination with label, icon, and active state.

subcomponents.name: BottomNavItem
subcomponents.type: { label: string; icon?: ReactNode; active?: boolean; badge?: ReactNode; showLabel?: boolean; render?: useRender.RenderProp } + button props
subcomponents.description: A single tab, placed as a child of BottomNav. `label` is the accessible name (aria-label) and optional visible label; `icon` is the glyph node (consumer swaps fill weight for the active state); `active` marks the current route (active ink + aria-current); `badge` overlays a corner dot/count on the icon; `showLabel` shows the label text beneath the icon — defaults to false (icon-only); turn it on when the icons alone are not self-evident; `render` renders as another element, e.g. render={<Link to="/x" />}.

motion.why: Fixed app chrome, present from the first paint of every screen. Animating it in on navigation would make each route change look like the app restarting.
The ink steps up on hover and the focus ring eases in, so a pointer or a keyboard on a tablet gets the same answer as every other control in the app.
On a phone there is no hover to say a tap landed, and a route can take a beat to paint. The settle on press is the receipt; without it people tap the tab a second time.
Changing tab eases the active ink out of one item and into the next. It is a cross-fade, not a travelling indicator: each item owns its colour, so there is no single mark to glide.
Navigation has no working state of its own. A slow route shows its pending state in the page it is loading, not in the tab bar.

a11y: BottomNav renders a <nav> landmark.
Each tab is a 44px minimum touch target with an aria-label.
Active tab carries aria-current="page".

examples.label: Tab bar
examples.code: <BottomNav><BottomNavItem icon={<Icon name="home" />} label="Home" active render={<Link to="/" />} /><BottomNavItem icon={<Icon name="bell" />} label="Notifications" badge={<NotificationBadge dot />} render={<Link to="/notifications" />} /></BottomNav>

components.name: Breadcrumbs
components.summary: Navigation trail showing the path to the current page. A labelled <nav> wraps an inline <ol> of crumbs — interactive ancestor links, separators, and a non-interactive current page. No Base UI.

usage.description: Use Breadcrumbs to show the user's location inside a hierarchy and provide lightweight parent navigation.

bestPractices.description: Use breadcrumbs when users can arrive deep in a nested structure.
Keep the current page as text so it reads as location, not another link.
Do not use breadcrumbs as a substitute for primary navigation or step progress.
Do not make the last crumb a link. It points at the page you are already on, and screen readers announce it as a destination; render it as the current page with aria-current.

anatomy.name: BreadcrumbItem
anatomy.description: A single step in the path.

anatomy.name: BreadcrumbLink
anatomy.description: A linked ancestor destination.

anatomy.name: BreadcrumbPage
anatomy.description: The current non-linked page.

anatomy.name: BreadcrumbSeparator
anatomy.description: The visual separator between steps.

props.name: Breadcrumbs
props.description: The trail root. Renders <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> around a flex <ol>. Pass the crumb parts as children.

subcomponents.name: BreadcrumbItem
subcomponents.description: A single crumb slot (<li>) holding a link or the current page.

subcomponents.name: BreadcrumbLink
subcomponents.description: An interactive ancestor crumb (<a>). Muted by default, brightens to foreground on hover/focus. render composes another element with the crumb's styling, e.g. a router link: render={<Link to="/library" />}, so navigating stays in the app.

subcomponents.name: BreadcrumbPage
subcomponents.description: The current-page crumb (<span aria-current="page">). Non-interactive, full-contrast.

subcomponents.name: BreadcrumbSeparator
subcomponents.description: Decorative divider (<li aria-hidden>) between crumbs. Defaults to a chevron-right icon; pass children to swap the glyph.

motion.why: The trail is page furniture, rendered with the page header. An entrance would replay on every navigation, which is exactly when the reader looks at it to get their bearings.
Ancestors are muted until hovered or focused. Easing the ink makes the trail read as links answering the pointer; a hard snap across a row of small text looks like flicker.
A breadcrumb has no state of its own. The current page changes by navigation, which replaces the trail; animating between two trails would imply the path itself moved.
It never works in the background. A route that is still loading says so in the page, not in its address.

a11y: The <nav> carries aria-label="Breadcrumb" so assistive tech announces the landmark.
Crumbs sit in an ordered list (<ol>) to convey hierarchy and position.
The current page uses aria-current="page" and is rendered as plain text, not a link.
Separators are aria-hidden so the chevron glyph is not announced.

examples.label: Three-level trail
examples.code: <Breadcrumbs><BreadcrumbItem><BreadcrumbLink href="/">Home</BreadcrumbLink></BreadcrumbItem><BreadcrumbSeparator /><BreadcrumbItem><BreadcrumbLink href="/library">Library</BreadcrumbLink></BreadcrumbItem><BreadcrumbSeparator /><BreadcrumbItem><BreadcrumbPage>Reports</BreadcrumbPage></BreadcrumbItem></Breadcrumbs>

components.name: Browser
components.summary: A generic, current browser window: one compact toolbar (window controls, back/forward/reload, a centered address field) around page content.

usage.description: Use Browser to frame a website or product surface preview when the browser chrome is part of the story.

bestPractices.description: Use it for documentation, product examples, and visual previews where the page context matters.
Keep the framed content simple enough to remain legible at the rendered size.
Do not use Browser for real navigation, real forms, or arbitrary card decoration.
Do not put a real, working URL in the address pill. It reads as a link, is not one, and invites a click that does nothing.

props.name: url
props.description: Address shown in the centered address pill. Omit for a blank pill.

props.name: children
props.description: Page content rendered inside the content region.

a11y: Purely presentational chrome; the framed content carries its own semantics.
The toolbar is drawn, not interactive, and hidden from assistive technology; the address is decorative text.

components.name: Bubble
components.summary: The surface a message's content sits on: four treatments, an align-aware tail, a readable measure cap, and an optional row of reaction pills.

usage.description: The tinted (or untinted) surface a turn's content sits on. Kept separate from Message because the row's layout and the content's surface change independently — an assistant's markdown answer wants no surface at all in exactly the same row a one-line reply wants a bubble.

bestPractices.description: Use `muted` for the other party and `primary` for the reader's own messages. Two treatments is the whole vocabulary a conversation needs to say who is speaking.

Reach for `variant="plain"` for long-form assistant output — rendered markdown, code blocks, tables. A tinted box around three paragraphs reads as a quote block rather than as a turn, and `plain` drops the measure cap with the surface.
Pass the same `align` you gave the enclosing Message, so the tail lands on the speaker's side.

Set `tail={false}` on the continuation bubbles in a grouped run — the tail marks where a speaker starts, and repeating it on every line makes a block of one person's messages look like four separate turns.

Let the register size it. Inside `<Density value="compact">` a Bubble sets itself in the workspace prose tier automatically — a docked agent panel needs no per-call-site sizing, and hardcoding one defeats the mechanism.
Do not remove the measure cap to fill a wide window. ~42rem is a reading measure; a bubble spanning a 1600px viewport is a paragraph at 140 characters per line.
Do not put the timestamp or the author name inside the bubble. Those are Message's `header` / `footer`, which stay outside the surface and so still work under `variant="plain"`.
Do not use a Bubble for a system note or a streaming status. Those are `Marker`, which is deliberately quieter than the message tier.
Do not render reactions as static text. `BubbleReaction` is a toggle and reports `aria-pressed`, which is how a screen-reader user knows whether pressing it adds or removes their own reaction.

anatomy.name: Bubble
anatomy.description: The surface itself. Holds the variant, the side, and the tail.

anatomy.name: BubbleReactions
anatomy.description: The row of reaction pills, just under the bubble at the message column's small gap, so it reads as belonging to that message rather than the next row.

anatomy.name: BubbleReaction
anatomy.description: One reaction pill — emoji, count (hidden at 1), and pressed state. Celebrates when it becomes the reader's own.

anatomy.name: BubbleReactionAdd
anatomy.description: The add-reaction pill at the end of the row: opens a ReactionPicker above it.

props.name: variant
props.description: Surface treatment. `muted` for the other party, `primary` for the reader's own messages, `outline` for a quieter own-side, `plain` for long-form output that should not sit in a box (also drops the measure cap and padding).

props.name: align
props.description: Which side of the conversation the bubble is on — puts the tail on the speaker's side. Match it to the enclosing Message.

props.name: tail
props.description: Draw the tail: a small ear off the speaker-side top corner, which goes square to meet it. The same 5px in every theme's radius language, flat through fully pilled. The bubble keeps the ear's space either way, so turning it off for the continuation bubbles in a grouped run keeps the run aligned.

props.name: ...div props
props.description: Spread onto the surface element.

subcomponents.name: BubbleReactions
subcomponents.description: Row container for reaction pills. Match `align` to the Bubble so the row hangs off the same edge.

subcomponents.name: BubbleReaction
subcomponents.type: { emoji: ReactNode; label?: string; count?: number; active?: boolean; motion?: MotionLevel } & ComponentPropsWithRef<"button">
subcomponents.description: One reaction pill. A toggle, not a label: `active` drives `aria-pressed` as well as the styling, `label` names it ("Party, 3"), and `count` is hidden at 1 because the pill already says "one". When it turns on — pressed, or newly added already on — the emoji blooms, copies of it burst out and the count rolls; pills the page loads with stay still.

subcomponents.name: BubbleReactionAdd
subcomponents.type: { reactions?: Reaction[]; selected?: string[]; onSelect?: (emoji: string) => void; label?: string; motion?: MotionLevel } & ComponentPropsWithRef<"button">
subcomponents.description: The add-reaction pill: a smiley that opens a ReactionPicker above it. Choosing an emoji closes the picker and calls `onSelect`; add the emoji to the row and its new pill celebrates on arrival.

motion.why: A bubble arrives with its Message row, which owns how a new message enters the transcript. A reaction pill that the reader just added arrives with its own celebration (below).

Reacting is the reader's choice, so it is answered like a like: the emoji grows from nothing past its size and settles, while copies of it spray outward and fade (Burst with the emoji as its particle, the way chat apps answer a reaction). Plays when a pill turns on and when a pill mounts already on into a row that has rendered — never for the pills a page loads with. Pills inherit Pill's motion-interactive and motion-press.

The count rolls with NumberTicker as people react. Turning a reaction off is quiet: the tint eases out and the count rolls back, with no burst. Under `subtle` or reduced motion the bloom and the spray are dropped and the tint and count alone answer.
A bubble is static content; a message still being written is StreamingText or a Marker, not a state of the surface.

a11y: The surface is a plain container with no imposed role — a bubble is presentation, and announcing one as a region would put a landmark around every line of a conversation.

Reaction pills are real buttons reporting `aria-pressed`, so the reader's own reaction is state rather than colour alone. Give each a `label`: it is named "Party, 3", with the emoji and its burst hidden from AT. The add-reaction pill is named "Add reaction" and opens a toolbar picker.
`whitespace-pre-wrap` and `break-words` keep pasted logs, long URLs, and hard-wrapped text inside the surface instead of overflowing the conversation.
Every variant meets AA against its own surface, including `primary`, which pairs the primary fill with its paired foreground token rather than a hardcoded white.

</>

components.name: Button
components.summary: Pill-shaped action primitive (theme-driven radius via --button-radius, defaults to full). Neutral tiers (primary/secondary/ghost/outline), plus destructive and link, and three on-color tiers (on-color/on-color-outline/on-color-ghost) that paint with the surrounding ink so a button reads on any tone or brand fill. Optional loading state shows a spinner and disables the button.

usage.description: Use Button when the user commits an action, submits a form, opens UI, or confirms a decision. Use the visual tier to communicate priority: one primary action per local decision area, then secondary, ghost, outline, or link for lower-emphasis choices.

bestPractices.description: Use a single primary button in a view or dense panel so the action hierarchy stays obvious.

For a copy control, pair an icon Button with `useCopy(text, { timeout? })`. It takes the text when the hook is called and returns `{ copy, copied }`; `copy()` takes no argument, so pass the value the button copies to the hook, not to `copy`. Text that costs something to produce (a file to fetch) goes in as a function, `useCopy(() => fetch(url).then((r) => r.text()))`, called only on click. Keep both glyphs mounted in a `motion-icon-swap` cell so the copy mark visibly becomes a check (a `copied ? "check" : "copy"` swap snaps between frames and is easy to miss), and say "Copied" in a polite `role="status"` region: the glyph change is silent to a screen reader.
Write labels as actions, such as "Save changes" or "Delete draft", instead of vague labels like "OK".
Use loading with loadingLabel for async work so the action cannot double-fire and the state is announced.

Put icons in iconStart / iconEnd rather than as children, so the button applies its optical padding. Start icons say what the action is (plus, share); end icons say where it goes (chevron-right, external).

Set bleed on a ghost or link button that sits at the start or end of a row, so its LABEL lines up with the content edge the row shares ("View all" over a grid, "Add task" under a list, "Resend code" at a card footer's end). The box moves out by exactly its own padding; the hit area and hover fill stay full size and run past the edge. SectionHeader, PageHeader (back and actions) and CardAction already do this for their outermost ghost/link child — don't add it there, and use bleed="none" to opt one out.

Pull a ghost button onto an edge with -ms-3 / -me-3 classNames. That number is one size's padding: it is wrong at xs, md and cta, wrong on a side carrying an icon, and wrong once a preset retunes the spacing. bleed reads the button's own padding var. And don't bleed a filled or outlined button — its visible edge is what aligns, so bleed is a no-op there.
Use destructive for reversible or low-risk actions; reserve it for operations with real loss or danger.
Use a button for plain navigation. Compose with render={<a />} when the element should behave like a link.

Use secondary on a tinted surface — inside a Note, a soft Banner, or any tone fill. `secondary` is a near-background surface token (in some themes within 2% of the page), so on a tint it reads as a hole punched in the fill rather than as a control sitting on it. On a soft tint use outline or ghost; on a full-strength fill use the on-color tiers.

On a coloured fill — a solid Banner, a bg-tone-* or bg-primary band, an inverse (bg-foreground) section, a brand panel — use variant="on-color" for the main action and on-color-outline / on-color-ghost for the rest. They paint with the band's inherited ink (currentColor), so the surface must set its paired ink (text-tone-info-foreground, text-primary-foreground, text-background…), which it already should. Name the fill once on the surface, e.g. [--on-color-fill:var(--tone-info)], and the solid button's label takes the fill colour; unnamed, it falls back to black or white against the ink. Both clear 4.5:1 in every shipped theme and mode.

Use the on-color tiers on the page, a Card, a Note, or a soft tint — there the ink is the page foreground and the normal tiers already fit. And don't restyle a normal variant with bg-*/text-* classNames to make it read on a band; that hard-codes colours per theme and skips the contrast and focus handling on-color carries.

anatomy.name: Container
anatomy.description: The rounded hit target that carries the visual tier, focus ring, disabled state, and loading affordance.

anatomy.name: Label
anatomy.description: Visible action text and the default accessible name. Icon-only buttons still need an aria-label.

anatomy.name: Leading icon
anatomy.description: An optional semantic Icon that reinforces the label without replacing it.

anatomy.name: Spinner
anatomy.description: Displayed during loading and paired with aria-busy plus disabled activation.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis tier. One primary per screen. The on-color tiers are for buttons ON a coloured fill: they paint with the inherited text colour (the fill's ink) — on-color is solid (ink background, fill-coloured label via the optional --on-color-fill var, else black/white), on-color-outline and on-color-ghost are transparent with an ink label. Never use them on page or card surfaces. floating is for a control that sits OVER content (carousel arrows, a marquee pause, a jump-to-latest over a conversation): its own edge, lift and translucent popover fill, so it reads on arbitrary content beneath. field is for a button docked in a workspace panel among xs fields: the inset panel-field fill and the field's corner, so a picker trigger or an add action reads as one of the row's controls; pair it with size xs or icon-xs.

props.name: size
props.description: Reads the density ladder, so every value differs by register: page 28/32/40/44, workspace 24/28/32/36. xs and icon-xs were added in 0.31.0 for the workspace control floor and are the sizes tool chrome wants; md is the default everywhere. icon/icon-sm/icon-xs are square.

props.name: render
props.description: Compose with another element/component through the Base UI render prop.

props.name: loading
props.description: Show a Spinner while an action is in flight and refuse presses. The spinner takes the iconStart slot when there is one; otherwise it lays over the label, which fades out in place, so the button keeps its width. Sets aria-busy and aria-disabled, never the native disabled: disabling the focused button sent focus to <body>, so a sheet the action opened had nowhere to return it.

props.name: onClick
props.description: May return a promise: the button shows `loading` until it settles and ignores further presses meanwhile, from the first click on. Prefer it to a `busy` flag in state, which takes effect a render late (three fast clicks ran three times).

props.name: badge
props.description: A corner indicator (usually <NotificationBadge dot /> or a count) overlaid on the top-end corner of the glyph. For icon-only sizes; never hand-position a badge over a Button with absolute offsets.

props.name: loadingLabel
props.description: Optional text shown in place of children while loading, with the spinner beside it. The width follows the new text, so prefer no loadingLabel where the row must not move.

props.name: iconStart
props.description: Icon before the label. The button takes one 2px step off its start padding so icon + label read as centred. Replaced by the spinner while loading.

props.name: iconEnd
props.description: Icon after the label (disclosure, external link, next). Same optical correction on the end side.

props.name: bleed
props.description: Optical alignment for a borderless button (ghost, link, on-color-ghost): a negative inline margin of exactly its own padding on that side — --button-px, or the icon side's optical padding when an icon sits there; an icon-only size bleeds by its inset to the glyph — so the label (or glyph) lands on the content edge. Hit area and hover/focus fill keep their full size. Logical sides, so it mirrors in RTL. A no-op on variants with a visible edge (primary, secondary, outline, destructive, floating, field, on-color, on-color-outline): a filled button aligns its edge, not its label. Unset, a borderless button renders data-bleed="auto" and SectionHeader, PageHeader and CardAction bleed it when it is their outermost child; none opts out.

motion.why: A button belongs to the layout it ships in. Whatever staged that region owns the entrance; a button that fades in on its own is a button that is briefly un-clickable for no stated reason.

Hover, focus ring and disabled fade all ease on one declaration. This is the reference case for the whole recipe: it lists scale and translate alongside the colours specifically so motion-press can add a transform without a second, conflicting transition-property.

The 0.97 settle on pointer-down is the only confirmation the press registered before the action's own result arrives — which on a slow network is the difference between waiting and clicking again. It skips disabled elements, so a dead button stays visibly dead.

Going busy is the one state change a button has. The spinner fades in where it mounts — in the icon slot, or laid over a plain label that fades out beneath it and keeps its place — so the width never changes and the row does not shift under the pointer that just pressed it. The label fades back when the work settles. A toggling control is a Switch or a Toggle; those carry their own transition.
Pending work is passed in via `loading`, which renders a Spinner — the activity motion lives there rather than being duplicated here.

a11y: Renders a native <button> by default (keyboard + role free).
Focus-visible ring uses the --ring token at 50% opacity.
Use render={<a/>} for link semantics rather than onClick navigation.
On-color tiers replace the --ring focus ring with one drawn in the band's ink past a transparent 2px gap, so focus stays visible on any fill (ink-on-fill is the theme's own tested pair).

On-color contrast is measured in button.test.tsx for every shipped theme and mode on each tone, primary, destructive, success, highlight and inverse fill: solid label at rest and hover, and outline/ghost label on the hover wash, all at least 4.5:1.
bleed moves only the box, never the hit target: the full padded area stays clickable and the focus ring still draws around the whole button, past the content edge.
loading sets aria-busy and disables activation (disabled on a native button, aria-disabled on a render element) so the action can't double-fire.

components.name: ButtonGroup
components.summary: Buttons joined into one control: a split button (an action beside the chevron that opens its menu) or a short run of related actions. The children stay ordinary Buttons; the group squares their inner corners, collapses bordered seams into one hairline, and draws a seam between filled ones.

usage.description: Use ButtonGroup when one action has close alternatives (Copy page, with Open in… behind a chevron) or a few actions belong together as one object (zoom out, reset, zoom in). Use ToggleGroup for a choice that stays selected, and Tabs to switch views.

bestPractices.description: Give the children one height: `size="sm"` with `size="icon-sm"`, `md` with `icon`. The group aligns them but cannot reconcile two heights into one edge.
For a split button, put the main action first and a Menu whose trigger is the chevron Button second, with an aria-label on the trigger ("More page actions").
Name the group with aria-label when the buttons alone do not say what they act on.
Do not round or border the children yourself to make them meet; that is the group's job, and an override breaks under a theme's button shape.
Do not use it for a selection that stays on. That is ToggleGroup, which carries the pressed state.

props.name: role
props.description: Group semantics, so a screen reader announces the buttons as one set. Pass `toolbar` when it carries arrow-key navigation of your own.

props.name: className
props.description: Layout classes for the group (margins, alignment). The children's look comes from their own variants.

props.name: ...props
props.description: All native <div> attributes, including aria-label.

a11y: Renders role="group", so assistive tech announces the buttons as one set; name it with aria-label.
Each child keeps its own focus stop and label; a focused child is raised above its neighbour so its ring is drawn whole.
An icon-only chevron that opens a menu needs its own aria-label, such as "More page actions".
