examples.code: <Field label="Password"><InputGroup trailing={<Button variant="ghost" size="icon-sm" aria-label={shown ? "Hide password" : "Show password"} aria-pressed={shown} onClick={() => setShown(!shown)}><Icon name={shown ? "eye-off" : "eye"} /></Button>}><Input type={shown ? "text" : "password"} autoComplete="current-password" /></InputGroup></Field>
examples.imports: import { Button, Field, Icon, Input, InputGroup } from "@sableui/react"

components.name: Kbd
components.summary: A keyboard key indicator. Renders a raised <kbd> key cap sized from the surrounding text, so one Kbd fits body copy, menus and tooltips; KbdGroup sets one cap per key for a combo. `mod` renders the platform modifier (⌘ or Ctrl); `variant="ghost"` is the bare label for menu rows and tooltips.

usage.description: Use Kbd to display keyboard keys or shortcuts in help text, menus, and docs.

bestPractices.description: Use it only for literal keyboard input such as Cmd, Enter, or Esc.
Show a combo as one cap per key inside KbdGroup — `<KbdGroup><Kbd mod /><Kbd>K</Kbd></KbdGroup>` — not several keys typed into one cap.
Use `variant="ghost"` where the shortcut sits on a surface of its own — a menu row's trailing slot, a tooltip — so it reads as a hint, not a second control.
Do not use Kbd as a decorative badge or button replacement.
Do not set a text size on a Kbd. It sizes itself from the text around it.
Do not hardcode ⌘ or Ctrl. The modifier differs by platform; use `<Kbd mod />`, which renders ⌘ on macOS/iOS and Ctrl elsewhere, or Windows users read Mac keys.

props.name: mod
props.description: Render the platform's shortcut modifier in place of children: ⌘ on macOS and iOS, Ctrl everywhere else. Server-rendered as Ctrl and corrected on hydration.

props.name: variant
props.description: `key`: a raised cap on the surface it sits on, with a heavier bottom edge as the key's lip. `ghost`: the bare label, for menu rows, tooltips and other surfaces that are already a frame.

props.name: className
props.description: Merge additional classes onto the key cap.

props.name: ...props
props.description: All native <kbd> attributes (children, ref, etc.).

a11y: Uses the semantic <kbd> element so assistive tech announces keyboard input.
KbdGroup is itself a <kbd> around the per-key caps — the HTML spelling of one key combination — so the combo is announced as a single piece of input.
Sized in em from the surrounding text, so it scales with the user's text size and never shrinks below 12px.

examples.label: Single keys
examples.code: <Kbd>Esc</Kbd>

examples.label: Combo
examples.code: <KbdGroup><Kbd mod /><Kbd>K</Kbd></KbdGroup>

examples.label: In a menu row
examples.code: <MenuItem>Search<KbdGroup className="ms-auto"><Kbd variant="ghost" mod /><Kbd variant="ghost">K</Kbd></KbdGroup></MenuItem>

components.name: Label
components.summary: Styled native <label>. Paired label typography via a size step (xs / sm / md / lg, all sentence case) or an uppercase eyebrow (eyebrow), non-selectable, dims when its peer control is disabled. Optional hint adds a dotted-underline tooltip affordance.

usage.description: Use Label to name a form control and create a clear accessible relationship with that control.

bestPractices.description: Use explicit, persistent labels for inputs, selects, textareas, and grouped controls.
Place helper text separately so the label stays short and direct.
Do not rely on placeholder text as the only label for a control.
Do not use it as a bare styled span. A Label without htmlFor or a wrapped control looks like a label and does nothing — clicking it will not focus the field, which is the entire point.

props.name: htmlFor
props.description: Associates the label with a control by its id (native <label for>).

props.name: size
props.description: Paired label typography step, all sentence case. xs is simply the smallest; for an uppercase eyebrow use eyebrow.

props.name: eyebrow
props.description: Set the label as an eyebrow: the uppercase, letter-spaced text-overline tier (themeable to sentence case). Replaces size. For a kicker above a group, not an ordinary field label.

props.name: hint
props.description: When set, the label gets a dotted-underline affordance and reveals this content in a tooltip on hover/focus.

props.name: className
props.description: Merge or override classes via cn().

a11y: Renders a native <label> — clicking it focuses/activates the associated control.
Associate with a control via htmlFor (matching the control's id) or by wrapping the control.

In a form, use Field: it renders this Label, wires htmlFor/id, and dims the label when the field is disabled. Hand-wired outside a Field, the label only dims via peer-disabled when the control carries `peer` AND precedes the Label in the DOM (Tailwind peer-* only matches a later sibling).
With `hint`, the label becomes focusable and the help text is announced via the tooltip's aria-describedby — so the affordance works for keyboard and screen-reader users, not just hover.

examples.label: With control
examples.code: <Stack gap={1}><Label htmlFor="name">Display name</Label><Input id="name" /></Stack>

examples.label: In a form
examples.code: <Field label="Display name" disabled><Input /></Field>

examples.label: With hint
examples.code: <Label htmlFor="discount" hint="Taken off every order this code is used on.">Discount</Label>

components.name: LikeButton
components.summary: A pressed-or-not toggle for a like, a star or a save, with its count. Pressing it on fills the glyph, which blooms while a ring and a spray of dots burst from it and the count rolls up; pressing it off is quiet.

usage.description: Use LikeButton for a personal, reversible endorsement that other people can see the tally of: liking a post, starring a repository, saving a recipe. It is the one place in Sable that celebrates, because the person chose it and it costs nothing to undo.

bestPractices.description: Pass the server's total as `count` and update it when the save lands. The button shows the viewer's own like at once, before the save, and goes back to `count` exactly whenever it changes, so a failed save that leaves `count` alone can also turn `pressed` back off.
Match the glyph, family and label to the meaning: `icon="star" tone="yellow" label="Star"` for a star. The label is the accessible name, so it must say what pressing does.
Use `format={{ notation: "compact" }}` once counts pass a few thousand, so a feed of buttons keeps one width.
Do not use it for a setting or a view switch (bold, mute, grid or list). Those are tools, not endorsements, and a burst on every press of a formatting control is noise; use Toggle.
Do not use it for a rating or a verdict on an answer (helpful, not helpful). That is a question with two sides; use Feedback.
Do not press it for the user. A burst is a reply to a person's choice — liking something on their behalf, or on load, turns delight into a notification.

props.name: count
props.description: The total, rolled when it changes. Pressing adds or removes the viewer's like at once; the button shows `count` exactly again whenever `count` changes. Omit it for a bare glyph (an icon-size button).

props.name: pressed
props.description: Controlled pressed state.

props.name: defaultPressed
props.description: Initial pressed state when uncontrolled.

props.name: onPressedChange
props.description: Called when the user presses it, with the new state.

props.name: icon
props.description: The glyph, by icon name. Its `solid` variant is shown while pressed.

props.name: tone
props.description: The palette family the glyph fills with while pressed, and the burst blooms from. A family, so it follows the theme.

props.name: label
props.description: The accessible name, read before the count.

props.name: format
props.description: How to write the count, e.g. `{ notation: "compact" }`.

props.name: variant
props.description: The Button surface.

props.name: size
props.description: A Button size; without a count, the matching icon size.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables it.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. The bloom and the burst are the flourish; the fill and the count changing stay.

motion.why: It arrives with the post or row it belongs to. A page that loads with likes already given must be still: nothing blooms on mount.

Pressing it on is the moment. The glyph is 16px, so it needs real amplitude to read as an event: it grows from nothing past its size and settles, after a 90ms beat in which the ring leads. Inherits Button's motion-press for the press itself. Pressing off has no bloom — taking a like back is not a celebration.

The follow-through: <Burst> draws a disc that hollows into a ring and shifts colour, then dots thrown outward in the theme's palette families. Expressive only — under `subtle` or reduced motion it renders nothing and the fill alone answers the press. The count rolls with NumberTicker.
There is no in-between state to show: the like is shown at once, before it is saved.

a11y: A native <button> through Button, with `aria-pressed`. Enter and Space press it.
The accessible name is the label then the count ("Like 1,301"); the burst is aria-hidden and the rolling digits are hidden behind the count's real text.
The pressed state is carried by the filled glyph and `aria-pressed`, never by colour alone.
Under reduced motion the glyph fills and the count changes at once; the bloom and the burst are dropped.

examples.label: A post's likes
examples.code: <LikeButton count={post.likes} defaultPressed={post.liked} onPressedChange={(on) => api.like(post.id, on)} />

examples.label: Star a repository
examples.code: <LikeButton icon="star" tone="yellow" label="Star" variant="outline" count={repo.stars} format={{ notation: "compact" }} />

examples.label: Bare glyph
examples.code: <LikeButton label="Save recipe" />

components.name: LineChart
components.summary: Lines over a sequence — for comparing how measures move. Smooth, linear or step curves, optional dots (coloured by series or by category) and value labels. Lines draw on as the chart scrolls into view.

usage.description: Use LineChart to compare how two or more measures change over the same sequence, or to show one trend precisely (with dots and labels). Unlike AreaChart, its value axis is fitted to the data rather than forced to zero, so small movements stay visible — say so if the axis is shown.

bestPractices.description: Turn on dots and labels for six or fewer points, when the exact values are the story.
Use curve="step" for values that hold until they change — prices, plan tiers, headcount.
Plot unordered categories (channels, products) as a line — the line implies a path between them; use BarChart.

Use it for data-heavy views — streaming or real-time data, thousands of points, zoom and brushing, trading charts. Those belong on a charting library (Recharts, visx, ECharts); Sable's charts are for dashboards, landing pages and decks.

props.name: data
props.description: The rows, in order along the category axis.

props.name: index
props.description: The datum field naming each row's category (a month, a day, a channel).

props.name: series
props.type: { key: string; label: string; tone?: ChartTone; color?: string; icon?: string }[]
props.description: The measures to plot: the datum field, its name in the legend/tooltip/table, and its colour (a tone by role, or any CSS colour). Omitted, series take the chart palette in order: --chart-1 … --chart-8, validated for colour-blind separation in light and dark; a theme may override the set.

props.name: label
props.description: What the chart shows. Its accessible name and the caption of the data table assistive tech reads.

props.name: className
props.description: Sizes the chart (plot + legend). Set a height: `h-72`, `aspect-video h-auto`.

props.name: valueFormatter
props.description: Format values everywhere (axis, labels, tooltip, table) — units like "$12,480". Default: compact on the axis, full elsewhere.

props.name: indexFormatter
props.description: Shorten category labels on the axis ("January" → "Jan"); the tooltip keeps the full value.

props.name: locale
props.description: BCP 47 locale for default number and date formatting.

props.name: tooltip
props.type: boolean | { indicator?: "dot" | "line" | "dashed" | "none"; hideLabel?: boolean; labelFormatter?: (label, datum) => ReactNode; showTotal?: boolean }
props.description: Show a tooltip on hover and keyboard focus, or configure it: the row marker, hiding the heading, rewriting it, adding a Total row.

props.name: legend
props.default: true when there is more than one series
props.description: Show the legend under the chart.

props.name: grid
props.description: Hairline gridlines along the value axis.

props.name: xAxis
props.default: true for columns; false for horizontal bars
props.description: The horizontal axis.

props.name: yAxis
props.default: false for columns; true for horizontal bars
props.description: The vertical axis.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. The arrival (lines drawing on) and the data-change morph are the flourish; the gliding cursor, dots and tooltip are the feedback `subtle` keeps.

props.name: animate
props.description: Play the arrival once the chart scrolls into view. Reduced motion shows the finished chart. `animate={false}` is `motion="subtle"`.
props.deprecated: motion="subtle" (what animate={false} now maps to: no arrival, hover kept) or motion="off"

props.name: activeIndex
props.description: The highlighted row (controlled); `null` for none.

props.name: defaultActiveIndex
props.description: The row highlighted at first — a tooltip already open before anyone hovers.

props.name: onActiveIndexChange
props.description: Called as the pointer or keyboard moves between rows.

props.name: curve
props.description: How the line runs between points. `smooth` is monotone: it never overshoots a value the data does not contain.

props.name: dots
props.description: Mark every data point with a dot.

props.name: colorBy
props.description: Colour the dots by series, or each by its category.

props.name: labels
props.description: Print each point's value above it.

motion.why: Once on screen each line draws on from the first point (stroke-dashoffset), series staggered, then the dots and labels fade in. On the motion tokens; reduced motion shows the finished chart. The arrival is expressive: it plays at the full motion level only, so `motion="subtle"` (or a subtle app policy) shows the finished chart while hover feedback stays.
Hover and focus move the cursor and tooltip instantly — a lagging cursor reads as a slow chart.

Geometry eases from the old shape to the new one through a CSS `d` transition on the motion tokens (no recipe animates path geometry); browsers without `d` transitions update in place. Expressive, like the arrival: under `subtle` new data swaps in place.
A chart has no indeterminate state; show a Skeleton while the data loads.

a11y: The drawing is aria-hidden; the same numbers are in a visually hidden data table (captioned by `label`) that the chart is aria-describedby, so assistive tech reads values, not shapes.

With a tooltip, the chart is one tab stop (role=group, aria-roledescription="chart"): arrow keys, Home and End step through the data, Escape clears, and each step is announced in a polite live region.
Colour is never the only key: series are named in the legend, tooltip and table.

examples.label: Compare two series
examples.code:
<LineChart
	label="Desktop and mobile visitors"
	data={visitors}
	index="month"
	series={[
		{ key: "desktop", label: "Desktop", tone: "primary" },
		{ key: "mobile", label: "Mobile", tone: "info" },
	]}
	indexFormatter={(m) => m.slice(0, 3)}
/>

examples.label: Dots and labels
examples.code:
<LineChart
	label="Desktop visitors"
	data={visitors}
	index="month"
	series={[{ key: "desktop", label: "Desktop" }]}
	curve="linear"
	dots
	labels
	grid={false}
/>

components.name: Marker
components.summary: A non-message row in a conversation: streaming status, system note, bordered notice, or a labelled rule for date breaks. Quieter than the message tier by design.

usage.description: Everything in a conversation that is not a message. Date breaks, "Carla joined", "Thinking…", "Ran search — 3 results", "Message failed to send". One component because they share one job: annotate the stream without competing with it.

bestPractices.description: Use `status` with `icon="spinner" spin` for work in flight, and add `shimmer` while text is actually streaming. The shimmer is scale-aware, so it freezes with the rest of the system under reduced motion.
Use `variant="separator"` for date breaks. The label sits between two rules, which reads as a division of the transcript rather than as another thing someone said.
Replace a status marker's text as the work progresses — "Thinking…" → "Searching the docs" → "Writing the answer". It is a live region, so each change is announced.
Reach for `bordered` only when a note needs containing — an error, an escalation, a retention notice. Boxing routine system events makes a transcript look like a list of alerts.
Do not style a Marker up to message weight. Its whole value is being below that tier; a marker as loud as a message competes with the conversation it is annotating.
Do not leave a status marker mounted after the work finishes. A permanent "Thinking…" is a live region that never resolves, which is worse than no status at all.
Do not use it for a message from a person or an assistant. That is `Message` + `Bubble` — a marker has no author and no side.
Do not set `live` on a `separator` or on a run of `note` markers. Announcing every date break and join event turns the live region into noise and buries the status that mattered.

props.name: variant
props.description: `status` for live activity, `note` for a system event, `bordered` for a note that needs containing, `separator` for a labelled rule.

props.name: icon
props.description: Semantic icon name shown before the label, resolved through IconProvider.

props.name: spin
props.description: Spin the icon — pair with `icon="spinner"` for work in flight.

props.name: shimmer
props.description: Sweep the label while something is streaming, via the scale-aware `motion-text-shimmer` recipe (freezes under reduced motion).

props.name: live
props.description: Announce the label to assistive tech as it changes. On for `status`, because a screen-reader user otherwise gets silence for the whole generation and no way to tell a slow answer from a dead one.

props.name: ...div props
props.description: Spread onto the row.

a11y: `status` markers render as `role="status"` with `aria-live="polite"`, so a change of activity is announced without interrupting whatever is being read.
The other variants are silent by default and can opt in with `live` — announcing every date break and join event would bury the status that mattered.
The separator's rules are `aria-hidden`, leaving only the label in the accessibility tree; the shimmer is decoration over readable text, not a replacement for it.

`motion-text-shimmer` keeps the label opaque through every frame — the gradient runs muted-foreground → foreground rather than fading to transparent, so the text never becomes unreadable mid-animation, and `--motion-scale` freezes it entirely under reduced motion.

examples.label: Streaming status
examples.code: <Marker icon="spinner" spin shimmer>Thinking…</Marker>

examples.label: Date break
examples.code: <Marker variant="separator">Yesterday</Marker>

examples.label: System note
examples.code: <Marker variant="note" icon="user">Carla joined the conversation</Marker>

examples.label: A notice that needs containing
examples.code: <Marker variant="bordered" icon="warning">This conversation will be archived in 7 days.</Marker>

examples.label: In a transcript
examples.code:
<MessageScroller className="h-96">
	<Marker variant="separator">Today</Marker>
	<Message messageId="m1"><Bubble>Can you summarise the release?</Bubble></Message>
	<Marker variant="note" icon="sparkles">Ran changelog — 12 entries</Marker>
	<Marker icon="spinner" spin shimmer>Writing the answer</Marker>
</MessageScroller>
examples.imports: import { Bubble, Marker, Message, MessageScroller } from "@sableui/react"

components.name: Marquee
components.summary: Seamless, constant-speed infinite loop (logos, tags, testimonials). Zero-dependency: duplicates children to fill the track and advances exactly one group + gap per iteration so it never seams. Pauses on hover/focus; freezes to a scroll region when motion is off/reduced.

usage.description: Use Marquee for decorative or ambient continuous content where motion supports the surface.

bestPractices.description: Use it for low-priority repeated content such as logos, tags, or lightweight highlights.
Respect reduced motion and keep the content understandable without relying on animation.
Do not put critical messages, controls, or required reading inside Marquee.
Do not put content that must be read in a Marquee. It moves continuously, so anything longer than a logo or a short label cannot be read reliably — and it must stop for prefers-reduced-motion.

props.name: direction
props.description: Scroll direction; up/down switch to a vertical loop, which needs a bounded height (e.g. className="h-56").

props.name: speed
props.description: Constant speed in px/s — independent of content length.

props.name: gap
props.description: Gap between items (any CSS length). Use a spacing-scale value (calc(var(--spacing) * n)) so it moves with density.

props.name: pauseOnHover
props.description: Pause while hovered or keyboard-focused (WCAG 2.2.2).

props.name: controls
props.description: Render a visible pause/play control — recommended for WCAG 2.2.2 when content auto-scrolls.

props.name: fade
props.description: Fade the leading/trailing edges with a mask.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label for the scrolling region.

a11y: Duplicate groups are aria-hidden, so screen readers read the content once.
Pauses on hover and focus-within; under prefers-reduced-motion / MotionProvider off it stops and becomes a normal scroll region.
Decorative by default — pass a label only when the row conveys meaning.

examples.label: Logo row
examples.code: {logos.map((l) => )}

examples.label: Reverse, faster
examples.code: <Marquee direction="right" speed={70}>{tags.map((t) => <Badge key={t} appearance="outline">{t}</Badge>)}</Marquee>

examples.label: Vertical
examples.code: <Marquee direction="up" className="h-64">{items}</Marquee>

components.name: MediaImage
components.summary: An image that fills its box and falls back to GradientArt seeded by the item when it has no source or the source fails — Avatar's image-load tracking, for covers, thumbnails and product shots instead of faces.

usage.description: Use MediaImage wherever content imagery may be missing or broken: a cover in a grid, a thumbnail in a row, a product shot. It fills the box it is given — an AspectBox for a cover, a sized and rounded box for a thumbnail — shows a quiet muted surface while the image loads, fades the image in once decoded, and paints GradientArt seeded by the item when there is no image to show, so a grid of missing covers still reads as distinct things. For a person use Avatar; for a whole tile with title and actions use MediaTile, which composes this.

bestPractices.description: Give the box the shape: `<AspectBox ratio={1} className="rounded-md"><MediaImage … /></AspectBox>`, or `size-14 rounded-md` on MediaImage itself for a thumbnail. It clips to whatever radius the box has.
Pass `seed` (the title or an id) when `alt` is empty, so the fallback art is the item's own and stays the same in every list it appears in.

Leave `alt` empty when a visible title sits next to the image — a tile, a row — and describe it when the image stands alone. A set `alt` also names the fallback, so the description survives a broken URL.
Set `position` when a cover crop would cut off the subject — a face high in a portrait, a product at one edge. Store the focus with the image (`"35% 50%"`) rather than re-cropping the file.
Do not hand-write ` setBroken(true)}>`. An image that fails before hydration never fires the handler on a prerendered page; MediaImage preloads off the DOM and catches it.
Do not use it for profile pictures. A person is a circle with initials — Avatar, whose `variant="art"` is the same fallback with the person's initials over it.

props.name: src
props.description: Image URL. Omitted, empty or failing to load ⇒ the fallback shows.

props.name: alt
props.description: Alt text. Empty is decorative — right beside a visible title. When set and no image shows, it names the fallback instead.

props.name: seed
props.description: Seeds the fallback art. Defaults to `alt`; pass the title or an id when `alt` is empty.

props.name: fallback
props.description: Replaces the GradientArt fallback — a glyph or monogram. Fills the frame under the same clipping.

props.name: fit
props.description: `cover` crops to fill (artwork, photos); `contain` letterboxes on the muted surface (a logo, a product that must not be cropped).

props.name: position
props.description: Where the image sits in its frame — CSS `object-position`, the sibling of `fit`. Under `cover` it is the part the crop keeps (`"50% 30%"` for a face, `"bottom"` for a horizon); under `contain` it is the side the letterbox gives way to.

props.name: srcSet
props.description: Responsive sources, passed to the ``.

props.name: sizes
props.description: The `sizes` attribute for `srcSet`.

props.name: loading
props.description: Native lazy loading. Use `eager` for the first row of a grid above the fold.

props.name: className
props.description: Sizing and rounding when MediaImage is the box itself (`size-14 rounded-md`). Inside an AspectBox it already fills.

motion.why: The image fades in over the muted surface once it has decoded, so a slow cover settles in instead of popping row by row as the grid loads.
Imagery, not a control. The tile or row around it answers the pointer.
Its only state change is loading → loaded or failed, which the arrival covers.
A loading image rests on a static muted surface; a shimmer per cover across a long grid would be noise.

a11y: `alt` defaults to empty (decorative), because the usual neighbour is a visible title that already names the item; describe the image when it stands alone.
When no image is on screen and `alt` is set, the frame takes `role="img"` with that label, so a broken URL does not erase the description. The fallback art itself is always aria-hidden.
The `` mounts only once it has loaded, so assistive technology never meets a broken-image icon.

examples.label: Cover with fallback
examples.code:
<AspectBox ratio={1} className="rounded-md">
	<MediaImage src={album.cover} seed={album.title} />
</AspectBox>

examples.label: No image yet
examples.code:
<AspectBox ratio={1} className="rounded-md">
	<MediaImage seed="Low tide, high noon" />
</AspectBox>

examples.label: Row thumbnail
examples.code: <MediaImage src={track.art} seed={track.title} className="size-12 shrink-0 rounded-sm" />

examples.label: Logo, never cropped
examples.code:
<AspectBox ratio={16 / 9} className="rounded-lg">
	<MediaImage src={brand.logo} alt={brand.name} fit="contain" />
</AspectBox>

examples.label: Crop focus per image
examples.code:
<AspectBox ratio={1} className="rounded-md">
	<MediaImage src={project.thumbnail} seed={project.title} position={project.focus ?? "center"} />
</AspectBox>

components.name: MediaTile
components.composition: AspectBox, MediaImage, a stretched link (or Card render), Badge appearance="overlay", Button
components.summary: A cover-first tile — square, 16:9 or poster artwork with an optional play-style action over it, then a title and a subtitle that can each be links — that is one link as a whole without nesting its other controls inside one.

usage.description: The item in a media grid or shelf: an album, a playlist, a video, a podcast, a film, a photo, a product. The cover leads and carries the weight; the title and subtitle sit underneath without a card around them. The whole tile follows the title's link, the subtitle can link somewhere else (the artist, the channel), and an action — usually play — floats over the cover's corner, revealed on hover and focus and always shown on touch. A missing or broken cover becomes GradientArt seeded by the title, so a grid of items without artwork still reads as distinct things.

bestPractices.description: Lay tiles out with `Grid` (`<Grid minItemWidth="10rem">`) or a horizontal `Scroller` for a shelf. The tile fills its cell; the grid decides the width.

Pass `render={<Link to="…" />}` (or `href`) for where the tile goes, and `subtitleRender` / `subtitleHref` for a second destination. Each stays a separate control; never wrap the tile in your own link.
Name the action for its item — `aria-label="Play Low tide, high noon"`, not "Play". A grid of twenty identical "Play" buttons is unusable from a screen reader's list of controls.
Use `titleAs="h3"` when the tiles sit under a section heading, so screen-reader users can move tile to tile by heading.
Do not build this from `Card render={<Link />}`. A card that is a link cannot hold a second link or a button — interactive content cannot nest — which is exactly what a media tile needs.

Do not put more than one action on the cover. A second control over the art is a toolbar on a thumbnail; move secondary actions (add to queue, share) into an OverflowMenu in the action slot or onto the item's page.
Do not use it for a framed commerce card with a price and a buy button — that is ProductCardBlock — or for a person, which is an Avatar.

anatomy.name: Cover
anatomy.description: An AspectBox holding MediaImage: the image, or GradientArt seeded by the title. Drawn first, read last.

anatomy.name: Title
anatomy.description: The item's name. When the tile links, this is the link, stretched over the whole tile.

anatomy.name: Subtitle
anatomy.description: The second line. Optionally its own link, raised above the stretched one.

anatomy.name: Action
anatomy.description: One control over the cover's bottom-end corner — usually play. Revealed on hover and focus; always visible on touch.

anatomy.name: Badge
anatomy.description: A static label over the cover's top-start corner — a duration, "New". Click-through.

props.name: title
props.description: The item's name. Seeds the fallback art when it is a string.

props.name: subtitle
props.description: The second line — an artist, a channel, a year.

props.name: meta
props.description: Lines under the subtitle, in its muted type: a price beside its sale price, a count of finishes, a status Badge. A wrapping block, where the subtitle is one truncated line. Use it for a product tile instead of building one.

props.name: src
props.description: Cover image URL. Without one, or when it fails, the cover is GradientArt seeded by the item.

props.name: srcSet
props.description: Responsive cover candidates, passed to the ``.

props.name: sizes
props.description: The cover's layout width for `srcSet`, e.g. `"(min-width: 64rem) 25vw, 50vw"`.

props.name: alt
props.description: Cover alt text. Empty by default: the title below already names the item.

props.name: seed
props.description: Seeds the fallback art. Defaults to `title` when it is a string.

props.name: position
props.description: Which part of the cover the crop keeps — CSS `object-position`, forwarded to the cover's MediaImage: `"50% 30%"` for a face, `"top"` for a poster's title. Store it with the image when each one frames differently.

props.name: aspect
props.description: The cover's shape: square (albums, podcasts), video (16:9), poster (2:3 — films, books), or any width / height ratio.

props.name: size
props.description: Moves the type tier, the cover-to-text gap, the corner and the overlay inset together.

props.name: href
props.description: Where the tile goes. The title becomes the link, stretched over the whole tile.

props.name: render
props.description: The title link's element, for a router: `render={<Link to="/albums/1" />}`. Takes precedence over `href`.

props.name: subtitleHref
props.description: Makes the subtitle its own link — a separate tab stop above the tile's.

props.name: subtitleRender
props.description: The subtitle link's element, for a router.

props.name: action
props.description: One control over the cover's bottom-end corner, usually a play Button. Hidden until hover or focus on hover-capable devices; always shown on touch.

props.name: badge
props.description: A static label on the cover's top-start corner — `<Badge appearance="overlay">`.

props.name: titleAs
props.description: The title's element. A heading one level below the section's lets screen-reader users move tile to tile.

props.name: loading
props.description: Native image loading. `eager` for the first row above the fold.

props.name: ...div props
props.description: Spread onto the root.

motion.why: The cover image fades in over a quiet surface once it decodes, so a grid loading on a slow connection settles tile by tile instead of popping.
Hovering the tile deepens the cover with a light scrim and lifts the action in (`reveal-on-hover`), so it is clear the whole tile is one target and where its action is.
A tile has no states of its own to move between; the action carries any (play / pause).
Nothing runs inside a tile; a now-playing indicator belongs to the player, not the grid.

a11y: No nested interactive content: the title is the tile's link, and its `stretched-link` overlay covers the tile, while the subtitle link and the action sit above it as separate controls.
Tab order is title → subtitle → action. The text comes first in the DOM and the cover is drawn above it with CSS `order`, so focus follows how a reader names the item.
Focusing the title link rings the whole tile, rounded like the cover, because the whole tile is what the link is; the subtitle link and the action ring themselves.

The action is hidden with opacity only, and only where the device can hover; it stays in the tab order and the accessibility tree, appears when anything in the tile has focus, and is always visible on touch.
The cover is decorative by default (`alt=""`), since the title names the item; the fallback art is aria-hidden.
Truncated titles keep their full text in the link's accessible name and in a `title` tooltip.

components.name: Menu
components.summary: Dropdown menu over Base UI Menu — roving focus, typeahead, ARIA menu/menuitem wiring, collision-aware positioning, Esc/outside dismissal. Trigger + portal-rendered popup with items, groups, and separators.

usage.description: Use Menu for a compact list of actions opened from a visible trigger.

bestPractices.description: Use it for secondary or grouped commands that do not need to be visible all the time.
Keep item labels action-oriented and easy to scan.
Do not use Menu for complex forms, persistent navigation, or arbitrary rich content.

Show a command's keyboard shortcut with `shortcut` on the row (`<MenuItem shortcut="Ctrl S">Save</MenuItem>`), not a span you push right yourself: the column stays aligned and muted under the highlight. A menu is where people learn the keys.
Do not build a Select out of it. A menu fires actions and has no value; a Select holds one and reports changes. Swapping them loses form semantics and keyboard type-ahead.

Inside a <Workspace> a Menu adapts automatically — its popup re-applies the compact density across the portal, so items render on the chrome type tier and the control ladder resolves to workspace sizes. Do NOT override the size per call site; that was necessary before v0.41 and is now drift.

anatomy.name: MenuTrigger
anatomy.description: The control that opens the menu.

anatomy.name: MenuContent
anatomy.description: The floating command surface.

anatomy.name: MenuItem
anatomy.description: One selectable command.

anatomy.name: MenuSeparator
anatomy.description: A divider between groups.

anatomy.name: MenuGroup
anatomy.description: A grouped set of menu items.

anatomy.name: MenuGroupLabel
anatomy.description: A label for a group of items.

props.name: Menu (Root)
props.type: Base UI Menu.Root props (open, defaultOpen, onOpenChange, modal, orientation, loopFocus)
props.description: Groups all parts and controls open state. Uncontrolled by default.

subcomponents.name: MenuTrigger
subcomponents.description: The button that opens the menu. Compose with render={<Button … />}.

subcomponents.name: MenuContent
subcomponents.type: Base UI Popup props + side: 'top' | 'right' | 'bottom' | 'left' + align: 'start' | 'center' | 'end' + sideOffset: number + className
subcomponents.description: Portal + Positioner + Popup. side picks which side of the trigger the popup renders against (auto-flips on collision; defaults to 'bottom'); align sets alignment along that side (defaults to 'start'); sideOffset is the gap in px between trigger and popup (defaults to 6).

subcomponents.name: MenuItem
subcomponents.type: Base UI Menu.Item props + className (disabled, closeOnClick, onClick) + variant?: "default" | "destructive" + icon?: ReactNode + description?: ReactNode + shortcut?: ReactNode
subcomponents.description: An interactive row. Highlights via data-[highlighted]; dims via data-[disabled]. variant="destructive" for a delete or irreversible action: it keeps the destructive ink when highlighted (never className="text-destructive", which the highlight repaints). `icon` leads the row; `description` adds a quieter second line saying what the action does, and the icon then sits in a small tile spanning both lines. `shortcut` ends the row with the key that runs the action from outside the menu ("Ctrl S", or ghost Kbd caps), muted and end-aligned so a column of them lines up; it is display only, so bind the key yourself.

subcomponents.name: MenuLinkItem
subcomponents.type: Base UI Menu.LinkItem props (href, target, closeOnClick) + className + icon?: ReactNode + description?: ReactNode
subcomponents.description: A row that navigates: a real <a>, so it opens in a new tab, middle-clicks and copies as a link. With target="_blank" it adds rel="noopener noreferrer" and a trailing ↗. Takes icon and description like MenuItem.

subcomponents.name: MenuSeparator
subcomponents.description: Hairline rule between item runs.

subcomponents.name: MenuSubmenu
subcomponents.description: A nested menu. Wraps a MenuSubmenuTrigger and its own MenuContent — pass side="inline-end" to that content so the submenu opens away from its parent in RTL as well as LTR.

subcomponents.name: MenuSubmenuTrigger
subcomponents.type: Base UI Menu.SubmenuTrigger props + value: ReactNode + icon: ReactNode + className
subcomponents.description: The row that opens a submenu: item styling, a trailing chevron, and an optional `value` showing the current choice so the row reads "Effort  High ›" rather than making the reader open it to find out. `icon` leads the row as MenuItem's does; give it one whenever the items around it have icons, or its label starts a column to their left.

subcomponents.name: MenuRadioGroup
subcomponents.type: Base UI Menu.RadioGroup props (value, defaultValue, onValueChange)
subcomponents.description: A single-choice group inside a menu. Controlled via value/onValueChange, uncontrolled via defaultValue.

subcomponents.name: MenuRadioItem
subcomponents.type: Base UI Menu.RadioItem props + className (value, disabled)
subcomponents.description: One option in a MenuRadioGroup, rendered as menuitemradio with a real checked state. The check sits in a reserved leading column so labels never shift sideways as the highlight moves.

subcomponents.name: MenuCheckboxItem
subcomponents.type: Base UI Menu.CheckboxItem props + className + shortcut?: ReactNode + { checked?: boolean; defaultChecked?: boolean; onCheckedChange?: (checked: boolean) => void; disabled?: boolean }
subcomponents.description: A toggling row, with the same reserved leading column as MenuRadioItem so a menu mixing the two keeps one text margin. Takes `shortcut` like MenuItem (View → Show ruler  Ctrl R).

subcomponents.name: MenuGroup
subcomponents.description: Groups related items; pair with MenuGroupLabel for an accessible group name.

subcomponents.name: MenuGroupLabel
subcomponents.description: The label for a MenuGroup — auto-associated with the group for screen readers.

a11y: Base UI provides role=menu/menuitem, roving tabindex, arrow-key navigation, and typeahead.
Esc and outside-press dismiss; focus returns to the trigger on close.
Animate open/close via data-[starting-style]/data-[ending-style] attributes.
MenuGroupLabel is auto-associated with its MenuGroup for screen readers.

A disabled MenuItem stays in the arrow-key order — Base UI keeps it focusable with aria-disabled so screen-reader users learn the command exists — but it cannot be activated, and it ignores the pointer.

components.name: Menubar
components.summary: An application's row of menus — File, Edit, View — over Base UI's Menubar. Each menu is an ordinary Sable Menu with a MenubarTrigger as its title; the bar joins them into one tab stop with ←/→ between titles, and once one menu is open, pointing at a neighbour opens it.

usage.description: Use Menubar for a tool or editor whose commands are too many for a toolbar and belong under named menus (File, Edit, View, Help). Use Toolbar for a row of direct actions, a single Menu or OverflowMenu for one set of options, and NavigationMenu-style links for site navigation.

bestPractices.description: Compose each menu from the Menu parts: `<Menu><MenubarTrigger>File</MenubarTrigger><MenuContent>…</MenuContent></Menu>`. Rows, groups, submenus, checkbox and radio items are the same parts a lone Menu uses.
Name the bar with aria-label ("Editor") so it is announced as the application's menus, not a list of buttons.
Keep titles to one short word each. A reader scans a menubar left to right; a phrase in the bar is a toolbar button.

Do not use MenubarTrigger outside a Menubar, or a plain MenuTrigger inside one. The bar's arrow keys and hover-to-switch work on the triggers it owns; a Button trigger in the bar looks like a menu title and behaves like a stray button.
Do not use a menubar for site navigation. Its items are commands in menus (role=menuitem), not links between pages.

anatomy.name: Menubar
anatomy.description: The bar: role=menubar, one tab stop, arrow keys between titles.

anatomy.name: Menu
anatomy.description: One per title; the ordinary Menu root.

anatomy.name: MenubarTrigger
anatomy.description: The title in the bar that opens its menu.

anatomy.name: MenuContent
anatomy.description: The menu's popup, with MenuItem / MenuSubmenu / MenuCheckboxItem rows inside.

props.name: orientation
props.description: The bar's axis. Arrow keys follow it: ←/→ along a horizontal bar, ↑/↓ down a vertical one.

props.name: loopFocus
props.description: Wrap from the last title back to the first with the arrow keys.

props.name: modal
props.description: While a menu is open, block pointer interaction outside it and lock page scroll, like a lone Menu.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disable every menu in the bar.

props.name: className
props.description: Layout classes for the bar. Titles take their look from MenubarTrigger.

subcomponents.name: MenubarTrigger
subcomponents.description: A menu's title in the bar. A small ghost Button in the control type tier, held in the accent wash while its menu is open (`sable-open:`), so the reader sees which title the popup belongs to.

a11y: Base UI renders role="menubar" with aria-orientation; each title is a menuitem with aria-haspopup and aria-expanded.
The bar is one tab stop. ←/→ move between titles (↑/↓ when vertical), ↓ or Enter opens a menu and moves into it, and Esc closes it and returns focus to its title.
With one menu open, pointing at another title opens that menu instead, so a reader can sweep across the bar, as in a desktop application.
Name the bar with aria-label; titles are their own text.

components.name: Message
components.summary: One row in a conversation: avatar gutter, side, and stacked header / content / footer. Layout only — the surface is Bubble, passed as children.

usage.description: The row a single turn occupies. It owns the geometry — which side, the avatar gutter, where the name and timestamp go, where reactions and receipts go — and nothing about how the content looks. That separation is the point: an assistant's markdown answer, a one-line reply, an attachment, and a tool-call card are all the same row with different children.

bestPractices.description: Set `messageId`. It is what MessageScroller reads for `scrollToMessage`, `initialScroll`, and visibility tracking — a message without one cannot be jumped to or marked as read.
Pass the same `align` to Message and to the Bubble inside it, so the flattened tail corner lands on the speaker's side.

Use `grouped` for consecutive messages from one author. It tightens the spacing and hides the avatar while keeping its column reserved, so the run reads as one block instead of stepping left. Pass `tail={false}` to the Bubble in each continuation too, so only the first message in the run carries a tail.
Match `avatarSize` to the `size` of the Avatar you pass (sm/md/lg line up 1:1). The gutter is declared, not measured, because it has to hold its width when `grouped` hides the avatar.
Do not justify the content to move a message to the right. `align="end"` already mirrors the whole row, gutter included; adding your own justification fights it.
Do not put the timestamp inside the Bubble. It belongs in `header` or `footer`, which stay outside the surface so `variant="plain"` content still has one.
Do not reach for Message to lay out a system note or a date break. That is `Marker`, which is deliberately quieter than the message tier.

anatomy.name: Avatar gutter
anatomy.description: Fixed-width column for the author's Avatar. Kept (but emptied) when `grouped`, which is what keeps a run aligned.

anatomy.name: Header
anatomy.description: Author name and timestamp, above the content.

anatomy.name: Content
anatomy.description: The children — usually a Bubble, but equally an Attachment, a tool card, or plain rendered markdown.

anatomy.name: Footer
anatomy.description: Reactions, delivery receipts, retry actions.

props.name: messageId
props.description: Stable id, published as `data-message-id`. The handle MessageScroller uses for scroll commands and visibility tracking.

props.name: align
props.description: Which side of the conversation. "start" is the other party or the assistant; "end" is the person reading. Mirrors the whole row, gutter included.

props.name: avatar
props.description: Avatar node for the gutter. Omit for a message with no author identity.

props.name: avatarSize
props.description: Gutter width, matching Avatar's own size scale 1:1 (32 / 40 / 48px). Declared rather than measured so it survives `grouped`.

props.name: header
props.description: Author name, timestamp — anything above the content.

props.name: footer
props.description: Reactions, receipts, retry actions — anything below the content.

props.name: grouped
props.description: This message continues a run from the same author: tightens the spacing (via `--message-gap`) and drops the avatar while reserving its column.

props.name: ...div props
props.description: Spread onto the row. Use `messageId` rather than `id` — the scroller matches on `data-message-id`.

a11y: A plain container with no imposed role — the conversation's semantics belong to the list or log element you wrap it in, not to each row.
`align` reverses the visual row without reordering the DOM, so reading order in assistive tech stays chronological regardless of which side a message is on.
The header and footer render at the secondary type step in muted ink, keeping both below the message tier in the visual hierarchy without dropping either below the AA contrast floor.

components.name: MessageScroller
components.summary: Scroll container for a conversation. Auto-follows new messages until the reader scrolls away, holds position when older history is prepended, and exposes scroll commands and visibility tracking through its ref.

usage.description: The scroll region a conversation lives in. It owns the scrolling and nothing else — not your messages, not your AI state, not your transport or persistence — so you bring the content renderer and it handles the behaviors that make streaming chat feel right: pinning to the newest message, releasing when the reader scrolls up, keeping the view still when older history loads above, jumping to a specific message, restoring a saved read position, and reporting what is actually on screen.

bestPractices.description: Building a whole chat? `sable docs building-a-chat` covers what the scroller does during a stream, what the app owns, and the failure states around it.

Bound it the way you would bound any scroll box — `flex-1 min-h-0` inside a flex column, or `max-h-96`. `className` lands on the element that actually scrolls, so the obvious bound is the correct one (same contract as Scroller).
Give every Message a `messageId`. It is the handle for `scrollToMessage`, `initialScroll`, and `onVisibleMessagesChange` — a message without one is invisible to all three.

Prepend older history directly into `children` when the reader reaches the top. The scroller anchors on the first rendered message and re-adds the height that appeared above it, so the view does not jump.
Set the rhythm between messages with the `gap` prop, not with a flex class on `className` — the messages are laid out in a column inside the scroll region, not directly on it.
Restore a reopened thread with `initialScroll={{ messageId: lastRead }}` instead of dropping the reader at the bottom of a conversation they have not finished.

Wrap a docked agent panel in `<Density value="compact">`. The scroller tightens its rhythm and every message inside it drops to the workspace type tier — one attribute for the whole conversation, no per-component sizing.
Do not call `scrollToBottom` on every incoming token. Auto-follow already does it, and doing it yourself fights the reader who scrolled up to read something.
Do not expect `ref` to be the DOM node — it is a command handle (`scrollToBottom`, `scrollToMessage`, `isFollowing`). Reach for `ref.current.element` when you genuinely need the element.

Do not wrap it in a positioned div to place a jump-to-latest button. It ships one, stuck to the bottom edge from inside the scroll region, which is why `className` gets to stay on the scrolling element.
Do not use it for an ordinary long list. That is `Scroller` — this one's follow-the-bottom behavior is wrong for content the reader is browsing rather than receiving.

anatomy.name: Scroll region
anatomy.description: The element that scrolls. Carries `className`: sizing, padding, and background.

anatomy.name: Message column
anatomy.description: The flex column holding the children, spaced by `gap`. Publishes `--message-gap` so `<Message grouped>` can close it.

anatomy.name: Jump to latest
anatomy.description: A control stuck to the bottom edge, shown only while the reader is scrolled away from the newest message.

props.name: ref
props.description: Imperative commands, not the DOM node: `scrollToBottom(opts)`, `scrollToTop(opts)`, `scrollToMessage(id, opts)` (returns false when the message is not rendered), `isFollowing()`, and `element` for the scrolling node itself. `opts` is `ScrollCommandOptions`: `{ animate?: boolean }` (default true, and off whenever motion is), not the DOM's `behavior`.

props.name: autoFollow
props.description: Keep the newest message in view as content arrives, until the reader scrolls away from the bottom. Set false for a transcript that must never move under the reader.

props.name: followThreshold
props.description: Distance from the bottom, in px, that still counts as following. A band rather than a pixel, so a token arriving mid-frame does not flicker the state.

props.name: onFollowChange
props.description: Notified when the viewport pins to, or releases from, the newest message.

props.name: initialScroll
props.description: Where a freshly mounted thread lands. Pass a messageId to restore a saved read position. Applied once, on mount — changing it later will not yank a reader mid-conversation.

props.name: jumpToLatest
props.description: Show the jump-to-latest control while the reader is scrolled away from the newest message.

props.name: jumpToLatestLabel
props.description: Accessible label and tooltip for that control.

props.name: gap
props.description: Vertical rhythm between messages. Also published as `--message-gap`, which `<Message grouped>` reads to collapse the gap within a run.

props.name: onVisibleMessagesChange
props.description: Ids of the messages currently intersecting the viewport, in DOM order. The hook for read receipts, mark-as-seen, and unread counters.

props.name: ...div props
props.description: Spread onto the scrolling element. `className` bounds and pads the scroll region; `onScroll` composes with the component's own.

a11y: Native overflow, so keyboard scrolling (arrows, Page Up/Down, Home/End) and the OS scrollbar work unchanged; the scrollbar is styled thin, not replaced.
Overscroll is contained, so a wheel gesture that runs out of conversation does not start scrolling the page behind it.
The jump-to-latest control is a real button with an accessible label, reachable by keyboard, and only present when there is somewhere to jump to.
Smooth scrolling is used only when motion is enabled — `prefers-reduced-motion` and <MotionProvider> off both collapse every scroll command to an instant jump.

components.name: Meter
components.summary: A role=meter reading over Base UI Meter, drawn as a bar or a ring — how full something is within a known range (storage, quota, strength), with a tone for good/caution/bad. Not task progress.

usage.description: Use Meter to show a static measurement against a known maximum — storage used, seats taken, API quota, password strength. It is announced as a meter, not a progress bar, so a screen-reader user hears a level rather than a task underway.

bestPractices.description: Label it and show the reading in units people use ("7.2 of 10 GB"), with MeterLabel and MeterValue. The bar shows proportion; the number is what gets acted on.
Pick `tone` from thresholds you own and apply them consistently across the page — warning near the limit, destructive at or over it. The component does not guess where good becomes bad.
Do not use Meter for a task in flight — an upload, an install, a step count. That is Progress; Meter tells assistive tech nothing is happening.
Do not use it for a value without a meaningful maximum (followers, total spend). A bar implies a full scale; an unbounded count is a stat.
Use shape="ring" when the reading is a score that belongs in a small, glanceable spot on a card. It is the same measurement drawn as a circular gauge, not a different component.

Use `segments` (a tick bar, ▮▮▮▮▮▮▯▯▯▯) for a discrete budget, score or quota read at a glance — a spend limit, credits left, an ICP lead score, months of data coverage. Pick a count that matches the unit when there is one (10 for a score out of 10, 12 for months) and otherwise size it to the track: a tick reads as a tick when it is taller than it is wide, about one per 8px of track (40 across a card row, 20 in a narrow table cell). Any reading above min shows at least one tick.

Do not segment a fine-grained continuous value where the exact proportion matters (disk at 73.4%) — ticks round it to the nearest mark; use the continuous bar. And do not use a tick bar for a task in flight or steps completed: that is Progress, or a Stepper for named steps.

anatomy.name: MeterTrack
anatomy.description: The rail that represents the full range.

anatomy.name: MeterIndicator
anatomy.description: The fill, sized from value and coloured by tone. Not used with `segments`: the track draws its ticks instead.

anatomy.name: MeterLabel
anatomy.description: The visible name; also names the meter for assistive tech.

anatomy.name: MeterValue
anatomy.description: The formatted reading.

props.name: value
props.description: The current reading, between min and max. Required.

props.name: min
props.description: The bottom of the range.

props.name: max
props.description: The top of the range.

props.name: tone
props.description: Fill colour, mapped to a semantic token. Choose it from your own thresholds.

props.name: shape
props.description: bar is a horizontal track; ring is a circular gauge for a small, glanceable reading — the same value, min, max and tones.

props.name: size
props.description: Ring diameter (40 / 64 / 96px at the default spacing; the centre value steps with it), or bar thickness on the same sm / md / lg rails as Progress.

props.name: showValue
props.description: Print the value in the ring's centre (formatted like MeterValue).

props.name: segments
props.description: Draw the bar as this many separate ticks instead of a continuous fill (a quota, score or spend limit). Filled ticks = round(share × N), at least one for any reading above min, none at min. Ticks take the tone; empty ones sit on the rail colour. The segmented track has its own, taller sm / md / lg ladder. Bar only: ignored for shape="ring".

props.name: strokeWidth
props.description: Ring stroke width, in viewBox units of 100.

props.name: format
props.description: Formatting for MeterValue and aria-valuetext (percent, unit, currency).

props.name: getAriaValueText
props.description: Human-readable reading for assistive tech ("7.2 of 10 gigabytes used").

props.name: locale
props.description: Locale for formatting. Defaults to the runtime locale.

subcomponents.name: MeterTrack
subcomponents.type: Base UI Track props + className + size
subcomponents.description: The rail. Rendered automatically when Meter has no children; renders a MeterIndicator by default — or, when the Meter has `segments`, its row of ticks (children are not rendered then).

subcomponents.name: MeterIndicator
subcomponents.type: Base UI Indicator props + className + tone
subcomponents.description: The fill. Inherits the Meter's tone unless given its own.

subcomponents.name: MeterLabel
subcomponents.description: Visible label; wires aria-labelledby on the root.

subcomponents.name: MeterValue
subcomponents.description: Formatted reading. Accepts a `(formatted, value) => ReactNode` child.

motion.why: A meter is a reading, present with the page that reports it. Animating the fill up from zero on load would act out a change that did not happen.
It reports and accepts no input. A bar that reacted to the pointer would read as a Slider the user could drag.

Width and colour ease on the motion tokens (no recipe animates width) when the reading changes — freeing space after a delete visibly shrinks the bar, so the user sees the cause and effect rather than a different bar.

With segments, the fill runs through the ticks from the edge it is leaving — left to right as it grows, right to left as it shrinks — each tick easing its colour on the fast token after a stagger that is a share of the slow token (a full sweep is one slow duration) × --motion-expressive. Every tick switching at once would read as a different bar, not the same budget moving; `subtle` lands them together and off is instant.
A meter has no indeterminate state; a reading is either known or not shown. Unknown-but-working is Progress with no value.

a11y: Base UI renders role=meter with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and aria-valuetext — distinct from Progress's role=progressbar.
Name it with MeterLabel or aria-label; an unnamed meter is announced as a bare number.
Tone is colour only. Say the state in text too ("Almost full") when it matters, and use getAriaValueText to give units.

components.name: MiddleTruncate
components.summary: Middle-truncates a long string (hash, address, signature) to `5J7s…8xQp`, keeping the start and end legible while preserving the full value on hover.

usage.description: Use MiddleTruncate when both the beginning and end of a long identifier must remain visible.

bestPractices.description: Use it for hashes, addresses, long filenames, URLs, or generated IDs.
Provide the full value through title text, copy action, or surrounding detail when needed.
Do not use MiddleTruncate for human prose where the middle words carry meaning.

Do not middle-truncate a value with no way to obtain it in full. Truncation removes characters from the page, so the value needs a copy affordance beside it: an icon Button with useCopy, as in the Copyable value example.

props.name: text
props.description: The full string to render. When it is truncated, the full value is also set as the title attribute (a pointer tooltip).

props.name: startChars
props.description: How many leading characters to keep before the ellipsis.

props.name: endChars
props.description: How many trailing characters to keep after the ellipsis.

a11y: When truncated, the visible abbreviation is aria-hidden and a visually hidden copy carries the full value, so screen readers announce the whole string. The title attribute holds it too, for a pointer tooltip only.
Renders the string verbatim when it is too short to benefit from truncation, so no value is hidden needlessly.

components.name: NavigationMenu
components.summary: A site header's primary nav over Base UI NavigationMenu: a bar of links and triggers, where a trigger opens a panel of links on hover, click or Enter. One shared panel glides between triggers and resizes to each one's content. Links take any router's link through `render` and mark the current page with `active`.

usage.description: Use NavigationMenu for a marketing or docs site's header: a few top-level destinations, some of which open a panel of related pages. Use Menu for actions rather than destinations, Tabs to switch views inside a page, Sidebar or SideNav for an app's persistent navigation, and AppHeader for an app's mobile top bar.

bestPractices.description: Keep the bar to a handful of entries. A trigger groups related pages; a destination with nothing beneath it is a plain NavigationMenuLink in its own item.

Give panel links a `description` when titles alone are ambiguous ("Sync" → "Offline first, conflict free"), and lay the Content out with layout classes (`grid w-[30rem] grid-cols-2`); the shared panel sizes itself to it.

Pass your router's link through `render` (`<NavigationMenuLink render={<Link to="/pricing" />}>`) and set `active` on the current page's link, so the bar shows where the reader is and announces it as `aria-current="page"`.

Below `md`, hide the bar and offer the same destinations in a Sheet opened from a menu Button: SheetContent side="left" holding a SideNav, its groups mirroring the panels. A hover panel has nothing to hover on a phone, and a bar of five entries does not fit one.
Do not put actions in it (Sign in, New project). Those are Buttons beside the nav; the nav holds places to go.
Do not assemble the panel yourself. The root renders the one Portal, Positioner, Popup and Viewport every trigger shares; a second one breaks the glide between triggers.

anatomy.name: NavigationMenu
anatomy.description: The `<nav>` root; also renders the shared floating panel.

anatomy.name: NavigationMenuList
anatomy.description: The bar: a `<ul>` the arrow keys rove across.

anatomy.name: NavigationMenuItem
anatomy.description: One `<li>`: a link, or a trigger with its content.

anatomy.name: NavigationMenuTrigger
anatomy.description: Opens its item's content; carries a chevron.

anatomy.name: NavigationMenuContent
anatomy.description: The links a trigger reveals, rendered into the shared panel.

anatomy.name: NavigationMenuLink
anatomy.description: A destination: a bar entry in an item, a two-line row in content.

props.name: NavigationMenu (Root)
props.type: Base UI NavigationMenu.Root props (value, defaultValue, onValueChange, delay, closeDelay, orientation) + className
props.description: The `<nav>`. `value` is the open item's value (null when closed); `delay` / `closeDelay` tune hover-to-open.

props.name: align
props.description: Alignment of the shared panel along its trigger.

props.name: sideOffset
props.description: Gap between the bar and the panel, in px. The pointer crosses it on a bridge, so the panel does not close on the way in.

subcomponents.name: NavigationMenuList
subcomponents.description: The bar of items, a `<ul>`. Arrow keys move between entries.

subcomponents.name: NavigationMenuItem
subcomponents.type: Base UI NavigationMenu.Item props + className + value?: string
subcomponents.description: One `<li>` holding either a NavigationMenuLink or a NavigationMenuTrigger with its NavigationMenuContent.

subcomponents.name: NavigationMenuTrigger
subcomponents.description: Opens its item's content on hover, click or Enter, with a chevron that turns while open. Styled like the bar's links: muted at rest, full ink when hovered or open.

subcomponents.name: NavigationMenuContent
subcomponents.type: Base UI NavigationMenu.Content props + className + keepMounted?: boolean
subcomponents.description: The item's panel content. Size and lay it out with layout classes; the shared panel follows its size and slides it in from the side it was reached from.

subcomponents.name: NavigationMenuLink
subcomponents.type: Base UI NavigationMenu.Link props + className + href?: string + active?: boolean + closeOnClick?: boolean + render?: ReactElement + description?: ReactNode
subcomponents.description: A destination. In an item it is a bar entry; in content it is a row with an optional `description` line. `active` sets `aria-current="page"`; `render={<Link to="…" />}` keeps the roving focus on your router's link.

motion.why: The panel fades and scales in from its trigger like a popover, but it also resizes as the reader moves between triggers, which motion-pop cannot express: Base UI measures each content into --popup-width/--popup-height and the popup transitions to them on the motion tokens.

Moving from one trigger to the next keeps one panel open: it glides along the bar and the new content slides in from the direction of travel, so the reader sees one surface changing rather than two popups swapping. Snaps on first open and on resize (data-instant), where a glide would mean nothing.
Bar entries and panel rows fill on hover and focus like the other interactive surfaces, so the bar reads as live before anything opens.
Nothing in a nav moves on its own.

a11y: The root is a <nav>; give it an aria-label when the page has more than one nav ("Main").
Arrow keys move across the bar; Enter, Space or ArrowDown opens a trigger's content and moves focus into it; Esc closes and returns focus to the trigger.
A trigger is a button with aria-expanded; its content is reachable by Tab in reading order once open.
`active` on a link sets aria-current="page" and gives it full ink, so the current page is announced as well as shown.
Panel motion runs on the motion tokens, so reduced motion (or MotionProvider "reduced") collapses the glide and resize to instant.

examples.code:
<NavigationMenu aria-label="Main">
	<NavigationMenuList>
		<NavigationMenuItem>
			<NavigationMenuTrigger>Product</NavigationMenuTrigger>
			<NavigationMenuContent className="grid w-[30rem] grid-cols-2">
				<NavigationMenuLink href="/editor" description="Write and review together.">Editor</NavigationMenuLink>
				<NavigationMenuLink href="/sync" description="Offline first, conflict free.">Sync</NavigationMenuLink>
			</NavigationMenuContent>
		</NavigationMenuItem>
		<NavigationMenuItem>
			<NavigationMenuLink href="/pricing">Pricing</NavigationMenuLink>
		</NavigationMenuItem>
	</NavigationMenuList>
</NavigationMenu>

	<NavigationMenuList>
		<NavigationMenuItem>

		</NavigationMenuItem>

components.name: Note
components.summary: Callout / admonition box. Its tone follows the shared status-tone vocabulary (neutral/info/success/warning/destructive), pairing a soft tone fill with a matching leading icon. Optional title.

usage.description: Use Note for helpful supporting information that should sit near the relevant content — including a caveat or warning attached to a form, a dialog, or a section. It is the in-context callout; Banner is the page-level strip.

bestPractices.description: Use it for tips, caveats, or secondary context that improves understanding.

Reach for Note rather than Banner when the message qualifies something on the page — a warning inside a dialog, a caveat above a submit button. Banner is a full-width announcement strip for page- or app-level state; inside a form it reads as a slab, and its soft fill carries no border or tone-colored icon, so the severity stops being visible.
Keep tone calm and concise so the note does not compete with primary content.

When the reader can resolve the state, pass `action` rather than putting a Button in children. The prop is data — label plus handler — so the callout owns the placement and weight; a Button dropped into children inherits neither, floats in the box's padding, and (in `secondary`) punches a near-background hole in the tone fill.
Do not use Note for state the whole page or app is in (an outage, an offline session, a blocked account) — that is Banner — or for a message tied to one field, which is the field's own error text.
Do not give a Note two actions. One remedy reads as the sentence's next move; two make it a decision point, which is a Dialog's job.
Do not stack several in a row. Three notes together are a wall of asides; if everything is called out, nothing is.

props.name: action
props.type: { label: string; onClick?: () => void; href?: string }
props.description: A single remedy, rendered below the body and aligned to the text column. Deliberately data, not a slot: Note owns the placement, weight, ink and motion, so the action cannot be styled into a button that outweighs the sentence explaining it. Use onClick for an in-place action (renders a button, no glyph) or href for a link (renders an anchor with a trailing chevron) — the chevron means navigate, so it appears only when the action genuinely goes somewhere.

props.name: tone
props.description: Severity tone — drives the border, fill, and leading icon color/name. The shared status-tone vocabulary (STATUS_TONES).

props.name: title
props.description: Optional bold lead-in rendered above the body (text-title-sm).

props.name: icon
props.description: Override the variant glyph: a string swaps the icon name (keeping the tone color), a ReactNode replaces it, null removes it; omit for the variant default.

motion.why: A note is part of the content it annotates and renders with it. A callout that animated in would pull the eye before the reader has reached it in the flow.
The action's focus ring eases in, and its underline thickens on hover. Inside a block of guidance, that is what separates the one thing to do from the prose around it.
A note's action usually navigates or opens something; the small settle on press is the only confirmation before the next surface paints.
A note has no states to move between: its tone is fixed when it renders. A note that changes tone is a new message, and should arrive as one.
Static guidance. Work in progress belongs in a Progress or a Spinner, not in a callout.

a11y: Rendered with role="note" so assistive tech can announce it as an aside.
Color is never the sole signal — the leading icon and optional title reinforce severity.

examples.code: <Note tone="info">Reports refresh every hour.</Note>

components.name: NotificationBadge
components.summary: An unread indicator. Renders a bare dot or a count pill (capped as "{max}+"), or nothing when there's nothing to show. A changing count rolls to its new number, and a badge that appears after being empty pops in. overlay pins it to the corner of a relative host; it is aria-hidden, so the host's name carries the count.

usage.description: Use NotificationBadge to show a compact unread count, alert count, or attention marker.

bestPractices.description: Place it on or near the item that owns the notifications.
Use compact counts and cap large numbers when exact precision is not useful.
Do not use NotificationBadge as a standalone status label or category marker.
Do not show a bare dot when the count is meaningful. A dot says "something"; if the user can act on "how many", show the number.
Do not put a neutral badge on a secondary host. Both are the secondary surface, so the badge disappears; use primary or destructive there.

props.name: dot
props.description: Render a bare dot indicator with no number. Takes precedence over count.

props.name: count
props.description: Unread count. Renders nothing when <= 0 and dot is unset.

props.name: max
props.description: Cap before showing "{max}+".

props.name: tone
props.description: Fill color. destructive for alarming counts; primary/neutral for non-alarming ones.

props.name: size
props.description: Scales the dot/pill on the spacing scale (count pill: sm 16px, md 18px, lg 20px at the default density).

props.name: overlay
props.description: Pin to the top-end corner of the nearest relative host (an icon button) — one placement for every caller instead of hand-tuned absolute offsets.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. Under `subtle` the count updates in place and the badge fades in without the pop.

motion.why: A badge that shows up after being empty is the news — something just arrived — so it fades and scales in where it sits instead of popping into existence. Never on first paint: a badge that mounts with a count is content, and a page of them popping on load is noise.
It is decorative and not interactive; the host it sits on answers the pointer.

The count rolls to its new number through NumberTicker (expressive), so 3 → 4 reads as one more arriving rather than a different badge. Past the cap the ticker holds at max with a static "+", so a count climbing beyond 99 does not keep rolling a badge that has not changed.
An unread count has no working state.

a11y: The badge is aria-hidden: a count rendered on a control is not associated with it, so the host needs an accessible name that includes the count — "Notifications, 3 unread" — or a screen-reader user hears "Notifications, button" and never learns there is anything new. Pass aria-hidden={false} only for a standalone badge whose number is the information.

A dot carries no number and no words: on its own it tells a sighted user only that something changed, and tells everyone else nothing. Pair it with a label that says what is new, and never make its colour the only difference between two states.

examples.label: Dot + counts
examples.code: <Row gap={3}><NotificationBadge dot /><NotificationBadge count={3} /><NotificationBadge count={128} /></Row>

examples.label: Overlay on an icon button
examples.code: <Button variant="secondary" size="icon" aria-label="Notifications, 5 unread" className="relative"><Icon name="bell" /><NotificationBadge count={5} overlay /></Button>

components.name: NumberField
components.summary: Numeric input with decrement/increment steppers over Base UI NumberField — keyboard arrows, scroll, scrub-to-change, min/max clamping, locale formatting, and form integration. Styled like Input; drops straight into a Field.

usage.description: Use NumberField for numeric values that benefit from validation, min/max bounds, or step controls.

bestPractices.description: Use it for quantities, thresholds, percentages, and other real numeric values.
Set sensible min, max, and step behavior when the domain has bounds.
Do not use NumberField for identifiers such as phone numbers, ZIP codes, or credit card numbers.

Do not use it in a property grid with steppers left on. Its two 32px stepper buttons (36px each with their inset) put a ~110px floor on a control that needs ~44px there — pass steppers={false}, or use ScrubField.

props.name: min
props.description: Lower bound. Clamps typing, arrows, scroll and scrub alike, so the value cannot leave the range by any route.

props.name: max
props.description: Upper bound, clamped on every input route the same way as `min`.

props.name: value / defaultValue
props.description: Controlled / uncontrolled numeric value.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Fired when the value changes (null when cleared).

props.name: step / smallStep / largeStep
props.description: Increment amount; smallStep applies with the meta key, largeStep with shift.

props.name: format
props.description: Locale formatting (currency, percent, units, …).

props.name: steppers
props.description: Show the decrement / increment buttons. Turn off in a dense property grid — the two 32px stepper buttons (36px with their inset) put a ~110px floor on the control; without them the value left-aligns.

props.name: disabled / readOnly / required / name / id
props.description: Standard form-control props. Base UI applies id + required to the input, so it labels and validates correctly.

a11y: Decrement / Increment are labelled buttons (Decrease / Increase); the input is a spinbutton with aria-valuenow/min/max from Base UI.
Routes aria-describedby / aria-invalid onto the input, so a Field's helper + error are announced for it.

examples.label: Bounded
examples.code: <NumberField defaultValue={1} min={0} max={99} />

examples.code: <Field label="Quantity"><NumberField min={1} defaultValue={1} /></Field>
