components.name: RadarChart
components.summary: Several measures compared around a centre: one polygon per series over a polygon or circular web, filled or outline only, with optional dots, a radius scale and a tinted web. Polygons grow from the centre as the chart scrolls into view.

usage.description: Use RadarChart to compare the shape of a profile across five to eight dimensions — skills, product scores, a cycle of months — for one to three series. The shape is the message; for exact values or more than three series, BarChart is easier to read.

bestPractices.description: Keep every spoke on the same scale and direction (more is better on all of them).
Use filled={false} when two polygons overlap heavily, so both outlines stay visible.
Use fewer than five spokes — three or four make a triangle or square that says little; use BarChart.

Use it for data-heavy views — streaming or real-time data, thousands of points, zoom and brushing, trading charts. Those belong on a charting library (Recharts, visx, ECharts); Sable's charts are for dashboards, landing pages and decks.

props.name: data
props.description: One row per spoke.

props.name: index
props.description: The datum field naming each spoke.

props.name: series
props.type: { key: string; label: string; tone?: ChartTone; color?: string; icon?: string }[]
props.description: The measures to plot: the datum field, its name in the legend/tooltip/table, and its colour (a tone by role, or any CSS colour). Omitted, series take the chart palette in order: --chart-1 … --chart-8, validated for colour-blind separation in light and dark; a theme may override the set.

props.name: label
props.description: What the chart shows. Its accessible name and the caption of the data table assistive tech reads.

props.name: className
props.description: Sizes the chart. Set a height.

props.name: grid
props.description: The web behind the polygons.

props.name: gridFill
props.description: Tint the web's outer area.

props.name: filled
props.description: Fill each polygon; `false` draws outlines only.

props.name: dots
props.description: Mark every vertex with a dot.

props.name: radiusAxis
props.description: Print the ring values along the top spoke.

props.name: legend
props.default: true when there is more than one series
props.description: Show the legend.

props.name: tooltip
props.type: boolean | { indicator?: "dot" | "line" | "dashed" | "none"; hideLabel?: boolean; labelFormatter?: (label, datum) => ReactNode; showTotal?: boolean }
props.description: Show a tooltip on hover and keyboard focus, or configure it: the row marker, hiding the heading, rewriting it, adding a Total row.

props.name: valueFormatter
props.description: Format values everywhere (axis, labels, tooltip, table) — units like "$12,480". Default: compact on the axis, full elsewhere.

props.name: locale
props.description: BCP 47 locale for default number and date formatting.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. The polygons growing in and morphing are the flourish; the hover highlight is the feedback `subtle` keeps.

props.name: animate
props.description: Grow the polygons from the centre when the chart scrolls into view. `animate={false}` is `motion="subtle"`.
props.deprecated: motion="subtle" (what animate={false} now maps to: no arrival, hover kept) or motion="off"

props.name: activeIndex
props.description: The highlighted row (controlled); `null` for none.

props.name: defaultActiveIndex
props.description: The row highlighted at first — a tooltip already open before anyone hovers.

props.name: onActiveIndexChange
props.description: Called as the pointer or keyboard moves between rows.

motion.why: Once on screen each polygon grows from the centre and fades in, series staggered, on the emphasized easing. On the motion tokens; reduced motion shows the finished chart. The arrival is expressive: it plays at the full motion level only, so `motion="subtle"` (or a subtle app policy) shows the finished chart while hover feedback stays.
The hovered spoke's vertices and label highlight at once.

Geometry eases from the old shape to the new one through a CSS `d` transition on the motion tokens (no recipe animates path geometry); browsers without `d` transitions update in place. Expressive, like the arrival: under `subtle` new data swaps in place.
A chart has no indeterminate state; show a Skeleton while the data loads.

a11y: The drawing is aria-hidden; the same numbers are in a visually hidden data table (captioned by `label`) that the chart is aria-describedby, so assistive tech reads values, not shapes.

With a tooltip, the chart is one tab stop (role=group, aria-roledescription="chart"): arrow keys, Home and End step through the data, Escape clears, and each step is announced in a polite live region.
Colour is never the only key: series are named in the legend, tooltip and table.

examples.label: Two profiles
examples.code:
const scores = [
	{ skill: "Speed", a: 86, b: 65 },
	{ skill: "Quality", a: 72, b: 90 },
	{ skill: "Support", a: 64, b: 80 },
	{ skill: "Price", a: 90, b: 55 },
	{ skill: "Docs", a: 70, b: 85 },
	{ skill: "Ecosystem", a: 60, b: 75 },
]

<RadarChart
	label="Product scores compared"
	data={scores}
	index="skill"
	series={[
		{ key: "a", label: "Atlas" },
		{ key: "b", label: "Beacon" },
	]}
/>

examples.label: Circular web, outlines only
examples.code:
<RadarChart
	label="Atlas scores"
	data={scores}
	index="skill"
	series={[{ key: "a", label: "Atlas" }]}
	grid="circle"
	gridFill
	filled={false}
	dots
/>

components.name: RadialChart
components.summary: Progress or share as rings: one ring per row against a muted track, a full circle or a gauge (`sweep`), one ring split between rows (`stacked`), ring labels and a value in the middle. Rings draw round as the chart scrolls into view.

usage.description: Use RadialChart for progress toward goals (several rings), a single score or usage gauge (`sweep={180}` with `centerLabel`), or a split of one total along a gauge (`stacked`). For one reading in a form or settings row, Meter's ring shape is lighter.

bestPractices.description: Set max to the goal, so a full ring means "done".
Pair a gauge with centerLabel stating the value in words or units.
Compare more than four rings — inner rings are shorter for the same value, which misleads; use BarChart.

Use it for data-heavy views — streaming or real-time data, thousands of points, zoom and brushing, trading charts. Those belong on a charting library (Recharts, visx, ECharts); Sable's charts are for dashboards, landing pages and decks.

props.name: data
props.description: One row per ring, outermost first.

props.name: index
props.description: The datum field naming each ring.

props.name: valueKey
props.description: The datum field holding each ring's amount.

props.name: label
props.description: What the chart shows. Its accessible name and the caption of the data table assistive tech reads.

props.name: categories
props.type: Record<string, { label?: string; tone?: ChartTone; color?: string; icon?: string }>
props.description: Labels, tones and icons per ring, keyed by the ring's name.

props.name: className
props.description: Sizes the chart. Set a height.

props.name: max
props.default: the largest value (stacked: the total; labelled: the largest value ÷ 0.75, leaving room for the labels)
props.description: The value a full ring stands for.

props.name: sweep
props.description: How far round a full ring runs, in degrees: 360 for a circle, 180 for a gauge.

props.name: stacked
props.description: Split ONE ring between the rows instead of a ring each.

props.name: track
props.description: Draw each ring's full track behind it.

props.name: labels
props.description: Name each ring at its start.

props.name: centerLabel
props.description: A value and caption in the middle. On a full ring the value holds the centre and the caption hangs below it. A number is formatted for you: in full up to 9,999, compact from 10,000 (10.2K); pass a string for units ("7.2 GB", "72%").

props.name: legend
props.description: Show the legend.

props.name: tooltip
props.type: boolean | { indicator?: "dot" | "line" | "dashed" | "none"; hideLabel?: boolean; labelFormatter?: (label, datum) => ReactNode; showTotal?: boolean }
props.description: Show a tooltip on hover and keyboard focus, or configure it: the row marker, hiding the heading, rewriting it, adding a Total row.

props.name: valueFormatter
props.description: Format values everywhere (axis, labels, tooltip, table) — units like "$12,480". Default: compact on the axis, full elsewhere.

props.name: locale
props.description: BCP 47 locale for default number and date formatting.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. The draw-on, the ring morph and the rolling centre number are the flourish; the hover dim is the feedback `subtle` keeps.

props.name: animate
props.description: Draw the rings round from their start when the chart scrolls into view. `animate={false}` is `motion="subtle"`.
props.deprecated: motion="subtle" (what animate={false} now maps to: no arrival, hover kept) or motion="off"

props.name: activeIndex
props.description: The highlighted row (controlled); `null` for none.

props.name: defaultActiveIndex
props.description: The row highlighted at first — a tooltip already open before anyone hovers.

props.name: onActiveIndexChange
props.description: Called as the pointer or keyboard moves between rows.

motion.why: Once on screen each ring draws round from its start (stroke-dashoffset on a round-capped arc), staggered outside in. On the motion tokens; reduced motion shows the finished chart. The arrival is expressive: it plays at the full motion level only, so `motion="subtle"` (or a subtle app policy) shows the finished chart while hover feedback stays.

The hovered ring stays full strength and the others dim at once — mixed toward the surface rather than faded, so a dimmed ring stays solid over its track instead of turning muddy. Essential: `subtle` keeps it.

A numeric centre value rolls to its new total digit by digit (NumberTicker) when the data changes, so the headline is seen moving with the rings instead of being found different afterwards. Expressive: under `subtle` it updates in place.

Geometry eases from the old shape to the new one through a CSS `d` transition on the motion tokens (no recipe animates path geometry); browsers without `d` transitions update in place. Expressive, like the arrival: under `subtle` new data swaps in place.
A chart has no indeterminate state; show a Skeleton while the data loads.

a11y: The drawing is aria-hidden; the same numbers are in a visually hidden data table (captioned by `label`) that the chart is aria-describedby, so assistive tech reads values, not shapes.

With a tooltip, the chart is one tab stop (role=group, aria-roledescription="chart"): arrow keys, Home and End step through the data, Escape clears, and each step is announced in a polite live region.
Colour is never the only key: series are named in the legend, tooltip and table.

examples.label: Goal rings
examples.code:
<RadialChart
	label="Weekly goals"
	data={[
		{ goal: "Move", progress: 82 },
		{ goal: "Exercise", progress: 64 },
		{ goal: "Stand", progress: 91 },
	]}
	index="goal"
	valueKey="progress"
	max={100}
	labels
/>

examples.label: Gauge with a value
examples.code:
<RadialChart
	label="Plan usage"
	data={[{ plan: "Used", gb: 7.2 }]}
	index="plan"
	valueKey="gb"
	max={10}
	sweep={180}
	centerLabel={{ value: "7.2 GB", label: "of 10 GB" }}
	legend={false}
/>

components.name: Radio
components.summary: Single-select control over Base UI RadioGroup + Radio (roving focus, arrow-key nav, ARIA radiogroup wiring, form integration). RadioGroup + Radio.

usage.description: Use Radio when a user must choose exactly one option from a visible set.

bestPractices.description: Use it when all options should be visible for comparison.
Keep option labels mutually exclusive and easy to understand.
Do not use Radio for independent toggles or multiple selection; use Checkbox or Switch.
Do not use a radio group with only one option, and do not omit the Fieldset. Without the fieldset the options share no accessible name, so a screen reader reads the choices with no question attached.

anatomy.name: RadioGroup
anatomy.description: The grouped set that manages one selected value.

anatomy.name: Radio
anatomy.description: One selectable option in the group.

props.name: Radio
props.type: Base UI Radio.Root props (value, disabled, readOnly, required) + className
props.description: A single radio button. value pairs it with the group's selected value. Renders a native button with radio semantics, the ring and an inner Indicator dot. A custom non-button render must also set nativeButton={false}.

subcomponents.name: RadioGroup
subcomponents.type: Base UI RadioGroup props (value, defaultValue, onValueChange, name, disabled, readOnly, required) + className
subcomponents.description: The group container that wraps Radio items and shares selection state across them. Controlled via value + onValueChange; uncontrolled via defaultValue. Lays its Radio items out in a vertical stack.

motion.why: Radios arrive with the form they belong to. Animating each one in turns a question into a title sequence.
The ring's edge and focus ring ease, so arrowing through a group — which moves the selection with focus — reads as one choice moving down the list.

The dot grows from the centre on a spring and shrinks out of the radio being left. A group's selection moves from one option to another, and the paired grow and shrink is what makes it read as moving rather than two dots blinking.
A radio commits instantly. A slow write belongs to the surrounding form's pending state, not the control.

a11y: Base UI provides the radiogroup/radio roles, aria-checked, hidden native inputs, and roving tabindex.
Arrow keys move and select between items; Space selects the focused item; Tab enters/leaves the group.
Checked state styling reads from the data-[checked] attribute; disabled items from the disabled state.

Focus-visible draws a 2px ring on the focused item. Wrap each Radio in <Field label orientation="horizontal"> so the label names it, is part of the hit target, sits on the first line, and dims with it when disabled — do not hand-build a <label> row.

examples.label: Basic
examples.code:
<Fieldset>
	<FieldsetLegend>Post type</FieldsetLegend>
	<FieldsetContent>
		<RadioGroup defaultValue="standard">
			<Field label="Standard" orientation="horizontal"><Radio value="standard" /></Field>
			<Field label="Poll" orientation="horizontal"><Radio value="poll" /></Field>
		</RadioGroup>
	</FieldsetContent>
</Fieldset>
examples.imports: import { Field, Fieldset, FieldsetContent, FieldsetLegend, Radio, RadioGroup } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: With a disabled option
examples.code:
<Fieldset>
	<FieldsetLegend>Post type</FieldsetLegend>
	<FieldsetContent>
		<RadioGroup defaultValue="standard">
			<Field label="Standard" orientation="horizontal"><Radio value="standard" /></Field>
			<Field label="Poll" orientation="horizontal" disabled><Radio value="poll" /></Field>
		</RadioGroup>
	</FieldsetContent>
</Fieldset>
examples.imports: import { Field, Fieldset, FieldsetContent, FieldsetLegend, Radio, RadioGroup } from "@sableui/react"

components.name: RadioCard
components.summary: A selectable card option (radio-card) over Base UI RadioGroup + Radio. RadioGroup shares selection state; each RadioCard is a card with a radio indicator, title, and description. Add an icon to switch to the richer two-dimensional card, and a tone to give the selected state a semantic colour identity.

usage.description: Use RadioCard for visual choice cards when users compare a small set of named options.

bestPractices.description: Use it when labels, descriptions, or icons make options easier to understand.
Make the selected state explicit and preserve keyboard access through the group.
Do not use RadioCard for dense menus, long lists, or simple yes/no settings.
Do not use a single RadioCard on its own. It is a radio, so one option cannot be deselected — a lone one is a switch, and should be a Switch.

anatomy.name: RadioCard
anatomy.description: One selectable option card.

anatomy.name: RadioGroup
anatomy.description: A grouped set of related choice cards.

props.name: value
props.description: The unique value that pairs this card with the group's selected value.

props.name: title
props.description: The card's primary label (rendered as text-title-sm).

props.name: description
props.description: Optional supporting copy beneath the title (text-body-sm, muted).

props.name: trailing
props.description: End-aligned on the title's line: a price, a delivery date, a count. The title takes the rest of the row.

props.name: icon
props.description: Leading icon (e.g. a solid <Icon>). Its presence switches to the two-dimensional card — icon top-left, indicator top-right, copy below — and the glyph is rendered as a solid-fill icon in the tone colour.

props.name: tone
props.description: Semantic colour the selected state carries across the border, radio, and icon glyph. Neutral uses the primary ring with a muted wash.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Dims the card and blocks selection. The group skips it during keyboard navigation.

props.name: titleClassName
props.description: Merged onto the title span (default text-title-sm) — e.g. to tighten copy in a two-column layout.

props.name: descriptionClassName
props.description: Merged onto the description span (default text-body-sm text-muted-foreground).

subcomponents.name: RadioGroup
subcomponents.type: Base UI RadioGroup props (value, defaultValue, onValueChange, name, disabled, readOnly, required) + className
subcomponents.description: The group container that wraps the RadioCard cards and shares their selection state. Controlled via value + onValueChange; uncontrolled via defaultValue. Lays its cards out in a single column by default; override with className (e.g. 'grid sm:grid-cols-3') for a grid — the group is a flex column, so a grid-cols-* class alone does nothing.

motion.why: Cards arrive with the form. A plan picker that animated each card in would delay the choice it exists to make.
The edge steps toward the ring colour on hover, eased. On a card-sized target a hard snap across the whole border reads as the layout flickering.
The settle on press confirms a click anywhere in the card — the radio is small, and without it a click in the card's body can feel like it missed the control.
Checking eases the tone ring and wash onto the new card as the old one releases, so the choice reads as moving between cards rather than two cards repainting.
The radio dot grows in on a spring, the same mark as Radio, so a card and a plain radio confirm a choice the same way.
A choice commits instantly. A slow write belongs to the surrounding form's pending state.

a11y: Base UI provides the radiogroup/radio roles, aria-checked, hidden native inputs, and roving tabindex.
Arrow keys move and select between cards; Space selects the focused card; Tab enters/leaves the group.
Checked state styling reads from the data-[checked] attribute; disabled cards from data-disabled.
focus-within draws a 2px ring on the focused card; the whole card is the hit target.
The icon is decorative — the title labels the card — so selection meaning never relies on colour alone (the border ring and the filled radio both shift; the neutral tone adds a muted fill).

examples.label: Post type (tone + icon)
examples.code: <RadioGroup defaultValue="starter" className="grid sm:grid-cols-3"><RadioCard value="starter" tone="3" icon={<Icon name="plus" />} title="Starter" description="Free for one person" /><RadioCard value="studio" tone="2" icon={<Icon name="gem" />} title="Studio" description="For small teams" /><RadioCard value="business" tone="1" icon={<Icon name="image-stack" />} title="Business" description="SSO and audit log" /></RadioGroup>

examples.label: Plan picker (plain)
examples.code: <RadioGroup defaultValue="pro"><RadioCard value="free" title="Free" description="For trying things out." /><RadioCard value="pro" title="Pro" description="For growing teams." /><RadioCard value="enterprise" title="Enterprise" description="Custom limits and support." /></RadioGroup>

examples.label: With a disabled option
examples.code: <RadioGroup defaultValue="free"><RadioCard value="free" title="Free" description="For trying things out." /><RadioCard value="enterprise" title="Enterprise" description="Contact sales to enable." disabled /></RadioGroup>

components.name: ReactionPicker
components.summary: The quick row of emoji you react to a message with: a toolbar of large emoji toggles that bloom in one after another as it opens and magnify under the pointer, with MenuReactions as the same row inside a right-click menu.

usage.description: Use ReactionPicker wherever a reader chooses a reaction for something: in a Popover from an add-reaction control (BubbleReactionAdd is that, ready-made), or as a hover bar over a message. Use MenuReactions for the same row as the first group of the menu a message opens on right-click or long-press, above Reply and Copy. Both report which emoji the reader has already used, so choosing one again removes it.

bestPractices.description: Keep the quick set short — six to eight. It is the reactions people actually use; a full emoji catalogue belongs behind a trailing "more" control passed as children.
Give every reaction a `label`. It is the accessible name and the menu's typeahead, and an emoji's own spoken name differs between platforms.
Pass `selected` so the reader's own reactions show pressed, and toggle in `onSelect`: choosing a reaction you already gave takes it back.
Offer the right-click menu and a visible add-reaction control together. A context menu is invisible until you know it is there; the pill is how a first-time reader finds reactions.
Do not put a ReactionPicker inside a Menu or ContextMenu. A toolbar is not a menu item, so the menu's arrow keys would skip it; use MenuReactions there.
Do not use it to rate an answer or collect a verdict. Reactions are social and many-valued; a helpful / not-helpful question is Feedback.

anatomy.name: ReactionPicker
anatomy.description: The toolbar: one tab stop, arrow keys move between emoji, each a toggle with `aria-pressed`.

anatomy.name: MenuReactions
anatomy.description: The same row as a group of checkbox menu items, for MenuContent and ContextMenuContent. Choosing one closes the menu.

props.name: reactions
props.description: The choices, in order. The default is 👍 ❤️ 😂 🎉 😮 😢 🙏.

props.name: selected
props.description: The emoji the reader has already reacted with: shown pressed, and choosing one again removes it.

props.name: onSelect
props.description: Called with the emoji the reader chose. Toggle it in or out of `selected`.

props.name: children
props.description: ReactionPicker only: trailing controls after the emoji, such as a button that opens a full emoji picker.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: The name of the toolbar or menu group.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps the press and drops the wave of emoji blooming in and the magnify, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down.

subcomponents.name: MenuReactions
subcomponents.type: { reactions?; selected?; onSelect?; motion? } & ComponentProps<typeof Menu.Group>
subcomponents.description: The quick row as checkbox menu items, for the first group of a MenuContent or ContextMenuContent. Same props as ReactionPicker, without children.

motion.why: Opening the picker is the reader's own action, so the emoji answer it: each blooms in 24ms after the one before, a short wave from first to last. The surface it sits in (a Popover or a menu) arrives with its own motion-pop. Expressive only — under `subtle` the emoji are simply there.

The emoji under the pointer or the keyboard highlight magnifies to 1.25 on a fast standard ease, so you can see which one a release will choose; each cell also carries motion-interactive and motion-press. The magnify rides an inner layer so it never fights the bloom over `scale`.
Pressed and not pressed differ by a tint, eased by motion-interactive. The celebration belongs to the reaction that lands under the message (BubbleReaction), not to the picker that chose it.
Choosing is instant; there is no in-between state to show.

a11y: ReactionPicker is a Base UI toolbar: one tab stop, Left/Right move between emoji, Home/End jump to the ends.
Each emoji is a button named by its `label` and reporting `aria-pressed`, so a screen-reader user hears whether choosing it adds or removes their reaction. The glyph itself is aria-hidden.
MenuReactions renders checkbox menu items (`menuitemcheckbox` with `aria-checked`), reached by the menu's arrow keys and typeahead like every other row.
Under reduced motion the emoji appear at once and do not magnify; pressed state is carried by `aria-pressed` and a tint, never motion.

examples.label: In a popover
examples.code:
<Popover>
	<PopoverTrigger render={<Button variant="ghost" size="icon-sm" aria-label="Add reaction" />}>
		<Icon name="emoji" />
	</PopoverTrigger>
	<PopoverContent side="top" className="w-auto rounded-full p-1">
		<ReactionPicker selected={mine} onSelect={toggle} />
	</PopoverContent>
</Popover>
examples.imports: import { Button, Icon, Popover, PopoverContent, PopoverTrigger, ReactionPicker } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: In a right-click menu
examples.code:
<ContextMenu>
	<ContextMenuTrigger render={<Bubble />}>See you at 6.</ContextMenuTrigger>
	<ContextMenuContent>
		<MenuReactions selected={mine} onSelect={toggle} />
		<ContextMenuSeparator />
		<ContextMenuItem>Reply</ContextMenuItem>
		<ContextMenuItem>Copy text</ContextMenuItem>
	</ContextMenuContent>
</ContextMenu>
examples.imports: import { Bubble, ContextMenu, ContextMenuContent, ContextMenuItem, ContextMenuSeparator, ContextMenuTrigger, MenuReactions } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: A custom set
examples.code:
<ReactionPicker
	reactions={[
		{ emoji: "✅", label: "Done" },
		{ emoji: "👀", label: "Looking" },
		{ emoji: "🚀", label: "Shipped" },
	]}
	selected={mine}
	onSelect={toggle}
/>

components.name: RelativeTime
components.summary: A human relative timestamp (e.g. "3 minutes ago") that reveals the full absolute date/time on hover or focus. Renders a native <time> element wrapped in our Tooltip; the absolute time is formatted with date-fns format(date, 'PPpp') (e.g. "Apr 29, 2025, 4:05:12 PM").

usage.description: Use RelativeTime to show recent activity or timestamps in conversational relative language.

bestPractices.description: Use it for feeds, audit summaries, comments, and activity streams.
Expose the exact timestamp when precision matters.
Do not use RelativeTime as the only date format for legal, billing, or audit-critical records.

Do not render it during SSR without a stable absolute fallback. "2 minutes ago" computed on the server differs from the client's value, which is a hydration mismatch — and it silently drifts as the page sits open.

props.name: date
props.description: The instant to render. Accepts a Date, an ISO/parseable string, or an epoch number (ms). Coerced to a Date for date-fns.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged onto the <time> trigger element (the visible relative label).

props.name: ...time props
props.description: Remaining native <time> attributes pass through to the trigger. dateTime is set automatically from the parsed ISO value.

motion.why: It is a word in a line of text and arrives with that line.

The only hover change on the timestamp is a dotted underline, and text-decoration-line is discrete: CSS cannot tween it, so a transition here would animate nothing and imply the snap had been handled.
The pointer's real answer is the absolute time, which arrives in a Tooltip on its own fast pop. That short entrance is what makes the full date read as belonging to the word under the cursor.
The label does not tick: it is computed when the component renders, so it never changes in front of the reader. A timestamp rolling from one minute to two would pull the eye off the content it dates.
A timestamp has nothing to wait for.

a11y: Renders a semantic <time> element with a machine-readable dateTime (ISO) attribute.

The <time> carries tabIndex=0 (it is not focusable natively), so the absolute time — exposed via Base UI's Tooltip, which opens on keyboard focus as well as hover and wires aria-describedby — is reachable from the keyboard.
It inherits the type size of the surrounding text rather than setting its own, so it sits inside a meta row or message header without changing tier.
Wrap the page or a group in <TooltipProvider> to share open/close delays.
Relative phrasing is supplementary; the dateTime attribute remains the canonical machine value.

examples.label: Basic
examples.code: <TooltipProvider><RelativeTime date={new Date()} /></TooltipProvider>

examples.label: From an ISO string
examples.code: <TooltipProvider><RelativeTime date="2025-04-29T16:05:12Z" /></TooltipProvider>

components.name: Scroller
components.summary: Scroll container that fades its leading/trailing edges when content overflows. Tracks scroll position to toggle the fades.

usage.description: Use Scroller to create a contained overflow region for content that naturally extends beyond the viewport.

bestPractices.description: Use it for chip rows, media strips, or comparison sets where horizontal browsing is expected.
Keep scroll affordances visible enough that overflow is discoverable.

Put everything on `className` — sizing (`max-h-80`, `h-64`, `flex-1 min-h-0`) and chrome (`rounded-lg border`, `bg-card`) alike. It styles the Scroller's outer box, and the scrolling element inside it is `flex-1 min-h-0`, so a cap on the Scroller is still a cap on what scrolls.

Pass `label` on any Scroller with real content. It is a focusable region, and an unnamed one announces as a bare group — "Tags" or "Recent covers" costs a word and is the difference between navigable and not.
Do not use Scroller to hide primary page layout or required controls.
Do not add your own wheel handler to make a horizontal strip mouse-scrollable — it already is. A second handler double-scrolls and usually loses the end-release, which traps the page.
Do not reach past it with a child selector (`[&>div]:snap-x`). The scrolling element is addressable by name: `viewportClassName`.
Do not use it to hide overflow you should have laid out. It exists to make an intentionally scrolling strip legible, not to contain content that overflowed by accident.

props.name: orientation
props.description: "vertical" scrolls and fades top/bottom; "horizontal" scrolls and fades left/right.

props.name: wheelScroll
props.description: On a horizontal Scroller, let a vertical mouse wheel scroll it sideways. Ignored when vertical. Turn it off only if the region is inside something that owns the wheel itself (a map, a canvas).

props.name: smoothWheel
props.description: Ease mouse-wheel steps toward their target, on either axis: the inertia a smooth-scroll library such as Lenis adds, scoped to this region. Only a mouse wheel is eased; trackpads and touch keep their own momentum, keys and scrollbar drags stay native, and reduced motion (the OS preference or MotionProvider) turns it off. Anything else that moves the region (scrollIntoView, a stick-to-bottom chat) stops the easing at once. For a scroll container of your own, `useSmoothWheel()` returns the same behaviour as a ref callback.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the scroll region. The region takes focus, so it should say what it contains; without one a screen reader announces an unnamed group.

props.name: viewportClassName
props.description: Classes for the inner element that actually scrolls. Narrow on purpose — `className` is what you want almost always. This is for the few utilities that only mean something on the scrolling box: `snap-x`, `scroll-smooth`, `scroll-p-*`.

props.name: ...div props
props.description: Everything except `className`/`style` spreads onto the SCROLLING element — `role`, `id`, `aria-*`, `data-*` and event handlers all describe the thing that scrolls, and CommandMenu relies on it to make this component its listbox. `ref` and `onScroll` likewise address the scroller, and compose with the component's own.

motion.why: It is a region, not an event; its content arrives with whatever fills it.
The region is focusable so the keyboard can scroll it, and its focus ring eases in like any control's. It is the one sign the region, not the page, now takes the arrow keys.

The vertical bar (`scrollbar-quiet`) stays hidden until the region is hovered, focused or scrolled, then fades its thumb in on the motion tokens. A bar that appeared in one frame would flash every time the pointer crossed the list.

The edge fades switch on and off as you scroll, in the frame the content is already moving, so the change is carried by the scroll itself. They are a mask gradient, which CSS cannot interpolate without registered custom properties.
A scroll region does no work of its own. Content still loading inside it brings its own Skeleton or Spinner.

a11y: The edge fades are a CSS mask-image on the scrolling element, not overlay elements — there is nothing in the DOM to intercept a pointer or be read by assistive tech, and the content under a fade stays fully interactive.

Two boxes: a chrome box carrying `className` (border, background, radius, sizing) and, inside it, the element that actually scrolls and carries the fade mask. They are split because a `mask-image` applies to its element's own border — so with both on one box, a bordered Scroller watched its frame dissolve at the scrolling edge. The axis is published as `data-orientation`, not `aria-orientation`, which is invalid on `role="group"`.
The scroll region uses native overflow and contains overscroll, so a gesture that runs out of content does not scroll the page behind it.

It is focusable (`tabIndex=0`, `role="group"`) and handles arrows, Home/End and PageUp/PageDown along its own axis. Chrome 128+ and Firefox make scrollable regions focusable on their own; Safari does not, so a strip with a hidden scrollbar and no focusable children is unreachable there. Declaring it makes the behaviour a property of the component, not of the reader's browser. Pass `label` to name it — an unnamed focusable region announces as a bare group.

On a horizontal Scroller, a vertical mouse wheel scrolls it sideways, because most mice have no horizontal wheel and the content past the fold is otherwise unreachable on them. The strip releases the wheel at both ends so it never traps the page, and leaves trackpad `deltaX` gestures and `shift+wheel` to the browser.

Cross-axis arrow keys are deliberately not captured, and a consumer can take the arrows entirely by calling `preventDefault()` in their own `onKeyDown` — a strip of interactive chips usually wants them for roving focus.

components.name: ScrubField
components.summary: The compact numeric field a property grid is built from: a leading glyph inside the field that doubles as a drag-to-scrub handle, the value, and an optional unit.

usage.description: Use ScrubField for numeric properties in tool chrome — an inspector, a property grid, a panel. The leading icon or letter says what the number is and is also the thing you drag, which is why a value like opacity needs no slider. Reach for NumberField instead in page-register forms: it has steppers and locale formatting, and it renders at page-register height. Those two steppers put a ~112px floor on a control that needs to be about 44px in a property grid, which is why ScrubField exists rather than a NumberField size variant. The input is sized in ch, so each field is as wide as its longest value and a grid of them lines up without per-field tuning.

bestPractices.description: Give the field an icon or prefix when it stands alone, so the row has a drag affordance and the value has an identity.
Pass the unit as `suffix` rather than baking it into the label — it renders against the number the way reference tools show 100%.
Bracket undo with onGestureStart/onGestureEnd. A scrub fires per frame, so without it one undo rewinds a single pixel of the drag.
Set `step` to the real precision (0.01 for a normalised threshold). Display precision follows it, so a seed shows 1234 and never 1,234.
Add a separate drag gripper beside the glyph. The icon or prefix already is the scrub handle; a second one is the same affordance twice and costs width a 240px panel does not have.
Pair it with a Slider AND give it a glyph. The slider is already the drag affordance; two on one row is the same gesture twice. Omit icon/prefix when there's a slider.
Use it in a page form. It is chrome-sized and has no label, description, or error slots — that's Field plus Input or NumberField.

props.name: value
props.description: The current value (controlled).

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Fires on commit, arrow-key step, and every frame of a scrub.

props.name: min
props.description: Lower clamp, applied to typing and scrubbing.

props.name: max
props.description: Upper clamp, applied to typing and scrubbing.

props.name: step
props.description: Arrow-key and scrub increment, and the source of display precision. Shift multiplies arrows by 10 and divides scrubbing by 10.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the input. Required — the visible glyph is decorative.

props.name: icon
props.description: Semantic icon name rendered inside the field; doubles as the scrub handle. Any name the app's IconProvider resolves works — image tools typically supply their own checkerboard glyph for opacity, which is a domain icon rather than one Sable's contract carries.

props.name: prefix
props.description: Short text used instead of an icon (e.g. "X" / "Y"), with the same scrub role.

props.name: suffix
props.description: Unit rendered after the value inside the field (e.g. "%", "px").

props.name: onGestureStart
props.description: Fires once when a scrub drag begins — open an undo transaction here, and drop expensive downstream work (e.g. a GPU renderer) to a cheap preview quality; without it a pipeline re-renders at full quality on every pointer move and the drag stutters.

props.name: onGestureEnd
props.description: Fires when a scrub drag ends — close the undo transaction here and restore full render quality.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables typing and scrubbing.

props.name: id
props.description: Input id, for a PropertyRow's htmlFor.

motion.why: It arrives with the inspector row it sits in.
The shell eases its focus ring like every field, so tabbing through a column of numbers shows where the keyboard is without flicker.
The handle's ink brightens while the field is hovered. It is the only sign that the icon or prefix can be dragged, which nobody would guess from a label.
The number follows the drag pixel for pixel. Easing it — or rolling it with a NumberTicker — would show a value the pointer has already left, in a control whose whole point is precision.
Scrubbing is synchronous; there is nothing to wait for.

a11y: The input carries the accessible name via `label`; the glyph is aria-hidden because it is decorative.
Every scrub gesture is reachable from the keyboard: ArrowUp/ArrowDown step by `step`, Shift+Arrow by ten steps.
Enter commits, Escape reverts to the last committed value, and blur commits — so a partial edit is never silently kept.

examples.label: Opacity with a glyph handle

  <ScrubField label="Offset Y" prefix="Y" value={y} min={-128} max={128} onValueChange={setY} />
</PropertyPair>

  <ScrubField label="Block size" value={size} min={2} max={256} suffix="px" onValueChange={setSize} />
</PropertyRow>

components.name: SearchInput
components.summary: Styled search field with a leading magnifier and a clearable X. Soft-square (rounded-sm), the theme's field surface, 2px focus ring; the clear button appears only when there is a value. size md (form), sm (toolbar, matching Pill lg and Button sm) or xs (inset tool-panel field).

usage.description: Use SearchInput for text queries that filter or search a known content set.

bestPractices.description: Use a clear placeholder that names the content being searched.
Provide a visible clear affordance when query state persists.

When a button stands in for search (a header trigger that opens CommandMenu with ⌘K), use CommandMenuTrigger. It wears this field's shell from the same source, so the two cannot drift; a hand-styled button already did once, into a borderless chip that matched neither the field nor a button.

Light the query in the results it filters with `useMatchHighlight(query)` — a callback ref for the results container, with `selector` to keep it to titles. It paints on the `highlight` pair without wrapping matches in `<mark>`, the same paint Combobox and CommandMenu use for their rows.

In a toolbar beside filter chips, use size="sm" with Pill size="lg" (and Button size="sm" for actions). All three stand on --control-sm (32px, 28 compact), the rung the spacing doctrine gives toolbar controls, so the row is one height in either density. Keep md for a search field in a form or a page header beside md buttons, and xs for a filter inside a workspace panel, where it matches Input xs's inset surface.
Do not match a neighbour's height with h-* on className or inputClassName. The magnifier, padding and clear button would stay sized for the old rung; pick the size that shares the neighbour's rung.

Do not use SearchInput as a command palette; use CommandMenu for global commands, opened from the header by CommandMenuTrigger. A SearchInput that opens a dialog on focus is a text box you cannot type in.
Do not search on every keystroke against an expensive backend without debouncing. The user sees results flicker and reorder under them, and you send a request per character.

props.name: size
props.description: The rung of the control ladder, named as on Input, Select and Combobox. md is the form field (--control-md, 40px / 32 compact). sm is the toolbar field (--control-sm, 32px / 28 compact), the rung Pill lg and Button sm share, so filters + search + actions in one row are one height. xs is the tool-panel field (--control-xs, 28px / 24 compact) on Input xs's inset panel-field surface. The magnifier, inline padding and clear button scale with the rung and stay vertically centred.

props.name: value
props.description: Controlled value of the search field.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Uncontrolled initial value. The field tracks its own text, so the clear button still appears and empties it.

props.name: className
props.description: Sizes and places the whole field — magnifier, input and clear button together (e.g. max-w-80). A width cap here keeps the clear button inside the field.

props.name: inputClassName
props.description: Classes for the <input> element alone, for the rare input-only override.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called with the next string on every keystroke.

props.name: onClear
props.description: Called when the clear button is pressed. The component also fires onValueChange('') so a controlled value resets.

props.name: placeholder
props.description: Placeholder text shown when the field is empty.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Dims the control and blocks pointer interaction.

props.name: ...props
props.description: All native input attributes (name, autoFocus, ref, aria-invalid, …) pass through to the <input> except value/onChange, which are owned by value/onValueChange, className, which sizes the whole field, and the native numeric size attribute, which the size prop replaces.

motion.why: The X mounts as the first character lands. Fading and settling in from a smaller scale keeps it from popping into the corner of the eye on every new search; removal is instant so an emptied field does not wait on it.
The focus ring and invalid border ease in, so focus reads as the field answering rather than a repaint.
The field has no states of its own to move between — the clear button arriving is its only change, and arrival covers it.
Searching is the results' job: a list skeleton or a Spinner beside them, not a field that animates while you type.

a11y: Renders a native <input type="search"> — keyboard and form semantics come for free.
Associate a <label htmlFor> (or wrap) — the magnifier glyph is decorative, not a label.
The leading search Icon is pointer-events-none and purely decorative.
The clear button is a real <button> (Sable's ghost icon Button) with aria-label='Clear search' and a focus-visible ring. It is hidden while the field is disabled.
Focus-visible draws a 2px ring in the --ring token; aria-invalid raises the destructive border and ring.

components.name: SectionHeader
components.summary: The heading block for one section of a page: a title (h2 by default), an optional line of description, and actions on the title row — a "View all" link or a couple of buttons — that drop beneath the title only when the row runs out of room.

usage.description: Use SectionHeader to head each section below the page title — a home-page shelf with View all, a settings group, a list with its own actions. PageHeader is the route's single h1; every section under it takes a SectionHeader, with titleId wired to the section's aria-labelledby.

bestPractices.description: Wrap the header and its content in a `<section aria-labelledby={titleId}>` (a flex column with a gap, or a Stack inside it) so the section is a named region and the header's title is its name.

Pick titleAs by the document outline (h2 under the page h1, h3 inside an h2 section) and size by visual weight: lg for an editorial page's sections under a PageHeader size="lg", md for a page's sections and shelves, sm for denser groups like settings.

Keep actions to one or two `size="sm"` buttons — the title is centred on that height. A shelf's "View all" is a ghost Button rendered as a link (`render={<a href=… />}`), named for what it opens when the label alone is ambiguous (aria-label="View all new releases").

Pass a ghost or link action as a plain Button and let the header align it: the last direct child bleeds by its own padding at the end, so "View all" sits on the edge of the grid below, and the first bleeds at the start, which is the edge once the actions wrap beneath the title. Filled buttons keep their edge on the line. Set bleed="none" on the Button to opt one out.

Nudge a View all onto the edge with -me-3, or wrap the actions in your own div: the header aligns direct children only, and only by each button's real padding. If you must wrap them, set bleed on the Button inside instead.

Use a second PageHeader for a section — that is a second h1, and the outline then reports two documents. And do not hand-build `<div className="flex justify-between"><h2 className="text-heading-3">…` per shelf: it misses the wrapping, the aria wiring and the shared rhythm.
Use SectionHeader to title a Card (use CardHeader + CardTitle) or a docked tool panel (use PanelSection). It heads a section of the page, not a surface.
Add margin to the header to space it from its content. It has no outer spacing on purpose; the section's gap owns that rhythm, so every section on the page keeps the same one.

anatomy.name: Title
anatomy.description: The section's heading (h2 by default), wrapping rather than truncating. Its id names the section.

anatomy.name: Description
anatomy.description: One line of supporting copy under the title, capped at the prose measure.

anatomy.name: Actions
anatomy.description: Buttons or links at the title row's end; they move beneath the title when the row is too narrow for both. A borderless (ghost/link) Button at either end of the group is optically aligned: its label, not its invisible padding, meets the content edge.

props.name: title
props.description: The section's title.

props.name: description
props.description: One line of supporting copy beneath the title, capped at the prose measure.

props.name: actions
props.description: Trailing actions on the title row — a View all link or a couple of buttons, size="sm". They stay on the title's row and drop beneath it only when the row runs out of room; the title wraps rather than truncating. A ghost or link Button that ends the group bleeds by its padding at the end (and one that starts it, at the start — the edge once wrapped), so its label lines up with the content below; Button bleed="none" opts out. Direct children only.

props.name: titleAs
props.description: The heading element, chosen by the document outline: h2 for a section under the page's h1, h3 for a subsection inside one.

props.name: titleId
props.description: The title's id, so the section it heads can point at it: <section aria-labelledby={titleId}>. Generated when omitted.

props.name: size
props.description: Visual weight, independent of the heading level: lg (text-heading-2 over a text-body-md description) for an editorial page's sections, under a PageHeader size="lg"; md (text-heading-3) for a page's sections and shelves; sm (text-heading-4) for denser sets — settings groups, subsections. lg stops at heading-2: heading-1 is the page title's, one per route. The actions stay centred on the title's first line at every size.

motion.why: A heading arrives with the section it names; animating it separately would make the section's title lag its content.
The header itself is not interactive; the Buttons passed as actions carry their own response.
It has no states of its own to move between.
It never does indeterminate work.

a11y: Renders a real heading (h2 by default); choose titleAs by the outline, never to get a size — size sets the look.
The title always carries an id (titleId, or a generated one). Point the section at it with aria-labelledby so the section is announced as a named region and appears in landmark navigation.
A repeated "View all" is ambiguous in a links list; name each one for its section (aria-label="View all new releases") or keep the visible label specific.

components.name: SectionRail
components.summary: A slim vertical rail of dots, one per section of a long page, that shows where the reader is and jumps to any section. The current section's bar glides as the page scrolls; a shared tooltip names each dot.

usage.description: Use SectionRail beside a long, single-column read — a case study, an essay, a long landing page — so the reader can see which section they are in and jump to another without leaving the text. It follows the scroll by itself (useActiveSection); pass value when the parent already knows the current section.

bestPractices.description: Give every section an id that matches its entry, and keep the list to the page's top-level sections — about ten at most, so the rail stays shorter than the viewport.

Place it with layout classes — usually `fixed top-1/2 left-6 z-(--z-nav) -translate-y-1/2` — and hide it below the width where it would overlap the text (`max-lg:hidden`). Offer the same links another way on narrow screens, such as a Collapsible list at the top of the page.

Pass `root` when the content scrolls inside an element (a Scroller, an inset AppShell main) rather than the window, and give sections `scroll-mt-*` when a sticky header would cover their tops after a jump.
Set `side="right"` when the rail sits on the right edge, so labels open toward the content.
Use it for app navigation between pages; that is SideNav or Sidebar. A SectionRail only moves within one page.
Use it to show the steps of a task or a flow; that is Stepper, which shows progress through steps rather than position in a read.
Use it for a handful of switchable views in one place; that is Tabs.

anatomy.name: Rail
anatomy.description: The `<nav>` landmark: a rounded muted track holding one link per section.

anatomy.name: Dot
anatomy.description: A link to `#id`, drawn as a small dot that grows under the pointer or focus.

anatomy.name: Marker
anatomy.description: One primary bar that sits on the current section's dot and glides to the next.

anatomy.name: Label
anatomy.description: A shared tooltip that names the hovered or focused dot and travels between dots.

props.name: sections
props.description: The sections, in document order. `id` is the section element's id (the link goes to `#id`); `label` is the tooltip and the link's accessible name.

props.name: value
props.description: The current section's id, when the parent decides it. Leave it unset and the rail follows the scroll itself.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called with the new id when the reader scrolls into a section or picks one.

props.name: offset
props.description: Where the reading line sits, as a fraction of the viewport from its top. A section becomes current once its top crosses it.

props.name: root
props.description: The element that scrolls, when it is not the window.

props.name: side
props.description: Which edge of the page the rail sits on. The labels open on the other side, toward the content.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the marker's glide, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: The nav landmark's name. Name it for the page ("Case study sections") when it has other navs.

motion.why: Page chrome arrives with the page; the marker lands on the current section with no transition, because a bar sliding in on load narrates a move nobody made.
The dot darkens and grows under the pointer or focus, and the label travels between dots as one tooltip (TooltipGroup) rather than closing and reopening at each.

One bar travels to the new section as the page scrolls, so the change reads as movement down the page. A picked section holds the bar until the reader scrolls by hand, so it goes straight there instead of stepping through every section in between, and stays on the pick even when the page ends before that section can reach the reading line. Expressive: `subtle` moves it at once.
Navigation chrome has no working state.

a11y: Renders a <nav> landmark (default name "Sections") of real links to `#id`, so it works with no script, middle-click and copy-link.
Each link is named by its section's label; the current one carries aria-current="location".
Activating a link from the keyboard moves focus into the section, as following an anchor does, so the next Tab continues from there.
The tooltip opens on focus as well as hover; the dots are 44×32 targets.
Under reduced motion the jump is instant and the marker moves without travel.

examples.label: Fixed beside a long read
examples.code:
<SectionRail
  aria-label="Case study sections"
  sections={[
    { id: "overview", label: "Overview" },
    { id: "problem", label: "The problem" },
    { id: "process", label: "Process" },
    { id: "outcome", label: "Outcome" },
  ]}
  className="fixed top-1/2 left-6 z-(--z-nav) -translate-y-1/2 max-lg:hidden"
/>

examples.label: On the right edge
examples.code:
<SectionRail
  side="right"
  sections={[
    { id: "intro", label: "Introduction" },

components.name: SegmentedBar
components.summary: One bar split into the parts of a whole — revenue by type, storage by kind, results by outcome. Segments size by their share of the total; the bar is one labelled image to assistive tech.

usage.description: Use SegmentedBar when a stat card or row needs to show how a total divides into a few categories. Pair it with a legend you compose (StatusDot + label + share), placed where the card has room. For one reading against a range (storage used, quota), use Meter; for task completion, use Progress.

bestPractices.description: Keep it to two to six segments and give the same category the same tone everywhere it appears.
Show the legend's shares in text ("42%") — colour identifies a segment, but the number is what a reader compares.
Use it for a single value against a limit; that is Meter, which carries the meter role and its value.
Rely on tone order alone to tell segments apart; a legend row per segment, with its label, is required.

anatomy.name: Track
anatomy.description: The rounded bar; segments fill it edge to edge with a hairline gap.

anatomy.name: Segment
anatomy.description: One category, sized by its share of the total and filled with its tone.

props.name: segments
props.type: { label: string; value: number; tone?: SegmentedBarTone }[]
props.description: The categories, left to right. Values in any unit; zero or negative values are skipped.

props.name: label
props.description: What the bar breaks down. Prefixes the accessible summary of every segment's share.

props.name: size
props.description: Bar thickness — the same rails as Meter and Progress.

props.name: locale
props.description: Locale for the spoken percentages.

motion.why: A breakdown is a reading, present with the card that reports it; growing the segments in on load would act out a change that did not happen.
It reports and accepts no input.
Each segment's share and colour ease on the motion tokens when the data changes (no recipe animates flex-grow), so the reader sees which part grew.
No indeterminate state — an unknown breakdown is not drawn.

a11y: Rendered role=img with an aria-label built from `label` and each segment's share ("Revenue by channel: Direct 42%, Partners 27%"), so the whole breakdown is read in one stop.
Colour alone does not identify a segment: always show a legend with each segment's label beside the bar.

examples.label: With a legend
examples.code:
const sales = [ { label: "Direct", value: 42, tone: "1" }, { label: "Partners", value: 27, tone: "2" }, { label: "Referrals", value: 19, tone: "3" }, ] as const
    {sales.map((s) => (
  • {s.label} {s.value}%
    • ))}

examples.label: Test results — status tones
examples.code:
<SegmentedBar
	label="Test results"
	segments={[
		{ label: "Passed", value: 412, tone: "success" },
		{ label: "Flaky", value: 9, tone: "warning" },
		{ label: "Failed", value: 3, tone: "destructive" },
	]}
/>

components.name: Select
components.summary: Listbox over Base UI Select — typeahead, roving focus, collision-aware popup, ARIA option wiring, and form integration. Trigger shows the selected value; the popup portals to <body>.

usage.description: Use Select when users choose one value from a known, finite set. Use Combobox for searchable or user-entered values, Combobox `multiple` for several choices, and Radio when all options should remain visible.

bestPractices.description: Use clear item labels and pass label explicitly when children are richer than plain text.
Group long option sets with SelectGroup and SelectGroupLabel when categories improve scanning.
Wrap in Field when the select belongs to a form so label, helper text, and errors are wired automatically.
Use Select for very large or fuzzy lists. Use Combobox when typing is the primary way to find an option.
Use Select for binary on/off settings. Use Switch or Checkbox instead.

Leave the trigger's type alone on mobile. Below the sm breakpoint the md trigger renders text-body-lg (17px) so it matches the Input and Textarea beside it, which carry that tier because iOS Safari zooms the page when a focused field computes under 16px. A custom field in the same row should follow: a second paired tier under a max-sm: variant, never a hand-set font-size.

Inside a <Workspace> a Select adapts automatically — trigger and popup both pick up the compact density, including across the portal. Do NOT hand-size it per call site; that was necessary before v0.41 and is now drift.

anatomy.name: Root
anatomy.description: Owns value, open state, form integration, and item collection.

anatomy.name: Trigger
anatomy.description: The button that shows the selected value and opens the listbox.

anatomy.name: Content
anatomy.description: The positioned popup containing options and optional groups.

anatomy.name: Item
anatomy.description: A selectable option with selected and highlighted states.

props.name: items
props.type: Record<string, ReactNode> | { value: string; label: ReactNode }[]
props.description: value → label map (a record, or an array of { value, label }). Derived automatically from literal SelectItem children; pass it explicitly when the items are generated in a loop, or a closed trigger renders the raw value instead of the label.

props.name: Select (Root)
props.type: Base UI Select.Root props (value, defaultValue, onValueChange, open, defaultOpen, onOpenChange, disabled, required, name, multiple, items)
props.description: Controls the selected value and open state. Uncontrolled by default. When `items` isn't passed, it is derived from the SelectItem children so the closed trigger shows display text instead of the raw value; pass `items` explicitly when item children aren't plain strings.

subcomponents.name: SelectTrigger
subcomponents.type: Base UI Trigger props + placeholder?: ReactNode + size?: "md" | "xs" + className
subcomponents.description: The button. Composes Trigger + Value + a chevron Icon that flips on open (data-[popup-open]). `size="xs"` is the property-grid rung — height, padding, radius AND surface move together, which is why it is a prop and not a className: the xs trigger is an inset `bg-panel-field` field with no border, matching ScrubField on the same row. A consumer overriding only the height gets an md-register 8px radius on a 24px box and a raised card sitting among inset fields; one inspector panel had eleven of those, and both tells are visible at a glance.

subcomponents.name: SelectContent
subcomponents.type: Base UI Popup props + side, align, sideOffset + className
subcomponents.description: Portal + Positioner + Popup + List. side="bottom", align="start", sideOffset=6 by default; matches trigger width.

subcomponents.name: SelectItem
subcomponents.type: { value: string; disabled?: boolean; label?: string } + className
subcomponents.description: An option. Composes Item + ItemText + a check ItemIndicator for the selected row. String children double as the item's `label`, so the closed trigger shows the display text — pass `label` explicitly only when children are richer than a string.

subcomponents.name: SelectGroup
subcomponents.description: Optional grouping of related options.

subcomponents.name: SelectGroupLabel
subcomponents.description: The heading associated with a SelectGroup for screen readers.

subcomponents.name: SelectValue
subcomponents.type: Base UI Value props (children render fn) + placeholder
subcomponents.description: Renders the selected option's label with a placeholder fallback. Already composed inside SelectTrigger; exported for advanced layouts that render the value outside the default trigger.

subcomponents.name: SelectSeparator
subcomponents.description: A thin themed divider between groups of items. Decorative — Base UI marks it aria-hidden.

motion.why: The popup's transform-origin follows Base UI's anchor, so it grows out of the trigger it belongs to. On a dense form with several selects in a column, that origin is the only thing identifying which field the open list is for.

Highlight follows both pointer and keyboard. Easing it means arrow-keying down a list is continuous motion rather than a background teleporting between rows, which is what makes a long list readable while moving.
Closing collapses back toward the trigger, so the reader's eye is returned to the field that now holds the value they just picked.
Select takes a resident list of options. Anything that has to be fetched or filtered as you type is Combobox, which owns that state.

a11y: Base UI provides listbox/option roles, aria-expanded, typeahead, roving focus, and a hidden form input.
Esc and click-outside dismiss; arrow keys and Home/End navigate the list.
Selected option carries data-[selected]; the highlighted option carries data-[highlighted].
Animate the popup via data-[starting-style] / data-[ending-style].

examples.label: Basic (controlled)
examples.code: <Select value={value} onValueChange={setValue}><SelectTrigger placeholder="Choose a font" /><SelectContent><SelectItem value="sans">Sans-serif</SelectItem><SelectItem value="serif">Serif</SelectItem><SelectItem value="mono">Monospace</SelectItem></SelectContent></Select>
examples.imports: import { Select, SelectContent, SelectItem, SelectTrigger } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: Grouped
examples.code: <SelectContent><SelectGroup><SelectGroupLabel>Weights</SelectGroupLabel><SelectItem value="regular">Regular</SelectItem><SelectItem value="bold">Bold</SelectItem></SelectGroup></SelectContent>
examples.imports: import { SelectContent, SelectGroup, SelectGroupLabel, SelectItem } from "@sableui/react"

components.name: Separator
components.summary: A hairline divider. Horizontal full-width rule or vertical 1px column, tinted with the border token. Optional centered label (horizontal) for a captioned section divider.

usage.description: Use Separator to divide related groups where spacing alone does not provide enough structure.

bestPractices.description: Use it sparingly between sections, menu groups, or dense rows.
Choose orientation based on the layout direction it separates.
Do not use Separator as decoration when hierarchy, spacing, or headings would explain the layout better.
Do not use it where space would do. A page whose every section is divided by a rule reads as a form; the rule should mark a real change of subject.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Axis of the rule. Vertical stretches to its flex parent's height.

props.name: label
props.description: When set (horizontal only), centers a muted caption between two hairline rules.

props.name: render
props.description: Compose with another element/component through the Base UI render prop. Ignored on the labeled variant.

a11y: Base UI sets role=separator and aria-orientation for assistive tech.
The labeled variant renders a div with explicit role=separator + aria-orientation (the caption is the visible context).
Purely decorative dividers can carry aria-hidden when adjacent content already conveys the grouping.

components.name: SettingsMenu
components.summary: A compact trigger that states the current settings, over a menu of rows that change them. Each row shows its own value and opens a submenu; with one setting, the menu opens straight to its options under the row's label.

usage.description: For a cluster of related settings that a reader checks often and changes occasionally — the model and effort on an AI composer, quality and format on an export control, density and sort on a table. It encodes one shape: summarise the state on the trigger, then open to a list of name → current value → submenu. It knows nothing about any particular domain; the AI-model case is one instance of it.

bestPractices.description: Put the current values in `summary`, not a noun. "5.6 Sol High" tells the reader where they are; a trigger reading "Settings" makes them open it to find out, which is the wrong trade for a control glanced at twenty times a session.
Give every SettingsRow a `value`. One glance at the open menu should answer every setting at once — a menu of bare names is a menu you have to explore.
Use `MenuRadioGroup` + `MenuRadioItem` inside a row for single-choice settings, so the current option is checked rather than merely remembered.
Reach for `variant="subtle"` when the trigger sits on a surface where a ghost control would float unanchored — inside a ChatComposer, for instance.
Do not use it for a single setting. One choice is a `Select`; the nesting only earns its cost when there are several related settings to summarise.
Do not put actions in it. Rows change state; a menu that mixes "Effort ›" with "Delete conversation" makes destructive commands look like preferences. That is `Menu` or `OverflowMenu`.
Do not nest more than one level deep. Past that the reader loses the path back, and the thing you have is a settings dialog wearing a menu.
Do not override the upward, end-aligned default without reason. Its home is the bottom of a composer or toolbar, where a downward menu opens off-screen.

anatomy.name: Trigger
anatomy.description: The summary control. States the current settings and carries a chevron; quiet at rest, so it does not compete with the primary action beside it.

anatomy.name: SettingsRow
anatomy.description: One setting: its name, its current value, and a submenu of options. Without children it renders flat, for a row that is a statement rather than a choice.

anatomy.name: Submenu contents
anatomy.description: Usually a MenuRadioGroup of MenuRadioItems, so the active option is checked.

props.name: summary
props.description: What the trigger reads when closed. Give it the current values, not a noun — the control should answer before it is opened.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the trigger, since the visible summary is data rather than a label.

props.name: variant
props.description: Resting treatment. `ghost` disappears into the surface at rest and shows its affordance on hover — right for a toolbar. `subtle` adds a fill for surfaces where a ghost trigger would float unanchored.

props.name: size
props.description: Trigger height, read off the density ladder so a compact scope retunes it with every other control.

props.name: side
props.description: Which side the menu opens on. Upward by default — its home is the bottom of a composer.

props.name: align
props.description: Alignment along that side.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disable the trigger.

props.name: ...Menu props
props.description: `open` / `defaultOpen` / `onOpenChange` and the rest of Base UI's menu root props.

subcomponents.name: SettingsRow
subcomponents.type: { label: ReactNode; value?: ReactNode; disabled?: boolean; children?: ReactNode }
subcomponents.description: One setting. With children it opens a submenu; without them it renders as a flat statement row.

subcomponents.name: MenuRadioGroup
subcomponents.type: { value?: string; defaultValue?: string; onValueChange?: (value: string) => void }
subcomponents.description: Single-choice group for a row's submenu. Exported from Menu; re-used here rather than duplicated.

subcomponents.name: MenuRadioItem
subcomponents.description: One option, with a check in a reserved leading column so labels do not shift as the highlight moves.

a11y: Base UI's Menu underneath, so roving focus, typeahead, Esc and outside-dismissal, and the full menu/menuitemradio ARIA wiring come for free — including submenu traversal with the arrow keys.

The trigger carries an explicit `label`, because its visible text is the current state rather than a name: without it, a screen reader announces "5.6 Sol High" with no indication that it is a control or what it changes.
Radio rows are `menuitemradio` with a real checked state, so the current choice is conveyed to assistive tech rather than only by a visible tick.
The check occupies a reserved column instead of appearing on selection, so labels never shift sideways as the highlight moves — a change that reads as motion to anyone tracking position.
Submenus open on the inline-end side, which flips correctly in RTL rather than always opening right.

examples.label: A model switcher in a composer
examples.code: {model.name}{" "}{effort}}> 5.6 Sol 5.6 Lite Low High } />
examples.imports: import { ChatComposer, MenuRadioGroup, MenuRadioItem, SettingsMenu, SettingsRow } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: Export options — the same shape, no chat involved
examples.code:
<SettingsMenu summary={`${format} · ${quality}`} side="bottom" align="start">
	<SettingsRow label="Format" value={format}>
		<MenuRadioGroup value={format} onValueChange={setFormat}>
			<MenuRadioItem value="PNG">PNG</MenuRadioItem>
			<MenuRadioItem value="SVG">SVG</MenuRadioItem>
		</MenuRadioGroup>
	</SettingsRow>
	<SettingsRow label="Quality" value={quality}>
		<MenuRadioGroup value={quality} onValueChange={setQuality}>
			<MenuRadioItem value="Draft">Draft</MenuRadioItem>
			<MenuRadioItem value="Final">Final</MenuRadioItem>
		</MenuRadioGroup>
	</SettingsRow>
</SettingsMenu>
examples.imports: import { MenuRadioGroup, MenuRadioItem, SettingsMenu, SettingsRow } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: A flat row for a setting with nothing to choose
examples.code:
<SettingsMenu summary="Standard">
	<SettingsRow label="Speed" value="Standard">
		<MenuRadioGroup value="standard">
			<MenuRadioItem value="standard">Standard</MenuRadioItem>
			<MenuRadioItem value="priority">Priority</MenuRadioItem>
		</MenuRadioGroup>
	</SettingsRow>
	<MenuSeparator />
	<SettingsRow label="Plan" value="Team" />
</SettingsMenu>
