components.name: Sheet
components.summary: Edge-anchored drawer over Base UI Drawer — focus trap, scroll lock, Esc/outside dismissal, portal backdrop, plus swipe-to-dismiss on touch. Slides in from a viewport edge via side and swipes back out toward the same edge.

usage.description: Use Sheet for secondary workflows that slide in while preserving context from the underlying page.

bestPractices.description: Use it for inspect, edit, filter, or create flows that relate to the current page.
Include clear title, close path, and footer actions for task-oriented sheets.

Give a bottom sheet snap points when it shows a summary first and detail on demand (a map result, a now-playing panel): `snapPoints={[0.4, 1]}`. The first stop is where it opens; put what matters at that height, because the rest is a drag away.
Do not use Sheet for simple confirmations or deeply nested workflows.
Do not use it on desktop where a Dialog fits. A sheet's affordance is edge-anchored travel for thumb reach; on a wide viewport it becomes a dialog that arrives from the wrong place.

anatomy.name: SheetTrigger
anatomy.description: The element that opens the sheet.

anatomy.name: SheetContent
anatomy.description: The sliding panel content.

anatomy.name: SheetClose
anatomy.description: An explicit close control.

anatomy.name: SheetHeader
anatomy.description: The title and description region.

anatomy.name: SheetTitle
anatomy.description: The sheet heading.

anatomy.name: SheetDescription
anatomy.description: Supporting context for the sheet.

anatomy.name: SheetList
anatomy.description: Edge-to-edge rows (Entity) aligned with the header — a queue, notifications, a picker.

anatomy.name: SheetFooter
anatomy.description: Footer actions for the workflow.

props.name: Sheet (Root)
props.type: Base UI Drawer.Root props (open, defaultOpen, onOpenChange, onOpenChangeComplete, modal, disablePointerDismissal, actionsRef, handle, snapPoints, snapPoint, defaultSnapPoint, onSnapPointChange, snapToSequentialPoints) — minus swipeDirection
props.description: Controls open state. Uncontrolled by default. The dismiss swipe direction is not a prop: it follows SheetContent's side. onOpenChange reports reason "swipe" when a swipe closed it. Records the element focused when the sheet opens, trigger or not, and returns focus there on close.

props.name: snapPoints
props.description: Stops a bottom sheet rests at, smallest first: a fraction of the viewport (0.4), pixels (320), or a px/rem string ("20rem"). The panel is the full stop's height and opens at the first stop; a swipe moves between stops and a swipe below the first closes it. side="bottom" only: other sides ignore them, with a development warning.

props.name: snapPoint
props.description: The active stop, controlled. Pair with onSnapPointChange; use defaultSnapPoint to open at a different stop uncontrolled.

props.name: onSnapPointChange
props.description: Fires when a swipe (or your code) moves the sheet to another stop.

props.name: snapToSequentialPoints
props.description: Move one stop per swipe, by distance. Off, a fast flick can skip past a stop.

subcomponents.name: SheetContent
subcomponents.type: Base UI Drawer.Popup props (initialFocus, finalFocus, …) + side: "right" | "left" | "top" | "bottom" + className
subcomponents.description: Backdrop + edge-anchored popup; portals to <body>. side picks which viewport edge the sheet anchors to and slides in from (defaults to "right"). Left/right are full-height side panels; top/bottom span the width up to 80vh. A bottom sheet with snapPoints is as tall as its highest stop allows (the viewport less a top gap), shows a drag handle, and translates down to the active stop; the part below the screen becomes bottom padding, so its scroll area and SheetFooter end at the visible edge. A bottom sheet rides above the on-screen keyboard (measured from visualViewport). On touch it swipes closed toward that same edge (right swipes right, left swipes left, top swipes up, bottom swipes down).

subcomponents.name: SheetTrigger
subcomponents.description: Element that opens the sheet. Compose via render prop.

subcomponents.name: SheetClose
subcomponents.description: Element that dismisses the sheet. Compose via render prop.

subcomponents.name: SheetHeader
subcomponents.description: Top section holding SheetTitle/SheetDescription.

subcomponents.name: SheetTitle
subcomponents.description: The sheet's accessible name — wires aria-labelledby on the popup.

subcomponents.name: SheetDescription
subcomponents.description: Muted supporting line; wires aria-describedby.

subcomponents.name: SheetList
subcomponents.description: Rows that run edge to edge in the sheet, Entity most often. It bleeds through the sheet's padding (--sheet-p) and hands it back to each row as --entity-px, so row content lines up with SheetHeader and a row's hover fill reaches the panel's edges. Without it a list of Entity rows sits 12px in from the header. The Sheet equivalent of CardList.

subcomponents.name: SheetFooter
subcomponents.description: Bottom row for actions, pinned after the scrollable body. In a bottom sheet it stacks: full width, the primary on top, every button at the cta height.

a11y: Base UI provides focus trapping, scroll lock, aria-modal, and labelled-by wiring (SheetTitle).
The panel scrolls its own content (thin scrollbar, contained overscroll) when it outgrows its bound — the full height on left/right, 80vh on top/bottom.
Esc and click-outside dismiss by default; on touch, a swipe toward the sheet's own edge dismisses too. A short or slow drag springs back.
Swipe is an extra path, never the only one: Esc, click-outside and SheetClose all still work.

Focus matches Dialog: the first tabbable on mouse/keyboard open, the panel itself on touch (so the virtual keyboard stays down). On close, focus returns to the element that held it when the sheet opened: the SheetTrigger, or your own button when it drives a controlled open. It is captured before the content mounts, so an autoFocus field inside cannot displace it; an explicit finalFocus on SheetContent wins.
Render a SheetClose inside SheetContent so screen-reader users can escape the popup.

Slide animation runs via data-[starting-style]/data-[ending-style] attributes on the motion-duration token; while swiping the panel tracks the finger directly, and a released swipe finishes on the same token (scaled by flick speed), so reduced motion makes it instant.
A mouse drag that starts on sheet content selects text rather than dragging the panel; mouse dragging only starts from the padding edge.

Snap points add stops, not a gate: at any stop the content scrolls within the visible part and every control stays reachable by keyboard, so nothing needs the drag. The handle is decorative (aria-hidden).

A bottom sheet stays above the on-screen keyboard: its bottom edge is lifted by the height the keyboard takes from the visual viewport, so a focused field is not covered. An app that sets interactive-widget=resizes-content in its viewport meta gets the same result from the browser, and the inset reads 0.

examples.label: List of rows (a queue)
examples.code: <Sheet><SheetTrigger render={<Button variant="secondary">Queue</Button>} /><SheetContent><SheetHeader><SheetTitle>Up next</SheetTitle></SheetHeader><SheetList>{queue.map((track) => <Entity key={track.id} leading={<GradientArt aria-hidden seed={track.title} className="size-10 rounded-sm" />} title={track.title} subtitle={track.artist} />)}</SheetList></SheetContent></Sheet>

components.name: ShowMore
components.summary: Collapsible content region that clips children to a collapsed height, fades the cut edge, and reveals the rest with a toggle.

usage.description: Use ShowMore to reveal additional content after an intentionally shortened preview.

bestPractices.description: Use it when the preview is useful on its own and the rest is optional.
Make the expanded state reversible when collapsing helps users regain context.
Do not place it on a card or tinted surface without checking the fade. The cut-edge gradient fades to the page background color, so on any other surface it reads as a visible band.
Do not hide required steps, important warnings, or primary actions behind ShowMore.
Do not use it to hide content search engines or screen readers need. Collapsed content is still in the DOM here, but if the user must read it to act, it should not be behind a toggle.

props.name: collapsedHeight
props.description: Collapsed height of the content region in px. The inner wrapper clips to this height until expanded. The toggle and fade only appear when the measured content is taller than this; content that already fits shows in full with no control. Expanding animates to the measured height.

props.name: collapsedLines
props.description: Collapsed height as a count of the content's own lines (measured from its line height). Wins over collapsedHeight, and is the one to prefer: the preview keeps the same number of lines when the type scale or density changes, where a px height shows fewer as type grows.

props.name: children
props.description: The content to collapse and reveal.

motion.why: The preview arrives with the content it clips. Its fade and toggle appear only once a measurement proves the content overflows.
The toggle is a link Button, so its hover and focus ease on Button's recipe.

The region eases its max-height between the collapsed and the measured full height on the slow motion token. motion-disclosure keys on Base UI's starting and ending styles, which this self-contained toggle does not have. The text unrolling in place keeps the reader's line; a snap drops them at a different scroll position.
The bottom fade dissolves as the region opens and returns as it closes, so the cut edge and the reveal read as one movement.
The chevron turns 180° in step with the region (motion-interactive lists `rotate`), so the toggle visibly points at what it will do next.
Expanding is local and instant; nothing loads.

a11y: The toggle is a real <button> with aria-expanded reflecting the open state.
The fade overlay is pointer-events-none and decorative; it never traps clicks.
Collapsed content stays in the DOM, so screen readers can still reach it.

components.name: Sidebar
components.summary: Desktop side-navigation rail (in-flow sticky, hidden below lg) with SidebarHeader / SidebarBrand / SidebarNav / SidebarGroup / SidebarItem / SidebarFooter / SidebarAccount parts, all on one set of columns. Items are router-agnostic via the `render` prop; an optional collapsed icon-rail mode reveals labels in tooltips.

usage.description: Use Sidebar for persistent desktop navigation or application chrome outside the main content region.

bestPractices.description: Use it for stable app destinations that should remain visible while content changes.
Keep item labels predictable and active state obvious.
Set surface="page" when a full-width top bar sits above the rail. A theme's tinted or dark rail is for a full-height rail that frames the app.
Keep surface="rail" inside AppShell frame="inset": the rail's tint becomes the ground the main panel floats on. Do not add a border-r class back — the gap is the divider.

Group items with SidebarGroup and end the rail with one SidebarAccount that opens the account menu (settings, appearance, sign out). Every part sits on the same icon and label columns, at either density.

Do not put SideNav, an Entity or a stack of ghost Buttons in the rail. Each brings its own insets, so the icons and labels land on four different columns. SideNav is the in-page section list; the rail has its own parts.
Do not put a Badge or pill in the account row. Its one quiet detail line carries the plan, role or 'Demo'.
Do not use Sidebar for page-local settings, filters, or temporary action groups.
Do not put page content in it. It is fixed-width chrome OUTSIDE the content grid, so anything in it is exempt from the page's measure and rhythm.

anatomy.name: Sidebar
anatomy.description: The persistent navigation container.

anatomy.name: SidebarItem
anatomy.description: One navigation destination or action.

props.name: collapsed
props.description: Collapse the rail to an icon-only width (--sidebar-width-collapsed). Items hide their label + badge and reveal the label in a hover tooltip; the content area reflows. Controlled — wire a toggle from app state. Read the state in custom header/footer content via useSidebar().

props.name: icons
props.description: Render the leading icon on each SidebarItem. Set false for a text-only rail. Ignored while collapsed (icon-only by definition).

props.name: variant
props.description: Where the rail lives. "app" is the page's chrome column — sticky, full viewport height, hidden below lg where AppHeader + BottomNav take over. "inline" is always visible and fills its parent's height, for a rail inside a bounded frame (a nested shell, an embedded preview). Use it instead of overriding the layout with !important classes.

props.name: surface
props.description: Which surface the rail is painted on. "rail" is its own --sidebar-* surface with a border — right for a full-height rail that frames the app, which a theme may tint or paint dark. "page" uses the page's surface and ink with no border — use it when a full-width header sits above the rail, where a tinted column starting under a page-coloured bar reads as pasted on. Use it instead of overriding bg-/text- classes, which the rail's re-pointed tokens defeat. In AppShell's sidebar slot with frame="inset", the rail's surface is also the shell's ground: from lg a "rail" rail drops its border (the gap around the main panel divides them) and either surface stretches to the shell's body row instead of sizing to the viewport. AppShell signals this to its sidebar slot only, so a Sidebar elsewhere in the page is unaffected.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the collapse ease and the current-page glide, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting.

subcomponents.name: SidebarHeader
subcomponents.description: The top of the rail, at least 64px tall (the chrome bar's height inside a compact Workspace, so it lines up with the WorkspaceBar beside it). It holds SidebarBrand and may take a second row under it, such as a search field or a notifications button: give that row basis-full and the header grows to hold it instead of clipping.

subcomponents.name: SidebarBrand
subcomponents.type: { mark: ReactNode; label: ReactNode; render?: useRender.RenderProp } + div props
subcomponents.description: The brand row, inside SidebarHeader, on the same grid as SidebarItem: mark in the icons' 24px slot, label on the labels' column, so a logo lines up with the nav below it without copying the rail's inset numbers. Collapsed, it shows the mark alone (named by a string label). render={<Link to="/" />} makes it the home link.

subcomponents.name: SidebarItem
subcomponents.type: { label: ReactNode; icon?: ReactNode; active?: boolean; badge?: ReactNode; render?: useRender.RenderProp } + button props
subcomponents.description: A single nav row, 44px on a page and 32px inside a compact scope such as a Workspace (the rail reads the density; nothing to set). label is the row text (inline when expanded, in a hover tooltip when collapsed); icon is the leading icon node (the consumer swaps fill weight for the active state); active marks the current route (accent fill + aria-current="page"); badge is a trailing node (e.g. a count) pushed to the row end and hidden when collapsed; render composes another element, e.g. render={<Link to="/x" />}.

subcomponents.name: SidebarGroup
subcomponents.description: A labelled run of SidebarItems inside SidebarNav ("Workspace", "Favorites"). The label starts on the items' icon column; collapsed, a hairline stands in for it and the label stays as the group's accessible name.

subcomponents.name: SidebarAccount
subcomponents.type: { avatar: ReactNode; label: ReactNode; detail?: ReactNode; indicator?: ReactNode | false; render?: useRender.RenderProp } + button props
subcomponents.description: The account row at the foot of the rail, inside SidebarFooter: the avatar in the icon slot (Avatar xs on a page rail, 2xs in a compact one), the label on the label column, one muted detail line, and an up-down chevron. Make it the trigger of the account Menu (render it through MenuTrigger render) and put Settings, appearance and sign-out there; it holds its fill while the menu is open. Collapsed, the avatar alone, with the label in a tooltip.

motion.why: The rail is the app's frame, present from first paint. It is not summoned, so it has no entrance.
Rows ease their hover fill (SideNav's row recipe on the rail rung), so moving down the nav reads as the pointer travelling rather than rows flashing.

The current-page fill is one element that travels to the new item when the page changes inside a persistent layout, so the marker reads as moving rather than one row dimming while another lights. It lands in place on first paint, and each item keeps its own fill as the server-render fallback. Expressive: `subtle` moves it at once.

Collapsing to the icon rail eases the width instead of jumping 192px in one frame, so the content beside it visibly takes the room the rail gave up. Nothing inside jumps — a collapsed row's centred icon and an expanded row's inset icon sit on the same column — and labels leave at once and fade back in on reopen, clipped to the rail meanwhile. It reflows the page for the length of the ease, which is acceptable for a deliberate user toggle and never happens on load. Expressive: `subtle` snaps.
Navigation chrome has no working state; a loading route shows it in the page.

a11y: SidebarNav renders a <nav> landmark.
Active item carries aria-current="page".
Items expose a focus-visible ring (sidebar-ring).
Collapsed: items take their accessible name from a string label (or aria-label) and reveal the visible label via the tooltip, so the rail stays usable by keyboard and screen readers.

components.name: SideNav
components.summary: A lightweight in-content vertical navigation list - the settings / docs sub-nav, distinct from the app-chrome Sidebar. Router-agnostic items, optional SideNavGroup sections, and an explicit active-state vocabulary for content rails or sidebar chrome.

usage.description: Use SideNav for vertical navigation inside a settings page, documentation area, dashboard rail, or sidebar chrome. It is router-agnostic: compose items with render={<Link />} and choose activeVariant based on whether the nav sits in content or app chrome.

bestPractices.description: Use aria-label on SideNav when a page contains more than one nav landmark.
Group related items with SideNavGroup when the rail has more than one conceptual area.
Use size='lg' and activeVariant='sidebar' when the nav is part of persistent app chrome.

Rows are rounded-sm, which nests in the usual rounded-lg p-2 frame. In any other rounded, padded frame give each item rounded-concentric-<outer>/<inset> — a same-radius row inset into a frame reads as a second system.
Use SideNav for bottom mobile navigation; use BottomNav in AppShell's bottomNav slot.
Mix content and sidebar active variants in the same rail unless individual items intentionally override the group.

anatomy.name: Nav
anatomy.description: The landmark container for the vertical navigation list.

anatomy.name: Group
anatomy.description: Optional labelled cluster of related navigation items.

anatomy.name: Item
anatomy.description: Interactive row with label, optional icon, optional badge, and active state.

anatomy.name: Badge
anatomy.description: Trailing count or state indicator aligned to the row end.

props.name: size
props.description: Density shared by all items. "md" (default) = the lightweight in-content sub-nav; "lg" = chrome-weight (larger label + icon, roomier rows) for a rail that pairs with the app Sidebar.

props.name: activeVariant
props.description: Active-state token vocabulary shared by all items. "content" uses bg-accent/text-accent-foreground for local rails inside the content area; "sidebar" uses bg-sidebar-accent/text-sidebar-accent-foreground for SideNavs rendered inside app chrome.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the current-page glide, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting.

subcomponents.name: SideNavItem
subcomponents.type: { label: ReactNode; icon?: ReactNode; active?: boolean; badge?: ReactNode; size?: "md" | "lg"; activeVariant?: "content" | "sidebar"; render?: useRender.RenderProp } + button props
subcomponents.description: A single row. label is the row text; icon is an optional leading icon; active marks the current sub-section (active fill + aria-current="page"); badge is a trailing node (e.g. a count) pushed to the row end; size and activeVariant override the enclosing SideNav per item; render composes another element, e.g. render={<Link to="/x" />}.

subcomponents.name: SideNavGroup
subcomponents.description: A labelled section within a SideNav - groups settings into areas. label renders an optional sentence-case caption heading above the group's items.

motion.why: In-page navigation arrives with the page it navigates.
Rows ease their hover fill and focus ring, so moving down a long nav reads as one pointer travelling rather than rows flashing in turn.

The current-item fill is one element that travels to the new row when the section changes inside a persistent layout, so the marker reads as moving rather than one row dimming while another lights. It lands in place on first paint, each row keeps its own fill as the server-render fallback, and the active row's heavier weight lands at once — font weight does not ease. Expressive: `subtle` moves it at once.
Navigation chrome has no working state; a loading section shows it in the content.

a11y: SideNav renders a <nav> landmark; pair multiple navs with aria-label to distinguish them.
The active item carries aria-current="page".
Items expose a focus-visible ring; the active state is reinforced by weight + fill, not colour alone.
Use activeVariant="content" for local in-page rails and activeVariant="sidebar" when a SideNav is placed on Sidebar chrome.

components.name: Skeleton
components.summary: Loading placeholder — a muted, shimmering block (rounded-md bg-muted motion-shimmer). Shape it with utility classes; rounded-full for circles.

usage.description: Use Skeleton to reserve space and hint at the shape of content while data is loading.

bestPractices.description: Match the approximate size and rhythm of the eventual content.
Use it for content regions where layout stability matters during loading.
Do not leave Skeleton visible after an error or empty state; switch to EmptyState (tone='destructive' for an error).
Do not use a skeleton whose shape differs from the content that replaces it. A mismatched placeholder causes a visible jump, which is worse than a brief spinner.

props.name: ...props
props.description: All native div props plus className. Size and shape the placeholder with utilities (h-*, w-*, size-*, rounded-full).

motion.why: A skeleton stands in for content that has not arrived; fading the placeholder in adds a wait before the wait.
Nothing here is interactive. A skeleton that reacted to the pointer would invite a click on a thing that cannot be clicked.
The skeleton has one state. Swapping it for real content is the parent's job, and the parent decides whether that swap is animated.

The sweep is the entire point of the component: it is what separates 'still loading' from 'loaded, and empty'. A static grey block is indistinguishable from a broken layout, which is why users reload the page. It is one band of light against the viewport, so every skeleton in a loading layout lights in sequence as a single wave rather than each block flashing at its own speed; each pass eases in, glides and settles, then rests off-screen before the next.

a11y: Purely presentational; the shimmer sweep is decorative, and it stops under reduced motion because motion-shimmer follows --motion-scale.
Mark the loading region with aria-busy="true" on a parent, and swap in real content (with the same layout) once loaded to avoid shift.

components.name: Slider
components.summary: Slider over Base UI Slider — pointer + keyboard control, ARIA slider wiring, and range support via multiple thumbs. The default export composes Root + Control + Track + Indicator + Thumb; pass an array value for a range.

usage.description: Use Slider for bounded numeric choices where approximate adjustment is faster than typing.

bestPractices.description: Use visible labels, min/max context, and value output when precision matters.
Choose steps that match the real granularity of the setting.
Do not use Slider when users must enter an exact arbitrary number; use NumberField.
Do not use it without showing the value. A slider with no numeric readout makes any precise choice guesswork — pair it with a ScrubField or a NumberField.

Do not resize the thumb's box on hover, focus, or drag. The thumb is a fixed-size hit target wrapping a decorative dot; only the dot scales. A target that grows under the cursor is a target nobody can learn, and WCAG 2.5.8 measures target size at rest. Restyle the dot, not the box.

anatomy.name: SliderRoot
anatomy.description: The controlled slider wrapper.

anatomy.name: SliderControl
anatomy.description: The interactive slider control region.

anatomy.name: SliderTrack
anatomy.description: The visible value range.

anatomy.name: SliderIndicator
anatomy.description: The filled portion of the track.

anatomy.name: SliderThumb
anatomy.description: The draggable handle.

anatomy.name: SliderValue
anatomy.description: A readable value display.

props.name: value
props.description: Controlled value. An array renders a range slider with one thumb per entry.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Uncontrolled initial value. An array renders a range slider.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Fires on every value change. value is a number (or number[] for a range).

props.name: min
props.description: Minimum allowed value.

props.name: max
props.description: Maximum allowed value.

props.name: step
props.description: Granularity the slider steps through. Snaps to multiples.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Ignore user interaction and dim the control.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Axis the slider tracks along. A vertical slider has no intrinsic length — give it a height (h-40, or flex-1 in a column).

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Accessible name, applied to each thumb's input (the element with role=slider). A range also names its group with it.

props.name: getAriaLabel
props.description: Per-thumb name for a range ("Minimum price" / "Maximum price"). Wins over aria-label on the thumbs.

props.name: getAriaValueText
props.description: What a screen reader announces for the value when the number alone is wrong — a seek bar's "1:23 of 3:45". For units or percent, `format` (Intl.NumberFormatOptions) is enough.

subcomponents.name: SliderRoot
subcomponents.description: The unstyled Base UI Root for custom composition — owns the value state and forwards value / defaultValue / onValueChange / min / max / step. Drag state surfaces via data-[dragging]. The default Slider export wires all the parts for you.

subcomponents.name: SliderControl
subcomponents.description: The interactive track lane — the positioning context the indicator and thumbs sit in; dims when disabled.

subcomponents.name: SliderTrack
subcomponents.description: The full-range rail beneath the indicator.

subcomponents.name: SliderIndicator
subcomponents.description: The filled portion from min (or the lower thumb) to the current value.

subcomponents.name: SliderThumb
subcomponents.description: A draggable handle: a fixed-size hit target wrapping a decorative dot. The dot rests small and scales to full size on hover, keyboard focus, and drag; the box never changes, so row metrics and the tap target hold. Range sliders render one per value; pass index for SSR. Interaction state surfaces via data-[dragging].

subcomponents.name: SliderValue
subcomponents.description: Formatted value readout for custom compositions (e.g. a live number beside the control).

motion.why: It arrives with the form or panel it sits in.

The thumb's dot grows from 12px to full size on hover and keyboard focus, and a little past it while dragging, on a spring. Only the paint resizes, never the hit target, so the growth says the thumb is live without moving where you have to aim.
The thumb and the filled range follow the pointer one-to-one, and keyboard steps land at once. An eased position would trail the drag and show a value the user has already moved past.
A slider commits as it moves; there is nothing to wait for.

a11y: Base UI provides role=slider, aria-valuemin/max/now, and arrow-key / Page Up-Down / Home-End control.

Each thumb is a focusable input[type=range] nested in the thumb element; keyboard focus raises a 2px ring on the thumb via has-[:focus-visible] (a bare focus-visible: on the thumb never fires, since the div itself is not focusable).

The thumb's hit area is a fixed 16px box at every state. Only the decorative inner dot resizes — rest 12px, full 16px on hover, keyboard focus, and drag — so the target a pointer or finger must land on never moves or changes size. Keyboard users, who never hover, get the enlarged dot from focus-visible.

The rest-to-full transition uses the motion duration/easing tokens, so it collapses to an instant state change under prefers-reduced-motion or MotionProvider off. The size change itself still happens: it reports interaction state, it is not decoration.
Range sliders get one thumb per value with minStepsBetweenValues honored.

Pass aria-label (or getAriaLabel for a range) so each handle has an accessible name. On Slider it reaches the thumb inputs; on a bare SliderRoot it only names the role=group — when composing, put aria-label / getAriaLabel on each SliderThumb, or label the Root with aria-labelledby or a Field, which Base UI does carry to the thumbs.
getAriaValueText sets aria-valuetext for values a number misreads (time, named steps).

<Slider value={range} onValueChange={setRange} aria-label="Price range" getAriaLabel={(i) => (i ? "Maximum price" : "Minimum price")} />

components.name: Sparkline
components.summary: A word-sized trend with no axes — a line, a line over a soft fill, or columns — sized by its container, for stat cards, table cells and sentences. Draws on as it scrolls into view.

usage.description: Use Sparkline next to a number to show where it has been — a KPI's last 30 days in a stat card, a row's trend in a table. It has no axes, tooltip or values to read off; when the reader needs those, use AreaChart or LineChart.

bestPractices.description: Pair it with the current value and its change in text; the sparkline shows only the shape.
Give it a label that names the measure and the period — the spoken summary adds the range and latest value.
Put two sparklines on one shared axis to compare them — each scales to its own data; use LineChart.
Use it as the only place a number appears; a shape without a value cannot be read off.

props.name: data
props.description: The values, oldest first.

props.name: label
props.description: What the line tracks ("Revenue, last 30 days"). The spoken summary adds the first and last values, low and high.

props.name: variant
props.description: A line, a line over a soft fill, or columns.

props.name: tone
props.description: Colour by role.

props.name: className
props.description: Sizes it; the drawing stretches to fit.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. Drawing on (or rising) is the flourish, so `subtle` and `off` show the finished line.

props.name: animate
props.description: Draw on (or rise) when it scrolls into view. `animate={false}` is `motion="subtle"`.
props.deprecated: motion="subtle" (what animate={false} now maps to) or motion="off"

props.name: locale
props.description: BCP 47 locale for default number and date formatting.

motion.why: Once on screen the line draws on (or the bars rise, in sequence). On the motion tokens; reduced motion shows the finished drawing. The arrival is expressive: it plays at the full motion level only, so `motion="subtle"` (or a subtle app policy) shows the finished line.
Not interactive: it has no tooltip or focus.
New data redraws in place; a word-sized chart animating on every update would distract from the number beside it.
No indeterminate state.

a11y: Rendered role=img with an aria-label built from `label` and the data: "Revenue, last 30 days: from 120 to 184, low 96, high 190".
It is not focusable and has no tooltip, so the number it accompanies must be in text beside it.

components.name: Spinner
components.summary: Pure SVG activity indicator. No Base UI, no icon dependency — a role=status ring (faint track + rounded-cap arc) that inherits the current text color. Size with the size prop (sm / md / lg), color with text-*.

usage.description: Use Spinner for short indeterminate waits where the user cannot know exact progress.

bestPractices.description: Use it in compact panels or places where layout is already stable. In a button, use Button's loading prop rather than placing a Spinner by hand — it disables the button, sets aria-busy and sizes the spinner to the button's icon.
Pair it with accessible loading text when the surrounding label is not enough.
Do not use Spinner as the only content for long waits or full page loading.
Do not use it without an accessible name or a nearby status message. A spinning icon is invisible to a screen reader, so the wait is announced as nothing at all.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label announced by screen readers while visible (sets aria-label on the role=status element).

props.name: appearance
props.description: ring is the default indicator; dots are three bouncing dots, softer, for chat and inline text.

props.name: size
props.description: One scale for both appearances: ring 14 / 16 / 24px, dots 4 / 6 / 8px.

props.name: className
props.description: Color (text-*); the ring's strokes use currentColor, so it follows the text color. Size with the size prop — a size-* class still overrides the ring for an off-scale context (Button sizes its own spinner this way), but is not the way to pick a size.

motion.why: A spinner already signals a wait. Fading it in delays the signal for exactly as long as the user most needs it.
It is a status indicator, not a control.
One state. Whatever replaces it on completion owns that change.

The rotation is the whole component — it is the only thing distinguishing 'working' from 'frozen'. motion-spin rather than Tailwind's animate-spin because the built-in ignores --motion-scale, so the reduced-motion policy cannot freeze it.

a11y: Wrapped in role=status, a polite live region, with an aria-label (default 'Loading').
Color comes from currentColor; pair with a text-* token for adequate contrast.
Spins with the motion-spin utility, which follows --motion-scale, so it slows and stops with the motion setting and reduced-motion.

components.name: StatusBar
components.summary: The bottom chrome strip of a Workspace: ambient document facts — dimensions, counts, sync state — in the micro type tier.

usage.description: Use StatusBar for the persistent facts about a document that otherwise have nowhere to live: size, counts, selection state, sync or connection status. Everything in it is ambient — it reports, it does not command. Pair it with Workspace's statusBar slot.

bestPractices.description: Put document-scoped facts here — dimensions, layer or record counts, saved/sync state — so panels stop competing for that space.
Use StatusBarGroup with align="end" for the trailing cluster, and StatusBarSeparator between related facts.
Render numeric facts in the UI num tier so a changing value doesn't shift the strip's layout.
Make it the only route to an action. It's ambient chrome at the micro tier — anything essential needs a real control elsewhere too.
Put zoom here. Anchor zoom to the canvas it acts on, which is where every reference tool puts it.
Use it for transient feedback like a save confirmation — that's Toast. A status bar states what is true, not what just happened.

Derive a fact here separately from the surface that shows it, or from something expensive to recompute. The strip re-renders with the document, so read the same value the canvas or panel uses: a status bar that reports max(asset sizes) while the canvas reports something else is a bug types cannot catch, because both are numbers.

anatomy.name: StatusBarGroup
anatomy.description: A cluster of items; align="end" pins it to the trailing edge.

anatomy.name: StatusBarSeparator
anatomy.description: A decorative dot between related facts; aria-hidden.

subcomponents.name: StatusBarGroup
subcomponents.description: A cluster of status items; `end` pushes it to the trailing edge.

subcomponents.name: StatusBarSeparator
subcomponents.description: A decorative middle dot between facts. aria-hidden, since order conveys grouping.

a11y: Renders a <footer>, so the strip is a discoverable region rather than an anonymous row of text.
Separators are aria-hidden — a screen reader announcing 'middle dot' between every fact is noise.
Micro-tier text is small by design; never put information here that exists nowhere else.

components.name: StatusDot
components.summary: A small colored status dot. Tone variants encode state via semantic tone tokens; sizes scale the diameter. Decorative (aria-hidden) — pair with text. Optional pulse adds a live ping ring.

usage.description: Use StatusDot as a compact visual state cue next to text, avatars, rows, or labels. It is decorative by design, so pair it with visible text or use `<Badge appearance="plain" dot>` when the label and dot should travel together — that is the labelled status line, not a hand-built row.

bestPractices.description: Place StatusDot beside a readable state label, person name, or row title.
Use pulse only for live or in-progress states that are actively changing.
Use the dot as the only status indicator; it is aria-hidden and color alone is not enough.
Mix many dot sizes in the same list. Keep row indicators visually consistent.

anatomy.name: Dot
anatomy.description: The small tone-colored circle. It is decorative and hidden from assistive tech.

anatomy.name: Pulse ring
anatomy.description: Optional motion ring for in-progress or live states.

props.name: tone
props.description: Semantic color of the dot, or a palette family (red … pink) for a category legend.

props.name: size
props.description: Dot diameter.

props.name: pulse
props.description: Wrap the dot in an animated ping ring to signal a live state.

a11y: Rendered aria-hidden — purely decorative. Convey status in adjacent text, not color alone.
A dot conveys state through colour alone, which fails for colour-blind users and announces as nothing. It must always sit beside text that states the same thing, or carry its own accessible name.

examples.label: Tones
examples.code: <Row gap={2}><StatusDot tone="3" /><StatusDot tone="info" /><StatusDot tone="warning" /><StatusDot tone="destructive" /></Row>

components.name: Stepper
components.summary: Where the user is in a multi-step flow — an ordered list of numbered steps, horizontal or vertical, each complete, current, upcoming or in error, with aria-current="step" on the current one. `indicator="dot"` turns it into a timeline of events (an order's delivery) with dots instead of numbers.

usage.description: Use Stepper above or beside a flow that is split into a known, small number of named steps — checkout, onboarding, an import wizard — so the user can see how far they have come and what is left. It reports position; the flow's own Back and Continue buttons move it.

bestPractices.description: Drive it from one number (`current`) and override a single step's `status` only for what a number cannot say — a completed step that now needs attention is `status="error"`.
Name steps with a word or two ("Shipping", "Payment"). Go vertical when steps need a description or there are more than five; horizontal titles truncate first.
Give completed steps `onSelect` only when going back to edit them actually works, and keep the user's later answers when they do.
Do not use Stepper for a task with unknown length or for a percentage. That is Progress; a stepper promises a fixed set of named stops.
Do not use it as navigation between independent sections. Sections the user can visit in any order are Tabs; a stepper implies each step depends on the one before.
Do not make upcoming steps pressable to skip ahead. A step that looks reachable but is not is worse than one that is plainly locked.

anatomy.name: Stepper
anatomy.description: The ordered list. Takes `current` and `orientation`, and an aria-label naming the flow.

anatomy.name: StepperItem
anatomy.description: One step: a numbered disc (a check when complete, a warning mark on error) — or, with `indicator="dot"`, a dot centred on the title's first line — a title, and an optional description.

anatomy.name: Connector
anatomy.description: The line to the next step, filled once this step is complete. Drawn automatically between items.

props.name: current
props.description: Zero-based index of the current step. Earlier steps derive complete, later ones upcoming.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Horizontal for a short flow across the top of a form; vertical for long flows, narrow columns or steps with descriptions. A horizontal stepper narrower than 28rem (a phone) compacts itself: every disc stays, only the current step's title shows, and the other titles stay for screen readers. No breakpoint code needed.

props.name: indicator
props.description: `number` for a flow the user moves through; `dot` for a timeline of events (delivery tracking, a document's history) where the position number adds nothing. The dot centres on the title's first line and scales with its type at every density.

props.name: statusLabels
props.description: Screen-reader status words appended to each title (Completed, Current step, Not started, Needs attention). Override to localize.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the flow ("Checkout progress"). Every Stepper needs one.

subcomponents.name: StepperItem
subcomponents.type: { title: ReactNode; description?: ReactNode; status?: StepStatus; onSelect?: () => void } + li props
subcomponents.description: One step. `status` overrides the derived state; `onSelect` makes the disc and title a button for returning to the step.

motion.why: The stepper frames the flow and is on screen before any step is. Animating it in would compete with the step content, which is what changed.
Only steps with onSelect respond, and the eased underline is what tells a returning user that this completed step can be reopened while the upcoming ones cannot.
When the user continues, the disc they leave fills and its connector darkens. Easing the colour makes that read as one step completing rather than the whole bar re-rendering.
A step is a place, not a process. Saving or validating between steps belongs on the Continue button's loading state; a pulsing disc would suggest the step itself is busy.

a11y: Renders an ordered list, so assistive tech announces the step count and each step's position.
The current step carries aria-current="step"; every title also gets a visually hidden status word (Completed, Not started, Needs attention), so state never depends on colour or the disc glyph.
Discs and connectors are aria-hidden — the number is already the list position.
Steps with onSelect render as native buttons with a visible focus ring; steps without it are not focusable.

examples.label: Checkout
examples.code:
<Stepper current={1} aria-label="Checkout progress">
	<StepperItem title="Cart" />
	<StepperItem title="Shipping" />
	<StepperItem title="Payment" />
	<StepperItem title="Review" />
</Stepper>

	<StepperItem title="Invite team" description="3 people invited" />
	<StepperItem title="Connect data" description="Choose a source to import from" />
	<StepperItem title="Launch" />
</Stepper>

<Stepper orientation="vertical" indicator="dot" current={2} aria-label="Delivery status">
	<StepperItem title="Order placed" description="Oct 9, 10:14 AM" />
	<StepperItem title="Printed and packed" description="Oct 10, 4:02 PM" />
	<StepperItem title="Out for delivery" description="Arriving today by 6 PM" />
	<StepperItem title="Delivered" />
</Stepper>

	<StepperItem title="Cart" onSelect={() => console.log("cart")} />

</Stepper>

components.name: StreamingText
components.summary: Prose arriving from a live source, a token at a time. Each token resolves out of blur, the trailing edge stays soft while more is coming, and a steady caret marks the write head.

usage.description: Use StreamingText for text whose final length is unknown while it renders — a model's answer, a live transcript, a log line being written. It is the counterpart to ThinkingOrb and Spinner: those cover the wait BEFORE the first token, this covers the arrival of the tokens themselves.

bestPractices.description: In a chat, read `sable docs building-a-chat`: one status drives `streaming` and the composer, a regenerated answer takes a new key (the text is append-only), and the finished turn is announced once.

Grow `text` and let the component do the rest. It assumes an append-only string and keys units by index, so React mounts only the new spans — re-rendering a longer string animates what was added and leaves what the reader has already read alone.
Drop `streaming` to false the moment the source closes. That is what removes the caret and the softened tail, and their disappearance is the only signal the reader gets that the answer is complete.
Turn `caret` off when something adjacent already reports the wait — a spinner in the message header, a status row beneath. Two indicators for one wait read as two things happening.

Do not use it for text that is already complete. Staging known text on scroll is TextReveal (a `motion` export, not a component folder), which computes a stagger from the full string; StreamingText cannot, because nothing here knows the length. Using it for static prose animates the whole paragraph on every mount and says 'still generating' about something that finished.
Do not wrap it in an aria-live region. Every token would be announced, which is unusable; the component sets `aria-busy` instead. Announce once when the turn settles, from whatever owns the turn.

Do not pass `split="char"` for paragraph-length text. It is one element per character — thousands of nodes for an answer, each with its own animation — and word-splitting is indistinguishable at prose reading speed. Reserve it for a headline-length string.

anatomy.name: Container
anatomy.description: The paragraph (or `as` element). Carries `aria-busy` while output is incomplete.

anatomy.name: Unit
anatomy.description: One word or character. Animates once on mount and never again; the newest one carries the softened tail while streaming.

anatomy.name: Caret
anatomy.description: The write head, shown while streaming. Steady rather than blinking — see `motion-caret`.

props.name: text
props.description: The text received so far. Assumed append-only: the component keys units by index precisely so a grown string mounts only its new spans.

props.name: streaming
props.description: Whether more is still coming. Drives the caret, the softened trailing edge, and `aria-busy`.

props.name: as
props.description: Render container element.

props.name: split
props.description: Split granularity. `char` is one element per character — short strings only.

props.name: caret
props.description: Show the caret while streaming. Turn it off when something adjacent already reports the wait.

motion.why: Each token resolves out of blur rather than fading. A fade makes every word a separate event; blur reads as the word coming into focus, so a paragraph arrives as one sentence being written instead of a queue of arrivals.
It is prose, not a control. Selecting and copying it is the only interaction, and both are native.

There is no state to move between — streaming to complete is marked by the caret and tail leaving, not by the text changing. Animating the whole paragraph on completion would re-stage text the reader already read.

The caret is the write head, and it is deliberately STEADY (`data-streaming="true"` suppresses the blink). A blink during arrival puts two rhythms on screen — text advancing at one rate, a caret flashing at another — and the flashing one carries no information the moving text has not already given.

a11y: The text is real text in the accessibility tree: units are ordinary spans, not aria-hidden fragments, so a screen reader concatenates them into the sentence.
`aria-busy` is set on the container while `streaming` is true, marking the output incomplete without announcing each token.
The caret is `aria-hidden` — it is a rendering of the write head, and a screen reader has no use for it.
Under reduced motion or with MotionProvider off, no unit animates and no tail is softened; text simply appears as it arrives.

examples.label: Streaming an answer
examples.code: <StreamingText text={answer} streaming={pending} />

examples.label: Inside a message, with the wait reported elsewhere
examples.code: <Message align="start"><StreamingText text={answer} streaming={pending} caret={false} /></Message>

examples.label: A headline resolving character by character
examples.code: <StreamingText as="h2" split="char" className="text-heading-2" text={headline} streaming={pending} />

components.name: Switch
components.summary: Binary on/off toggle for immediate-effect settings. Track fills with the primary tone when checked; the thumb slides on a spring-eased transform (mirrored in RTL). The thumb is white in both states, like every physical toggle, and turns dark only on a near-white track (a dark mode's light primary). Themes can set --theme-switch-thumb-on.

usage.description: Use Switch for immediate on/off settings that take effect as a persistent preference or mode.

bestPractices.description: Use it for binary settings where the label describes the enabled state.
Make the current state obvious through both position and accessible text.
Do not phrase the label as a negative, such as "Don't send read receipts". Turning off a negative is a double negative, and the user has to solve it before they can act.
Do not use Switch for one-time agreement, multi-select choices, or submit-only booleans.
Do not use a Switch whose effect is not immediately visible somewhere. A toggle flipped with no observable consequence gives no confirmation it worked, so the user flips it again to check.

props.name: checked
props.description: Controlled on/off state. Pair with onCheckedChange. Omit for an uncontrolled switch.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: Initial state for an uncontrolled switch.

props.name: onCheckedChange
props.description: Fired when the switch is toggled. Note: Base UI passes a second eventDetails arg — not the common (checked) => void, so a single-arg handler must widen its signature.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Dims the control and ignores user interaction.

props.name: readOnly
props.description: Prevents toggling while keeping the control fully visible.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the switch as required when inside a form.

props.name: name
props.description: Identifies the field when the enclosing form is submitted.

motion.why: Switches arrive as part of a settings list. Animating each one in turns a form into a title sequence.
The track is small and its hover change is subtle; without the ease the colour shift reads as a rendering glitch rather than a reaction.

The thumb sliding IS the affordance — it shows the control has two ends and which one you are now at. Teleporting the thumb makes on and off two unrelated pictures, and users re-read the label to work out which they are looking at. motion-interactive is the right recipe because it declares `translate`, so the thumb transform and the track colour ease on one timeline instead of two.
A switch commits instantly. If the write is slow enough to need a pending state, the surrounding form owns that, not the control.

a11y: Renders Base UI's Switch with a hidden native <input> — role, ARIA, and keyboard (Space/Enter) toggling come for free.
Focus-visible draws a 2px ring in the --ring token.
Disabled state sets cursor-not-allowed and 50% opacity; readOnly keeps full contrast but blocks changes.
Give it an accessible name: wrap it in <Field label=… orientation="horizontal">, which wires the label for you.

examples.label: Default (uncontrolled)
examples.code: <Switch defaultChecked />

examples.label: Controlled
examples.code: <Switch checked={on} onCheckedChange={setOn} />

examples.label: Disabled
examples.code: <Switch disabled defaultChecked />

examples.label: With a label
examples.code: <Field label="Reduce motion" orientation="horizontal"><Switch defaultChecked /></Field>

components.name: Table
components.summary: Styled native table subcomponents (Table, TableHeader, TableBody, TableFooter, TableRow, TableHead, TableCell, TableCaption). Horizontally scrollable frame, hairline row borders, hover-lift, and selectable rows via data-selected.

usage.description: Use Table for structured data with consistent columns and rows. Use DataTable when the table should be data-driven with sorting or empty state behavior, and use lists or cards when each item has a different shape.

bestPractices.description: Use TableCaption and TableHead so the table has a clear purpose and column semantics.
Keep cells concise and scannable; compose Badge, StatusDot, Avatar, or Button only when they clarify the row.
Use the built-in horizontal frame for overflow instead of squeezing columns until content becomes unreadable.

Put a table in a card with `<CardContent flush>`. The first and last columns then take the card's own padding (`--table-edge-px`), so they line up with the CardHeader at any density. Never hand-set `pl-6`/`pr-6` on edge cells.
Use Table for heterogeneous items with no stable columns. Use Card, Entity, or a list composition instead.
Put every possible action in every row. Use one primary row action, an OverflowMenu, or row detail navigation.

anatomy.name: Caption
anatomy.description: Accessible summary of what the table contains.

anatomy.name: Header
anatomy.description: Column labels rendered with TableHead cells.

anatomy.name: Body
anatomy.description: Rows and cells containing the tabular data.

anatomy.name: Footer
anatomy.description: Optional totals or summary row group.

props.name: className
props.description: The root renders a horizontally scrollable frame around a native <table>; forwards all native table attributes plus className. Each subcomponent likewise forwards its element's native attributes + className.

subcomponents.name: TableHeader
subcomponents.description: The header row group (thead).

subcomponents.name: TableBody
subcomponents.description: The data row group (tbody).

subcomponents.name: TableFooter
subcomponents.description: Summary row group (tfoot) with a muted fill.

subcomponents.name: TableRow
subcomponents.description: A row (tr) — hairline bottom border, hover lift, and a selected state via the data-selected attribute.

subcomponents.name: TableHead
subcomponents.description: A column header cell (th) in muted label styling. `numeric` marks a number column: end-aligned, tabular figures — set it on the column's cells too.

subcomponents.name: TableCell
subcomponents.description: A data cell (td). `numeric` end-aligns it with tabular figures, matching its column's header.

subcomponents.name: TableCaption
subcomponents.description: Accessible description of the table (caption), muted.

motion.why: A table renders with the page it sits in. Staggering rows in delays reading data someone opened to scan.
Body rows ease to a muted wash under the pointer. Across a wide row, the wash is what keeps the eye on the right line, and eased it follows the cursor down the table rather than strobing.
A `data-selected` row's fill eases in on every cell together, so the selected row reads as one band being set rather than a stamp.
Table is markup. Loading rows are Skeletons, which carry the shimmer.

a11y: Renders semantic native table elements (thead/tbody/tfoot/th/td/caption) preserving built-in table semantics.
Use TableHead (th) for column headers and TableCaption for an accessible description.
Mark the active row with the data-selected attribute for a visible selected state.

components.name: Tabs
components.summary: Tabs over Base UI Tabs (roving focus, arrow-key nav, ARIA tablist wiring) in two styles: underline (page sections) or pill (compact switchers), with one indicator that glides to the active tab. Tabs (Root) + TabsList + TabsTrigger + TabsPanel.

usage.description: Use Tabs to switch between related panels within the same page context.

bestPractices.description: Use tabs when each panel is peer content and users may compare or switch often.

In tool chrome (a WorkspaceBar, a compact panel header) use variant="pill" for a view switch such as Overview / Issues / Updates: it reads as a control beside the bar's other controls. Underline is the page-section idiom; inside a WorkspaceBar it sits on the bar's hairline rather than drawing its own.
Keep tab labels short and make the active tab unmistakable.
Use variant="pill" for a short switcher inside a card or toolbar (Preview / Code, List / Grid); keep the default underline for sections of a page.
Do not use Tabs for unrelated pages or primary navigation that needs distinct URLs.
Do not use tabs for sequential steps. Tabs are peer views the user returns to in any order; a process with an order needs a stepper, or the user will skip ahead.

anatomy.name: TabsList
anatomy.description: The list of tab triggers.

anatomy.name: TabsTrigger
anatomy.description: One selectable tab.

anatomy.name: TabsPanel
anatomy.description: The content associated with a trigger.

anatomy.name: TabsContent
anatomy.description: Compatibility alias for panel content.

props.name: Tabs (Root)
props.type: Base UI Tabs.Root props (value, defaultValue, onValueChange, orientation)
props.description: Controls the active tab. Uncontrolled via defaultValue; controlled via value + onValueChange.

props.name: motion
props.description: On Tabs: how much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the glide, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting.

subcomponents.name: TabsList
subcomponents.type: Base UI Tabs.List props (activateOnFocus, loopFocus) + variant?: "underline" | "pill" + className
subcomponents.description: The tablist row. variant="underline" (default) draws a divider rule beneath the triggers; variant="pill" drops the rule and fills the active trigger, which takes the theme's button shape (--button-radius). Triggers inherit the variant. It renders the gliding indicator (Base UI Tabs.Indicator) itself, so do not add one.

subcomponents.name: TabsTrigger
subcomponents.type: Base UI Tabs.Tab props (value, disabled) + className
subcomponents.description: A single tab button. value pairs it with the panel of the same value.

subcomponents.name: TabsPanel
subcomponents.type: Base UI Tabs.Panel props (value, keepMounted) + className
subcomponents.description: The content shown when the matching trigger is active.

subcomponents.name: TabsContent
subcomponents.description: Re-export of TabsPanel for consumers that prefer this name.

motion.why: Tabs arrive with the section they organise. An entrance of their own would announce navigation chrome louder than the content it navigates.
The label steps from muted to foreground under the pointer; the ease is what makes that read as an answer rather than a repaint.

One underline (or pill) travels to the new tab and stretches to its width. A mark that teleports makes the reader re-find the selection on every click; one that moves is tracked without looking. Expressive: motion="subtle" lands it in place. Each tab's own mark is the fallback until the indicator has measured, so the server render is already right.

The incoming panel fades in, opacity only, so a switch between two similar panels still registers. Skipped on first render (activation direction "none") so a page of tabs does not fade in on load, and the outgoing panel leaves layout at once so a quick second click never stacks both.
Switching tabs is synchronous. A panel that loads data shows its own Skeleton or Spinner inside the panel, where the wait is.

a11y: Base UI provides the tablist/tab/tabpanel roles, aria-selected, and roving tabindex.
Arrow keys move between tabs; Home/End jump to first/last; panels are linked via aria-controls.
Active tab styling reads from the data-active attribute; disabled tabs from data-disabled. Disabled tabs are skipped by arrow-key navigation.
Keyboard focus shows a ring on the focused trigger in both variants; the panel remains focusable.
The gliding indicator is role="presentation" decoration; aria-selected on the tab carries the state.

components.name: Textarea
components.summary: Styled native multi-line text control. Soft-square, the theme's field surface, --ring focus, and an aria-invalid destructive error state.

usage.description: Use Textarea for multi-line freeform text entry such as notes, descriptions, or messages.

bestPractices.description: Use labels, helper text, and character limits when expectations are specific.
Size it to the expected amount of input without making the page feel blocked.

Keep a focusable field at 16px or larger on mobile. iOS Safari zooms the whole page when a focused textarea computes under 16px and never zooms back out. Textarea handles this itself — below the sm breakpoint it renders text-body-lg (17px) and returns to text-body-md at sm and up. Build a custom field the same way: a second paired tier under a max-sm: variant, never a hand-set font-size.
Do not override the type with a page tier below 16px (text-body-md, text-body-sm) without a >=16px mobile arm — that reintroduces the iOS focus zoom.
Do not use Textarea for short single-line values; use Input.
Do not leave it at the default height for long-form input. A two-row textarea for a paragraph forces the user to write through a letterbox.

props.name: aria-invalid
props.description: When true, swaps the input border to the destructive token to signal a validation error.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Dims the control to 50% and blocks pointer interaction.

props.name: rows
props.description: Native textarea row count. The floor is min-h-20 on the spacing scale, so it moves with density.

props.name: autoResize
props.description: Grows to fit content via CSS field-sizing: content (no JS). The min-height stays the floor; browsers without field-sizing fall back to the fixed min-height.

props.name: ...props
props.description: All native textarea attributes (value, placeholder, onChange, name, ref, …).

a11y: Renders a native <textarea> — label association, keyboard, and screen-reader semantics come for free.
Renders through Base UI's Field.Control: inside a Field it picks up the label, description, error and validity wiring from context.
Pair with a <label htmlFor> (or aria-label) for an accessible name.
Set aria-invalid and reference an error message via aria-describedby to announce validation failures.
Focus-visible draws a 2px ring in the --ring token.

components.name: ThemeSelector
components.summary: A presentational radiogroup for choosing a Sable design theme from theme manifests — tiles that draw each theme as a miniature of its own interface (its colours, type and corner shape) for a settings page, or compact rows for tool chrome. Pair it with useSableTheme().themeId and setThemeId when the app uses SableThemeProvider.

usage.description: Use ThemeSelector wherever a person picks a theme. The default `cards` layout is page-register furniture: a miniature of each theme's interface (its background, "Aa" in its display face, a card, and a primary button in its own corner shape), with the name and a caption only where one distinguishes it (the default theme, or a single-mode theme). Use `layout="list"` in tool chrome, a popover, or any docked panel — five cards is the wrong object for a 256px surface, however it is sized. For colour mode (light/dark/system) use ThemeSwitcher, which is a segmented control and belongs in chrome as-is.

bestPractices.description: Use layout="list" in a popover, a menu, or a docked panel. Rows sit on the --control-sm ladder and still show a small tile of each theme, so the choice stays visible rather than described. Rows take `sable-frame-inner`, so host the list in a sable-frame (`sable-frame sable-surface sable-surface-popover sable-frame-popover` — PopoverContent is not one; give it that class list, or its p-4 leaves the rows unnested) and their corners nest concentrically.
Pass mode={useSableTheme().mode} so every preview renders in the colour mode actually in use, rather than in each theme's manifest default.

Use ThemeSelector when switching is free: it is a radio group, so arrow keys check the next theme and onValueChange fires on every press — the page restyles as you go, which is the point of a live theme switcher. When a switch has a cost (it opens a "discard changes?" confirm, loads fonts, or resets other settings), use a DisclosurePicker list instead, with a `ThemePreview size="sm"` as each option's `media`: arrows only move there, and Enter, Space or a click commits.

Load each theme's fonts in the host app. Every card carries a type specimen in that theme's own face so people can compare typography as well as color. A theme whose fonts are not loaded falls back to system-ui, and its specimen stops telling the truth.

Add a viewport breakpoint to force a column count — `className="sm:grid-cols-1"` or similar. `sm:` keys off the VIEWPORT, not this component's container, so on a wide screen it does nothing for a narrow parent. The cards grid already reflows on its own width via auto-fit.
Put the cards layout in workspace chrome. It was built for a settings page; in a 256px popover the cards clip their labels to a single character and grow to roughly twice their intended height.

Use ThemeSelector for light / dark / system colour mode. That is ThemeSwitcher — a segmented control. This picks the design theme, which is a different axis entirely, and the two are frequently confused.

anatomy.name: ThemeSelector
anatomy.description: The radiogroup of themes, as cards or list rows.

anatomy.name: ThemePreview
anatomy.description: The tile each option draws, exported for showing a theme outside the picker — the row naming the current theme, or the `media` of each option in a commit-on-Enter DisclosurePicker list.

props.name: value
props.description: The currently selected Sable design theme id.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called with the next design theme id when an option is chosen.

props.name: themes
props.description: Theme manifests to render. Defaults to Sable's built-in themes.

props.name: mode
props.description: Preview mode for each theme's tile. Pass useSableTheme().mode to match the current color mode; omitted cards use their manifest defaultMode.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label for the radiogroup.

props.name: layout
props.description: Presentation. "cards" is the page-register picker (~144px per card); "list" is one compact --control-sm row per theme, for chrome and popovers. A presentation variant, not a size — "list" is not "cards, smaller" — which is why it is a prop rather than a density scope.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged onto the outer radiogroup grid.

subcomponents.name: ThemePreview
subcomponents.description: The tile each option draws: the theme as a miniature of itself (background, "Aa" in its display face, a card, a primary button in its own corner shape), in its own scope. Exported for anywhere that shows a theme outside the picker, e.g. a row naming the current preset, or each option of a DisclosurePicker list where a pick has a cost. Sized in the caller's spacing unit, so it lines up with the row it sits in.

motion.why: It sits in a settings panel or a popover, which owns the entrance.
List rows ease their hover fill like Menu and Select rows, so a theme list beside a menu reads as the same kind of row.
In the grid, the theme's name brightens on hover, eased. The preview tile's outline steps rather than easing — outline is not in the recipe's transition list — so the name carries the motion.
The check fades into the chosen row and out of the old one, so the choice reads as moving, at the same moment the whole interface repaints in the new theme.
Applying a theme is synchronous: the whole interface repaints at once, and that repaint is the feedback.

a11y: The container is role="radiogroup" with an aria-label; each card is a role="radio" button with aria-checked reflecting the selected theme.

Standard radio keyboard: arrow keys move the check — calling onValueChange on each press — and Space checks the focused option. That instant switching is right for a free, reversible choice; where a switch has a cost, use a DisclosurePicker list (a listbox: arrows move, Enter commits) with ThemePreview tiles instead.
Focus-visible draws a 2px ring on the focused card.
The selected card wears the shared selection-card checked ring (the same as RadioCard and CheckboxCard), a muted fill and a check icon, so selection does not rely on colour alone.
Presentational only: it does not change the document theme; pass useSableTheme().setThemeId or apply the change in onValueChange.

examples.label: When a switch has a cost: a DisclosurePicker list of ThemePreview tiles
examples.imports: import { DisclosurePicker, DisclosurePickerList, DisclosurePickerOption, DisclosurePickerPanel, DisclosurePickerTrigger, ThemePreview, useSableTheme } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: With SableThemeProvider
examples.code:
const { themeId, setThemeId, themes, mode } = useSableTheme()
<ThemeSelector value={themeId} onValueChange={setThemeId} themes={themes} mode={mode} />

examples.label: Controlled

const [themeId, setThemeId] = useState<ThemeId>("sable")
<ThemeSelector value={themeId} onValueChange={setThemeId} />

// Five 144px cards is the wrong object for a 256px surface. Rows are.
<PopoverContent align="end" className="w-64 p-3">
  <ThemeSwitcher value={preference} onValueChange={setPreference} />
  <ThemeSelector layout="list" value={themeId} onValueChange={setThemeId} mode={mode} />
</PopoverContent>

components.name: ThemeSwitcher
components.summary: A segmented light / dark / system switch. Presentational: it renders the selected color preference and reports changes via onValueChange; pair it with useSableTheme() when the app uses SableThemeProvider. A radiogroup of three icon buttons (sun / moon / desktop).

usage.description: Use ThemeSwitcher for light, dark, and system color mode preference.

bestPractices.description: Use it where users expect appearance controls, such as app chrome or settings.
Respect persisted system or user preference when initializing the control.
Do not use ThemeSwitcher to choose brand themes or component style presets.

Do not hand-build another segmented capsule for a different choice. ThemeSwitcher wears the shared segmented look (lib/segmented); for any other single-select switch use ToggleGroup appearance="segmented".
Do not omit the `system` option or default to a hardcoded mode. Overriding the OS preference is the single most common accessibility complaint about theme controls.

props.name: value
props.description: The currently selected color preference.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called with the next color preference when an option is chosen.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label for the radiogroup.

props.name: motion
props.description: How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the glide, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged onto the outer radiogroup container.

motion.why: It arrives with the header or settings row it lives in; a theme control that announces itself competes with the page it themes.
The icon steps from muted to foreground under the pointer, which is what tells an icon-only segment it is a control.
A settle under the press confirms the tap on a 28px target before the theme change repaints the page around it.

One pill slides to the chosen mode, stepping by option + gap on the spacing scale, so light → dark reads as the same control moving, not three icons trading a fill. Expressive: motion="subtle" lands it in place.
Changing the theme is synchronous; the repaint is the feedback.

a11y: The container is role="radiogroup" with an aria-label; each option is role="radio" with aria-checked reflecting the selected value.
Each icon button carries an aria-label (Light / Dark / System) plus a title tooltip, since the visual is icon-only.
Focus-visible draws a 2px ring on the focused option; selection styling reads from aria-checked.
Presentational only: it does not change the document theme; pass useSableTheme().setPreference or apply the change in onValueChange.

examples.code:
const [theme, setTheme] = useState<ThemeMode>("system")
<ThemeSwitcher value={theme} onValueChange={setTheme} />

examples.code:

<ThemeSwitcher value={preference} onValueChange={setPreference} />
