examples.code: <ThemeSwitcher value="light" onValueChange={setTheme} />

examples.label: Subtle motion
examples.code: <ThemeSwitcher value={theme} onValueChange={setTheme} motion="subtle" />

components.name: ThinkingOrb
components.summary: Canvas dot-cloud 'agent is thinking' indicator. Three generated modes (orbit / globe / mesh) drawn from pure math — no icon dependency, no animation library. Ink follows currentColor; size steps are separately tuned.

usage.description: Use ThinkingOrb while an AI agent is working and there is nothing specific to report yet — before the first token streams, or between tool calls. It is a richer, more characterful sibling of Spinner for the one place in a product where the wait is the experience.

bestPractices.description: Reserve it for the single active agent state — the composer, the streaming message header, a standalone thinking screen. One orb on screen reads as intent; several read as decoration.

Switch mode to say what kind of work is happening: orbit for generic thinking, globe while searching or retrieving, mesh while relating sources or running tools. Pair it with a text status so the phase is legible without decoding the animation.
Use size="sm" inline in a message row or composer and size="lg" only when the orb is the main thing on screen. The size steps are separately tuned, not scaled, so the small one stays legible.

Do not put one on every row of a list or in a repeated skeleton. Each orb runs its own animation frame loop painting hundreds of arcs; use Skeleton for content-shaped waits and Spinner inside buttons.
Do not use it for a determinate wait. It carries no sense of how far along anything is — reach for Progress when a percentage exists.
Do not rely on the animation alone to announce the wait. Give the label a short constant phrase (it is the role=status announcement) or place a status message next to it.

Do not pass a label that changes while the orb is up. It is the accessible name of a live region, so every change re-announces the whole thing — feed it a per-token phase and a screen reader interrupts on each delta: "Chromatic drift" → "Chromatic drift · rgb-shift" → "Chromatic drift · rgb-shift → grain", which is unusable. The label names the wait ("Thinking"); the phase belongs in adjacent text, as in the "Inline with a status line" example. If the phase must be announced, announce it once when the turn settles from a separate live region — not per update.

props.name: mode
props.description: Which cloud to draw. orbit = generic working, globe = searching/retrieving (a scan band sweeps pole to pole), mesh = relating things (nodes wire to near neighbours and signals run the edges).

props.name: size
props.description: Rendered box on the spacing scale: sm 5 units (20px at the default spacing; inline in a composer or message row), md 8 (32px; beside a status line), lg 16 (64px; standalone). The box moves with density like the text beside it, and the canvas re-measures it. Each step has its own dot density, dot size and speed.

props.name: speed
props.description: Multiplier on top of the per-size tuned speed. Below ~0.5 the orb reads as stalled.

props.name: paused
props.description: Freeze on a representative still frame without unmounting.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label announced by screen readers while visible (sets aria-label on the role=status element). Must stay constant for as long as the orb is mounted — it names the wait, it does not report progress.

props.name: className
props.description: Set the ink with a semantic text-* token (the dots are drawn from the element's computed color). The box is sized by the size prop, not by className.

motion.why: The orb appears when work starts, and the point cloud is already in motion on its first painted frame. There is nothing to stage.
It reports state; it is not a control. A hover reaction would suggest the wait is something you can click your way out of.

Changing `mode` swaps the renderer on the next frame: the cloud is redrawn as the new shape, not morphed into it. The phase change is carried by the status text beside the orb, which is what a reader actually reads; a per-particle morph would be decoration on top of it.

The cloud is drawn per frame on a canvas by a single requestAnimationFrame loop — no CSS animation exists to name here. The loop reads the motion policy itself, which is the part worth checking when auditing: `custom` means the kill-switch is honoured in JS rather than by --motion-scale.

a11y: Wrapped in role=status, a polite live region, with an aria-label (default 'Thinking'); the canvas itself is aria-hidden.

Because that label is the live region's accessible name, it must not change while the orb is mounted — a name that churns re-announces on every change, so a phase recomputed per streamed delta becomes an interruption per delta. Keep the label constant and let the phase live in adjacent text; announce an outcome once when the work settles, from a separate region.
Ink is the element's computed color, so contrast is the consumer's token choice — pair with foreground or muted-foreground rather than a decorative tint.
Honours the motion policy: under prefers-reduced-motion or <MotionProvider> off, it paints one still frame and never starts an animation loop.
The loop also stops when the orb scrolls out of view or the tab is backgrounded, so a forgotten orb cannot burn a CPU core.

examples.code: <ThinkingOrb />

<ThinkingOrb mode="orbit" size="lg" />
<ThinkingOrb mode="globe" size="lg" />
<ThinkingOrb mode="mesh" size="lg" />

examples.code: <ThinkingOrb size="lg" className="text-primary" paused />

components.name: Toast
components.summary: Imperative notification system over Base UI Toast — auto-dismiss timers, swipe-to-dismiss, focus management, ARIA live-region announcements, and a limit-aware stack. Wrap the app in ToastProvider, then push toasts from anywhere with the global, Sonner-shaped toast() (toast.success/error/info/warning/loading/promise/dismiss) or the useToast() hook inside components.

usage.description: Use Toast for transient feedback caused by a user action: saved, failed, copied, queued, uploaded, or undone. Use Banner for persistent page/app state and InlineStatus or Field errors for feedback that must remain attached to content.

bestPractices.description: Mount one ToastProvider near the app root before any code calls toast() or useToast().
Use toast.promise for async actions so loading, success, and error states stay tied to one notification.
Keep toast copy short and outcome-focused. Add an action only when it is immediately useful, such as Undo.
Use Toast for critical blockers or persistent outages. Use Banner or Dialog when the user must notice and act.
Fire multiple toasts for one operation. Update the same toast when a task progresses.

Put the only path to an action in a toast that auto-dismisses. An Undo that expires on a timer is data loss on a schedule, so error toasts and any toast carrying actionProps default to timeout 0 and wait to be read — pass an explicit timeout only when the action is also reachable somewhere else. When a timeout exists at all, 5s is the floor: anything shorter cannot be read and acted on.

anatomy.name: Viewport
anatomy.description: The positioned live-region stack rendered by ToastProvider.

anatomy.name: Surface
anatomy.description: The individual ToastRoot containing title, description, action, and close affordance.

anatomy.name: Title
anatomy.description: Short outcome text, used as the accessible name.

anatomy.name: Description
anatomy.description: Optional detail or context beneath the title.

anatomy.name: Action
anatomy.description: Optional inline action such as Undo or Retry.

props.name: ToastProvider
props.type: { children, timeout?, limit?, closeIcon?, position?, stacked?, viewportClassName? }
props.description: Wraps Base UI Toast.Provider and renders the themed Viewport + toast list. Mount once near the app root, above any caller of useToast().

props.name: position
props.description: Screen anchor for the toast stack.

props.name: stacked
props.description: Stack the toasts like a deck of cards, the newest in front and the older ones peeking out behind it, a step smaller, instead of listing them one under another. Hovering or focusing the stack fans it out into the list. Use it when an app can raise several toasts in a row, so they don't take over the corner of the page.

props.name: viewportClassName
props.description: Extra classes merged LAST onto the fixed viewport region — for safe-area insets or an offset (e.g. clearing a sidebar).

props.name: timeout
props.description: Default auto-dismiss time in ms for toasts. 0 keeps a toast until it is dismissed. Error toasts, loading toasts, and any toast carrying actionProps default to 0 regardless of this value; a per-toast timeout overrides both.

props.name: limit
props.description: Maximum toasts shown at once; older toasts are pushed out when the limit is exceeded.

props.name: closeIcon
props.description: Override the dismiss-button glyph. The default already follows the injected icon set.

props.name: useToast / useToastManager
props.description: Manager hook for use inside components. add({ title, description, timeout?, type?, priority?, actionProps? }) returns the new toast id and applies the same persistence default as toast.* — an error, loading, or actionProps toast stays until dismissed unless you pass a timeout. close(id), update(id, opts), and promise(p, opts) round out the API.

props.name: toast
props.type: (message, options?) => string  &  { success, error, warning, info, message, loading, promise, dismiss, update, add, custom }
props.description: Imperative singleton callable OUTSIDE React (event handlers, utilities, non-React code) — the Sonner-shaped surface that makes migrating a lib/toast wrapper a near drop-in. Requires a mounted <ToastProvider> (it binds the shared manager). Each call returns the toast id; toast.dismiss(id?) closes one or all; toast.promise(p, { loading, success, error }) and toast.update(id, opts) handle async + in-place updates.

props.name: type (toast option)
props.description: Set by the toast.* helpers. Drives a leading status glyph from the shared tone list, the same one Note and InlineStatus use (success→success, error→destructive, warning→warning, info→info), which blooms in as the toast lands; loading shows a spinner, and the glyph blooms in its place when the toast settles. Both loading and error persist until updated or dismissed unless the call supplies a timeout.

subcomponents.name: ToastRoot
subcomponents.type: Base UI Toast.Root props + className (requires the `toast` object)
subcomponents.description: A single toast surface. Animates enter/leave via data-[starting-style]/data-[ending-style]; swipe-to-dismiss is wired by Base UI.

subcomponents.name: ToastContent
subcomponents.description: The toast's contents as one row. In a stacked viewport it fades on the cards behind the front one and returns when the stack fans out. Wrap a hand-composed toast's parts in it so a stacked viewport can hide them.

subcomponents.name: ToastTitle
subcomponents.description: The toast headline (text-title-sm). Auto-associated as the toast's accessible name.

subcomponents.name: ToastDescription
subcomponents.description: Supporting body copy beneath the title (text-body-sm, muted). Auto-associated as the toast's accessible description.

subcomponents.name: ToastClose
subcomponents.description: Dismiss button. Base UI handles the close and leave animation; labelled "Dismiss" by default.

subcomponents.name: ToastAction
subcomponents.description: Inline action button (e.g. Undo). The imperative path renders one on every toast and Base UI sources its label and handler from that toast's `actionProps`, rendering nothing when there are none — so `toast(msg, { actionProps })` is all an action needs. Reach for the component directly only when composing a toast by hand; compose with render={<Button … />}.

motion.why: A toast interrupts without being asked, so where it came from is the reader's first question. Sliding in from the viewport edge answers it and marks the toast as belonging to the edge rather than to whatever it happens to cover.
Toasts are on a timer, so the action has to look actionable at a glance — there is no time to hunt for the hit target.
Leaving the same way it entered keeps the stack legible when several dismiss at once; toasts that fade in place leave the remaining ones jumping to fill gaps with no visible cause.

A stacked toast arrives from the anchored edge in front of the others, which step back and shrink to make room; hovering fans the deck out into the list. Moving every card, rather than snapping them, shows that the new one went on top and the old ones are still there.

The glyph is what says how it went, so it lands as its own beat: it blooms in 120ms after the card, and blooms again in the spinner's place when a loading toast settles. A 16px glyph needs that amplitude to read as an answer; the card itself only slides.
A toast reports a result that has already happened. Anything still in flight belongs in the surface that started it, where the reader is still looking.

a11y: Base UI announces toasts through an ARIA live region — `low` priority is polite, `high` is assertive.
Auto-dismiss timers pause on hover/focus and while the window is hidden.
ToastClose is keyboard-focusable and labelled; Esc dismisses the focused toast.

ToastClose draws a 24px box (21px against the desktop root) and carries a 24x24+ POINTER TARGET behind it, per WCAG 2.5.8 — the glyph stays quiet because a dismiss control should not be the loudest thing in a toast. Base UI keeps the button out of the accessibility tree until the toast is focused; the toast itself is the announced element.

An action does NOT dismiss its toast — Base UI leaves that to the handler, so an action that opens a confirmation keeps the toast it is confirming. Call `toast.dismiss(id)` yourself when the action should close it.
Animate enter/leave via data-[starting-style]/data-[ending-style] rather than mount/unmount flips.

examples.label: Imperative (from anywhere)
examples.code: toast.success("Saved", { description: "Your post is live." })

examples.label: Promise (loading → success / error)
examples.code: toast.promise(publish(), { loading: "Publishing…", success: "Published", error: "Failed to publish" })

examples.label: Persistent loading, updated in place
examples.code: const id = toast.loading("Uploading report…"); /* later */ toast.update(id, { title: "Uploaded", type: "success", timeout: 4000 })

examples.label: Custom toast markup (composed parts)
examples.code:
const { toasts } = useToast() {toasts.map((t) => (
{t.title}{t.description}
))}
examples.imports: import { Icon, toast, ToastClose, ToastDescription, ToastRoot, ToastTitle, ToastViewport, useToast } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: Undo action
examples.code: toast.message("Post archived", { actionProps: { children: "Undo", onClick: () => restorePost() } })

examples.label: Stacked
examples.code: <ToastProvider stacked position="bottom-right">{children}</ToastProvider>

examples.label: Provider with app chrome
examples.code: <ToastProvider position="bottom-right" limit={3}><AppShell><Region max="feed"><Button onClick={() => toast.success("Saved")}>Save</Button></Region></AppShell></ToastProvider>

components.name: Toggle
components.summary: Pressed-state button over Base UI Toggle, plus ToggleGroup for shared single- or multi-select rows. Pressed styling reads from data-[pressed].

usage.description: Use Toggle for button-like controls that can be pressed on or off within a toolbar or compact control set.

bestPractices.description: Use it for transient UI modes such as bold, preview, pin, or favorite.
Make the pressed state visually and programmatically clear.
Use ToggleGroup appearance="segmented" for a single-select view switch (List / Grid). It is the same capsule ThemeSwitcher wears — do not hand-build a track around a row of toggles.
Do not use Toggle for persistent application settings; use Switch.
Do not leave an icon-only Toggle without an accessible name. It announces as "button, pressed", which tells a screen-reader user the state but never what the state applies to.

anatomy.name: Toggle
anatomy.description: A single pressed or unpressed control.

anatomy.name: ToggleGroup
anatomy.description: A coordinated group of toggle choices.

anatomy.name: ToggleGroupItem
anatomy.description: One toggle inside a group — an alias of Toggle, so <Toggle value="…"> inside a ToggleGroup is the same thing.

props.name: appearance
props.description: On ToggleGroup: `default` is a loose row of toggles; `segmented` draws the capsule segmented control (one track, the pressed option filled) shared with ThemeSwitcher. Single-select segmented draws ONE fill that glides to the pressed option and resizes to its label; multi-select keeps a fill per pressed option. Toggles inside inherit it.

props.name: multiple
props.description: On ToggleGroup: allow several toggles pressed at once. The default is single-select, which behaves like a radio group.

props.name: motion
props.description: On ToggleGroup: how much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the glide, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting.

props.name: Toggle
props.type: Base UI Toggle props (pressed, defaultPressed, onPressedChange, disabled, value) + className
props.description: A two-state button. Uncontrolled via defaultPressed; controlled via pressed + onPressedChange. Pass value to identify it inside a ToggleGroup.

subcomponents.name: ToggleGroup
subcomponents.type: Base UI ToggleGroup props (value, defaultValue, onValueChange, multiple, disabled, orientation, loopFocus) + appearance?: "default" | "segmented" + motion?: "full" | "subtle" | "off" + className
subcomponents.description: Groups child Toggles and shares pressed state across them — each Toggle inside carries a value. Defaults to multiple: false (single-select) — the fit for view-mode switches and segmented controls; pass multiple to allow several pressed at once, e.g. a row of formatting toggles.

subcomponents.name: ToggleGroupItem
subcomponents.description: Re-export of Toggle for group composition — a Toggle carrying a value is the group item.

motion.why: Toggles arrive with the toolbar or header they sit in. Animating each one in would make a row of controls ripple for no reason.
Hover and the pressed fill ease rather than flip, so pressing reads as the same button changing state, not a different button appearing.
The small settle under the finger confirms the press landed before the state change is read — the difference matters most on touch, where there is no hover.

In a single-select segmented group one fill travels to the chosen option and stretches to its label, so a view switch reads as one control now pointing elsewhere. Measured, because labels differ in width. Expressive: motion="subtle" lands it in place.
A toggle commits instantly. Work that follows from the new state shows where its result appears, not on the control.

a11y: Base UI sets aria-pressed on each Toggle and manages the pressed/disabled states.
ToggleGroup provides arrow-key roving focus across its items; loopFocus wraps at the ends.
Pressed styling reads from the data-[pressed] attribute; disabled items are dimmed and non-interactive.
Always supply an aria-label (or visible text) when a Toggle holds only an icon.

examples.label: Standalone
examples.code: <Toggle aria-label="Mute">Mute</Toggle>

examples.label: Single-select group

examples.code: <ToggleGroup appearance="segmented" defaultValue={["list"]} aria-label="View"><Toggle value="list" aria-label="List view"><Icon name="list" /></Toggle><Toggle value="grid" aria-label="Grid view"><Icon name="grid" /></Toggle></ToggleGroup>

examples.label: Segmented with labels, subtle motion
examples.code: <ToggleGroup appearance="segmented" motion="subtle" defaultValue={["week"]} aria-label="Range"><Toggle value="day">Day</Toggle><Toggle value="week">Week</Toggle><Toggle value="month">Month</Toggle></ToggleGroup>

examples.label: Multi-select group

components.name: Toolbar
components.summary: A row or column of controls that is one tab stop, with arrow-key movement between its items (role="toolbar"), over Base UI Toolbar. Items reuse Button's ghost variants and Input, so they follow density like every other control.

usage.description: Use Toolbar when three or more related controls sit together and act on the same thing — a text selection, a canvas, a document, a table. Tab lands on the toolbar once and the arrow keys move along it, so a keyboard user crosses an editor's twelve buttons in one keystroke instead of twelve. It works in both registers: ghost sm buttons on a page, compact icon-xs buttons inside a Workspace.

bestPractices.description: Give every Toolbar an aria-label that names what it acts on ("Text formatting", "Canvas"). With more than one toolbar on screen, that label is the only way a screen-reader user tells them apart.
Use size="icon-sm" (page) or size="icon-xs" (workspace) with an aria-label for icon-only ToolbarButtons, and keep one size across the row so the controls line up.
Split a long row into ToolbarGroups with a ToolbarSeparator between them — undo/redo, text style, insert. Groups give the eye the same structure the arrow keys already cross.

Compose triggers and toggles through ToolbarButton's render prop — render={<MenuTrigger />}, render={<PopoverTrigger />}, or render={<Toggle value="bold" />} inside a ToggleGroup — so they join the toolbar's arrow-key order.

Put a bare Button, Toggle or Input inside a Toolbar. It renders, but it is not a toolbar item: the arrow keys skip it and it takes its own tab stop, which is the inconsistency Toolbar exists to remove. Use ToolbarButton, ToolbarInput, or render through ToolbarButton.
Wrap one or two buttons, or a dialog's Cancel/Confirm pair, in a Toolbar. Those are independent actions; arrow-key movement there is a surprise, not a shortcut. A plain row of Buttons is right.
Use Toolbar for navigation between pages or views. Links that go somewhere are Tabs, SideNav or Breadcrumbs; ToolbarLink is for the odd link that sits among actions, like Help.
Give toolbar buttons primary or destructive fills by default. A toolbar is a quiet strip of tools; the ghost default keeps it from competing with the page's one primary action.

anatomy.name: Toolbar
anatomy.description: The root (role="toolbar"). Owns orientation, loopFocus and disabled for everything inside it.

anatomy.name: ToolbarButton
anatomy.description: An action. Button's ghost variants by default; `render` composes a menu trigger, popover trigger or Toggle into the toolbar.

anatomy.name: ToolbarGroup
anatomy.description: A run of related items. `disabled` disables the whole run.

anatomy.name: ToolbarSeparator
anatomy.description: A hairline between groups, oriented across the toolbar. Never a focus stop.

anatomy.name: ToolbarInput
anatomy.description: A compact Input that joins the arrow-key order — a search or find field in the bar.

anatomy.name: ToolbarLink
anatomy.description: An <a> styled like a ToolbarButton, for a link that sits among the actions.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Which arrow keys move focus (Left/Right or Up/Down) and which way the items stack. Separators turn to match.

props.name: loopFocus
props.description: Arrowing past the last item wraps to the first, and back.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables every item. Items stay focusable (aria-disabled) so the row keeps its shape under the keyboard.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the toolbar for assistive technology. Always set it.

props.name: className
props.description: Layout overrides — e.g. `flex-1` to let the toolbar fill a bar.

subcomponents.name: ToolbarButton
subcomponents.type: { variant?: buttonVariants variant (default "ghost"); size?: buttonVariants size (default "sm"); disabled?: boolean; focusableWhenDisabled?: boolean (default true); render?: ReactElement } + Base UI Toolbar.Button props
subcomponents.description: A toolbar action, styled exactly like <Button>. Disabled buttons stay focusable by default and carry aria-disabled. Pass size="icon-sm"/"icon-xs" plus aria-label for icon-only.

subcomponents.name: ToolbarLink
subcomponents.type: { href?: string; variant?: buttonVariants variant (default "ghost"); size?: buttonVariants size (default "sm"); render?: ReactElement } + Base UI Toolbar.Link props
subcomponents.description: An <a> in the toolbar's arrow-key order, styled like a ToolbarButton.

subcomponents.name: ToolbarInput
subcomponents.type: { disabled?: boolean; focusableWhenDisabled?: boolean (default true) } + Base UI Toolbar.Input / native input props
subcomponents.description: Sable's Input at the sm control height (w-40 by default; override with className). Arrow keys leave the field so it does not trap the row.

subcomponents.name: ToolbarGroup
subcomponents.type: { disabled?: boolean } + Base UI Toolbar.Group props
subcomponents.description: Groups related items; `disabled` disables all of them.

subcomponents.name: ToolbarSeparator
subcomponents.description: A hairline-strong rule across the toolbar's axis, exposed as role="separator" and skipped by the arrow keys.

motion.why: A toolbar is fixed chrome. It is present when its surface is; animating it in would leave the tools briefly unusable for no reason the user can see.
Inherited from buttonVariants: hover fill, focus ring and disabled dim ease together, so the item under the arrow keys reads as the one that moved.
Inherited from buttonVariants. Many toolbar actions change something off to the side (the canvas, the selection), so the settle on press is the confirmation that lands where the pointer is.
The toolbar has no state of its own. Pressed state belongs to a Toggle rendered through ToolbarButton, which carries its own transition.
A toolbar never works on its own. Pending work belongs to the surface the action targets, or to a Spinner in the button that started it.

a11y: Base UI renders role="toolbar" with aria-orientation, and a roving tabindex: the toolbar is one tab stop, the arrow keys move between items, Home/End jump to the ends.
Disabled items stay focusable by default and announce as disabled (aria-disabled), so arrowing along the row never silently skips a control. Set focusableWhenDisabled={false} on an item to opt out.
ToolbarSeparator is role="separator" with the orientation opposite the toolbar's, and is not a focus stop.
ToolbarInput lets the arrow keys move the caret and only leaves the field at either end of its text.
Always set aria-label on the Toolbar, and on every icon-only ToolbarButton.
A Toggle rendered through ToolbarButton keeps aria-pressed; a MenuTrigger keeps aria-haspopup/aria-expanded.

examples.label: Formatting toolbar
examples.code:
<Toolbar aria-label="Text formatting">
  <ToolbarGroup aria-label="History">
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Undo">
      <Icon name="arrow-left" />
    </ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Redo">
      <Icon name="arrow-right" />
    </ToolbarButton>
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToggleGroup multiple aria-label="Style">
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Bold" render={<Toggle value="bold" />}>
      <Icon name="bold" />
    </ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Italic" render={<Toggle value="italic" />}>
      <Icon name="italic" />
    </ToolbarButton>
  </ToggleGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarLink href="/help">Help</ToolbarLink>
</Toolbar>

examples.label: With a menu trigger and a search field

<Toolbar aria-label="Table">
  <ToolbarButton>Export</ToolbarButton>
  <Menu>
    <ToolbarButton render={<MenuTrigger />}>View</ToolbarButton>
    <MenuContent>
      <MenuItem>Compact rows</MenuItem>
      <MenuItem>Comfortable rows</MenuItem>
    </MenuContent>
  </Menu>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarInput aria-label="Search rows" placeholder="Search" />
</Toolbar>

  <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Select">
    <Icon name="arrow-up" />
  </ToolbarButton>

    <Icon name="edit" />

components.name: ToolCall
components.summary: One tool an agent called, as a quiet row inside its turn: a status glyph, what it did, the tool's name and where it is — with the arguments and result behind a disclosure.

usage.description: Use it for each tool call in an assistant's turn, so the person can see what the agent did and check any step. The row is the summary — glyph, a plain-words title, the tool's name, the status — and stays one line, so a turn with ten calls is still scannable. Input and output sit behind the disclosure, because they are read rarely and, when they are, in full.

bestPractices.description: Give it a `title` in plain words, in the tense of the status: "Searching the docs" while running, "Searched the docs" once done. The `name` stays beside it in mono for the person who wants to know exactly which tool ran.
Drive `status` from the call's real state and keep the same element mounted as it changes. The spinner swaps for the outcome in place, and the change is announced to screen readers once.
Pass `error` with `status="error"`. It shows under the row without opening anything, because a failure is the one result everyone needs to read.

Pass a rendered result as `children` when the output is something to look at — a list of hits, a diff — rather than data to inspect. It replaces the output's code view, and `input` still shows above it.
Do not put the approve and deny buttons in a ToolCall. A call held for permission is `status="awaiting"` here, and the decision itself is ApprovalBlock, which says what will happen and asks once.

Do not use it for the agent's thinking or a progress note. A wait with no tool behind it is ThinkingOrb or a Spinner with a status line, and a row that claims a tool ran when none did makes every other row less trustworthy.
Do not open every call by default. A turn whose calls all show their JSON buries the answer; leave `defaultOpen` for the one call the person is likely to check, if any.

anatomy.name: Status glyph
anatomy.description: Spinner while running, then the outcome: check, warning, clock (awaiting approval) or ×. The only part that moves.

anatomy.name: Title
anatomy.description: What the call does, in plain words. Without one, the tool's name leads.

anatomy.name: Name
anatomy.description: The tool's own name in mono, after the title. Hidden below the sm breakpoint when a title is present.

anatomy.name: Status
anatomy.description: One word for where the call is: Running, Needs approval, Done, Failed, Denied.

anatomy.name: Error line
anatomy.description: The failure message, under the row and always visible.

anatomy.name: Details
anatomy.description: Input and output as code, or a rendered result. A disclosure; the row is its trigger.

props.name: name
props.description: The tool's own name, as the model called it (`search_docs`). Shown in mono.

props.name: title
props.description: What the call does, in words a person reads. Leads the row; omit it and `name` leads.

props.name: status
props.description: Where the call is. `awaiting` is held for the person's approval; `denied` is one they declined.

props.name: statusLabel
props.description: Overrides the status word, for another language or a more specific phrase.

props.name: input
props.description: The arguments. A string shows as is; anything else as formatted JSON.

props.name: output
props.description: The result, shown the same way as `input`.

props.name: error
props.description: What went wrong, for `status="error"`. Always visible under the row.

props.name: children
props.description: A rendered result in place of `output`'s code view.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: Open the details on mount.

props.name: open
props.description: Controlled open state of the details.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.description: Called when the details open or close.

motion.why: It arrives as part of the assistant's turn, and the turn's own arrival covers it. A second entrance per call would make a busy turn twitch.
The header is the disclosure trigger but reads as a status row. The hover step is what tells the person it opens.

The spinner becoming a check or a warning is the moment the call settles, and it is the one change in the row worth catching from the corner of the eye. The swap reads as one mark replaced, not a flicker.
The height change connects the code that appears to the row that was pressed, in a thread where several rows look alike.
While the call runs, the spinner is what separates working from stuck. It pauses once the call settles, so a long thread of finished calls costs nothing.

a11y: With details, the header is a button with aria-expanded (Base UI Collapsible); its name is the title, the tool name and the status word, so it reads as one sentence.

A status change after mount is announced once through a polite role=status region ("Searched the docs: Done"). The status a call mounts with is not announced, so a thread restored from history stays quiet.
The glyph is aria-hidden: the status word beside it carries the meaning, so colour and shape are never the only signal.

examples.label: A finished call
examples.code:
<ToolCall
	name="search_docs"
	title="Searched the docs"
	status="complete"
	input={{ query: "date range picker" }}
	output={{ hits: ["DatePicker", "Calendar", "DateTile"] }}
/>

examples.label: Running, then failed
Waiting for approval
examples.code: <ToolCall name="send_email" title="Send the invoice to Ada" status="awaiting" input={{ to: "ada@example.com", subject: "INV-1042" }} />

components.name: Tooltip
components.summary: Hover/focus label over Base UI Tooltip (collision-aware positioning, ARIA wiring, delay grouping via TooltipProvider). Compact popover surface.

usage.description: Use Tooltip for brief nonessential hints tied to a specific control or piece of text.

bestPractices.description: Use it to name icon-only controls or clarify compact UI when the label cannot be visible.
Keep tooltip content short and noninteractive.
Do not put critical instructions, errors, or interactive content inside Tooltip.

Do not let a tooltip serve as an icon button's accessible name. A tooltip is not a name — without its own aria-label the button announces as "button", and the tooltip never opens for a screen reader at all.

anatomy.name: TooltipProvider
anatomy.description: Optional provider for shared tooltip timing.

anatomy.name: TooltipTrigger
anatomy.description: The element that owns the hint.

anatomy.name: TooltipContent
anatomy.description: The short hint content.

anatomy.name: TooltipArrow
anatomy.description: An optional pointer toward the trigger.

anatomy.name: SimpleTooltip
anatomy.description: A convenience wrapper for common tooltip usage.

props.name: side
props.description: On TooltipContent: which side of the trigger to render against. Flips automatically when there is no room.

props.name: Tooltip (Root)
props.type: Base UI Tooltip.Root props (open, defaultOpen, onOpenChange, disabled)
props.description: Groups the trigger and content. Uncontrolled by default.

subcomponents.name: TooltipProvider
subcomponents.type: Base UI Tooltip.Provider props (delay, closeDelay, timeout)
subcomponents.description: Wraps an app or group of Tooltips to share open/close delays. Once one tooltip is open, adjacent tooltips open instantly.

subcomponents.name: TooltipTrigger
subcomponents.description: The anchor element. Use render={<Button/>} to compose with another component.

subcomponents.name: TooltipContent
subcomponents.type: Base UI Popup props + side | align | sideOffset + className
subcomponents.description: Portals + positions + paints the popup. side ("top" | "bottom" | "left" | "right" | "inline-*") picks which side of the trigger to render against, defaults to "top", and auto-flips on collision; align ("start" | "center" | "end") defaults to "center"; sideOffset (gap between trigger and popup, in pixels) defaults to 6.

subcomponents.name: TooltipArrow
subcomponents.description: Optional pointer connecting the popup to its trigger — a popover-coloured square turned 45° that carries the border on its outward edges. Place inside TooltipContent.

subcomponents.name: SimpleTooltip
subcomponents.type: Base UI Tooltip.Root props + content: ReactNode + children: ReactElement + side | align | sideOffset
subcomponents.description: Shorthand wrapping Root + Trigger + Content for the common case. The single child becomes the trigger (via Base UI render); content sets the body; side / align / sideOffset forward to the content with the same defaults. Composition parts remain for advanced use. Inside a TooltipGroup it becomes a trigger of the group's shared tooltip instead.

subcomponents.name: TooltipGroup
subcomponents.description: One tooltip shared by every SimpleTooltip inside it — for a toolbar or a row of icon buttons. Moving the pointer along the row glides the tooltip to the next trigger and swaps its label (old fades out, new fades in, each sliding toward the direction of travel), instead of closing one tooltip and opening another a few pixels away. Renders no element. Each SimpleTooltip keeps its own content / side / align / sideOffset and `disabled`; root props such as open / onOpenChange belong to the shared tooltip and are ignored inside a group. `motion` turns it down: `subtle` jumps between triggers and only cross-fades the label. The composable Tooltip parts are unaffected.

motion.why: The transform-origin follows the anchor, so the tooltip appears to grow out of the element it describes. That is what binds it to its trigger — a bubble that materialises at full size near two possible triggers belongs to neither.
The tooltip is not a hover target; pointing at it is how you dismiss it. Styling it for the pointer would suggest otherwise.
Same recipe, exit direction — it collapses back toward the anchor. Content that fades from a fixed size on close reads as a second, unrelated element disappearing.
Tooltip copy is resident before the tooltip opens. Anything that has to be fetched is a Popover with its own loading state.

Moving between triggers in a group, the one tooltip glides to the next trigger, resizes to its label and cross-fades the text with a short slide toward the direction of travel. Separate tooltips would close here and open there, two surfaces blinking side by side; the glide says it is the same hint following the pointer. Base UI's handle + Viewport supply the shared popup and the previous/current content; the timing is the expressive glide (slow, emphasized), so `subtle` keeps only the cross-fade.

a11y: Base UI wires aria-describedby from trigger to popup and manages hover + focus open.
Opens on keyboard focus, not just hover; dismisses on Esc and blur.
Animate via data-[starting-style]/data-[ending-style] opacity attributes.
Tooltip text is supplementary — never put essential-only actions inside a tooltip.

examples.label: Basic
examples.code: <TooltipProvider><Tooltip><TooltipTrigger render={<Button variant="ghost" size="icon-sm" aria-label="Info"><Icon name="info" /></Button>} /><TooltipContent>Saved to your workspace.</TooltipContent></Tooltip></TooltipProvider>
examples.imports: import { Button, Icon, Tooltip, TooltipContent, TooltipProvider, TooltipTrigger } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: Sides
examples.code: <Tooltip><TooltipTrigger render={<Button variant="secondary">Right</Button>} /><TooltipContent side="right">Opens to the right</TooltipContent></Tooltip>
examples.imports: import { Button, Tooltip, TooltipContent, TooltipTrigger } from "@sableui/react"

examples.label: Shorthand (SimpleTooltip)
examples.code: <SimpleTooltip content="Saved to your workspace."><Button variant="ghost" size="icon-sm" aria-label="Info"><Icon name="info" /></Button></SimpleTooltip>

examples.label: One tooltip gliding along a toolbar (TooltipGroup)
examples.code: <TooltipGroup><Toolbar aria-label="Formatting"><SimpleTooltip content="Bold"><ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Bold"><Icon name="bold" /></ToolbarButton></SimpleTooltip><SimpleTooltip content="Italic"><ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Italic"><Icon name="italic" /></ToolbarButton></SimpleTooltip><SimpleTooltip content="Insert link"><ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Insert link"><Icon name="link" /></ToolbarButton></SimpleTooltip></Toolbar></TooltipGroup>
examples.imports: import { Icon, SimpleTooltip, Toolbar, ToolbarButton, TooltipGroup } from "@sableui/react"

components.name: Tree
components.summary: The object list a tool is built around — layers, scene graph, outline — on one shared grid, so every left edge in the panel resolves to the rail or an exact multiple of the indent step.

usage.description: Use Tree for the hierarchy panel in a workspace: layers, objects, an inspector outline. It owns the geometry that makes nesting legible — the rail, the disclosure and type columns, and the indent step — via the density ladder (scope the panel with data-density, e.g. data-density="compact"), so nothing in the panel computes its own inset. It is also the file tree: nest rows with `subtree`, let folders manage their own open state with `defaultExpanded`, and mark kind with the `icon` convention (folder for a row with a subtree, file for a leaf). Reach for Accordion when the content is prose sections rather than nodes in a hierarchy.

bestPractices.description: Give Tree an aria-label naming the hierarchy ("Layers", "Files"). It is a role="tree", and an unnamed tree is announced as just "tree".

In a layers panel, where the arrows should select, set `selectionFollowsFocus` (and aria-multiselectable when Shift extends) instead of handling ArrowUp/Down on the rows: the tree keeps Home/End, ←/→ and the tab stop, and the row's onClick stays the one selection path.

For a file tree, nest with `subtree` and use the icon convention: `icon={<Icon name="folder" />}` on a row with a subtree, `icon={<Icon name="file" />}` on a leaf. There are no folder/file presets — they would only bind those two props.
Give TreeAddRow the same depth as the rows it adds to, so its mark lands in their type column: one deeper than the parent for a child list, the parent's own depth for a sibling list.

Put mutable per-row state (visibility, solo, a row menu) in `actions`, on the right rail. Show it on hover with `reveal-on-hover` (the row is its `group`), and at rest only when its value is the non-default one.
Let section headers sit on the rail at the same height as a depth-0 row. Space and a hairline separate sections; TreeSection handles both, including dropping the divider on the first.
Hardcode a left inset anywhere in the panel. Use treeIndent(depth) or var(--tree-rail); a hand-written px value is how a tree ends up with four different left edges.
Redefine --tree-indent to anything other than --tree-column. A step smaller than the column puts a child's content left of its parent's and the nesting reads inverted.
Put the visibility toggle before the name. A leading toggle makes each row's visual start depend on its depth, so no two rows share an edge.
Hand-copy icon paths into a tree row. Use Icon and the shared semantic set, or provide an app-specific icon through the supported slot.
Use EmptyState inside a panel. It is page-register furniture (px-6 py-12 around a size-12 disc) and in 240px it spends 24px of inset and ~96px of height on nothing. Use TreeEmpty.
Show explanatory prose AND an add row in an empty section. That is two things to read where one carries the affordance; give TreeEmpty a one-line message and pass the add row as its action.

Leave a section actionable when its action cannot do anything yet — a document-level effect list with no content to apply to, for instance. Hide the section or its affordance until the thing it operates on exists.

anatomy.name: Tree
anatomy.description: The container. Does not scroll itself — put it in a scrolling Panel, or make it the scrolling region with className.

anatomy.name: TreeSection
anatomy.description: A titled group. Header on the rail, hairline above, divider suppressed on the first section.

anatomy.name: TreeRow
anatomy.description: One node: rail, disclosure column, type column, name, right-rail actions.

anatomy.name: TreeAddRow
anatomy.description: The affordance that ends a branch. Mark in the type column, label in the name column.

anatomy.name: TreeEmpty
anatomy.description: A section's empty state at panel scale: one line, one action, optionally a dashed drop region.

props.name: depth
props.description: Nesting level, on TreeRow and TreeAddRow. 0 sits on the rail; each level adds one --tree-indent.

props.name: expandable
props.description: Whether TreeRow renders a disclosure control. The column is reserved either way, so leaf and parent names stay aligned.

props.name: expanded
props.description: Controlled open state for a TreeRow. Pair with onExpandedChange; omit both for an uncontrolled row.

props.name: defaultExpanded
props.description: Uncontrolled initial open state, used when `expanded` is not passed. Pass false for a file tree's closed folders.

props.name: onExpandedChange
props.description: Called when a TreeRow opens or closes — from the disclosure, ArrowRight/ArrowLeft, or activating a row that has no onClick. Fires in both controlled and uncontrolled use.

props.name: subtree
props.description: The rows nested under a TreeRow, rendered after it while it is expanded. Nested rows inherit depth + 1 unless they pass their own `depth`, so a file tree never computes depth by hand.

props.name: selected
props.description: Selection fill and accent bar on a TreeRow. Inside a Tree it is exposed as aria-selected on the treeitem; a row rendered outside a Tree is a plain div and exposes aria-current instead.

props.name: toggleLabel
props.description: Names the thing being disclosed, for the toggle's accessible label — "Expand Background" rather than "Expand group". Every example passes it; a screen-reader user hearing twenty identical "Expand group" buttons has no way to tell them apart.

props.name: icon
props.description: The kind marker for a TreeRow, rendered in the type column at 1em. Use a semantic Icon so it follows the app icon set.

props.name: disclosureIcon
props.description: Replaces TreeRow's semantic chevron-down icon. Omit to use the chevron-down from the app's IconProvider set.

props.name: actions
props.description: Right-rail controls for a TreeRow: visibility, solo, a row menu.

props.name: label
props.description: TreeAddRow's visible label. Name what gets added — 'Add effect', not 'Add'.

props.name: motion
props.description: On Tree. How much motion this component uses: `full` (default) inherits the app's policy, `subtle` keeps feedback and drops the flourish, `off` stills it. It can only turn motion down — it never overrides a reader's reduce-motion setting. Under `subtle` expanded rows appear at once instead of unfolding; the chevron still turns.

props.name: selectionFollowsFocus
props.description: On Tree. The arrow keys select the row they land on, as a layers panel does, instead of only moving focus. The row is activated as a click carrying the key's Shift, so its own onClick (reading event.shiftKey for a range) extends the selection on Shift+Arrow; Ctrl/⌘+Arrow moves without selecting. Only rows with an onClick are selected — a disclosure-only row, a TreeAddRow or a row with selectOnFocus={false} is just focused. Pass aria-multiselectable on the Tree when more than one row can be selected.

props.name: selectOnFocus
props.description: On TreeRow. Pass false for a row whose click does more than select — it switches the active document, or opens itself — so the Tree's selectionFollowsFocus only focuses it as the arrows pass and the tree doesn't reshape under the cursor. Enter/Space and a pointer click still activate it.

subcomponents.name: TreeSection
subcomponents.type: { title: ReactNode; hint?: string; action?: ReactNode }
subcomponents.description: A titled group of rows, with the header on the rail.

subcomponents.name: TreeRow
subcomponents.type: { depth?: number; selected?: boolean; accent?: boolean; dimmed?: boolean; expandable?: boolean; expanded?: boolean; defaultExpanded?: boolean; onExpandedChange?: (expanded: boolean) => void; subtree?: ReactNode; toggleLabel?: string; disclosureIcon?: ReactNode; icon?: ReactNode; actions?: ReactNode }
subcomponents.description: One node in the hierarchy (role=treeitem inside a Tree). Controlled via expanded/onExpandedChange or uncontrolled via defaultExpanded; nest children with subtree. Always reserves both leading columns (disclosure and type), so a leaf's name lines up with its expandable siblings.

subcomponents.name: TreeAddRow
subcomponents.type: { depth?: number; label: ReactNode; icon?: ReactNode }
subcomponents.description: The add affordance, shaped as a row and aligned to the branch it adds to. Its mark sits in the type column (level with the siblings' kind markers), not the name column. `icon` replaces the built-in add mark.

subcomponents.name: TreeEmpty
subcomponents.type: { message: ReactNode; action?: ReactNode; dropTarget?: boolean; depth?: number }
subcomponents.description: A section's or a branch's empty state, at panel scale rather than page scale. One-line message, one action slot; dropTarget renders it as a dashed drop region and sets data-drop-target for styling. `depth` (inherited inside a subtree) starts the line on the edge of the rows that branch would hold.

subcomponents.name: treeIndent
subcomponents.description: The left inset for a depth, as a calc() expression reading the density ladder. Use this rather than computing pixels.

motion.why: Rows a user's expand reveals fade down into place in document order (a capped 18ms stagger), so the eye can follow where the children came from. An animation (motion-arrive) rather than a transition, because the rows already wear motion-interactive and a second transition list would fight it. Only on a user expand of a `subtree` — a tree that mounts open shows its rows at once, and rows added later to an open folder do not cascade. Expressive: `subtle` shows them at once.
Hover and selection fills ease, so sweeping the pointer down a dense panel reads as a highlight following it rather than rows flickering.
The chevron turns with the rows arriving under it; motion-interactive lists `rotate`, which is what -rotate-90 writes, so it no longer flips in one frame.
A tree has no indeterminate state of its own; a branch that loads its children should render a TreeEmpty or a loading row inside it.

a11y: Tree implements the ARIA tree view pattern: Tree is role="tree", each TreeRow and TreeAddRow is role="treeitem" with aria-level, expandable rows carry aria-expanded, and a TreeSection is a role="group" labelled by its heading. Rows stay flat in the DOM — hierarchy is aria-level — so the fills span the panel's full width.

Keyboard: exactly one row is in the tab order (roving tabindex, seeded on the selected row, else the first). ArrowUp/Down move between visible rows; ArrowRight expands a collapsed row, then steps to its first child; ArrowLeft collapses an expanded row, else steps to its parent; Home/End jump to the ends; Enter/Space activate the row — its onClick, or toggling it when it has none. Keys pressed inside a row's own controls (an action button, a rename field) are left to that control. Every key the tree handles is preventDefault-ed, so a page-wide arrow binding (a canvas nudge) should skip an event whose defaultPrevented is true rather than stopping propagation row by row.
With `selectionFollowsFocus`, selection moves with the arrows (Shift extends, Ctrl/⌘ moves focus only), matching the ARIA multi-select tree model; announce it with aria-multiselectable on the Tree.

Selection has one mapping: inside a Tree, `selected` is aria-selected on the treeitem; outside a Tree the row is a plain div, where aria-selected is invalid, so it falls back to aria-current. A navigation tree that wants aria-current="page" passes it through props.
Each treeitem is named by its own label (aria-labelledby the name), never by the text of its icon or action buttons.

The disclosure is a real button with aria-expanded and a label naming what it discloses, and it stops propagation so collapsing a group never changes the selection. Inside a Tree the treeitem carries aria-expanded and the arrow keys, so the button becomes a pointer target only: aria-hidden, out of the tab order, and it leaves focus where it was when clicked.

The disclosure's POINTER TARGET is bigger than the mark it draws. `--tree-column` is 20px comfortable and 18px compact, both under WCAG 2.5.8's 24x24 floor, so a centred pseudo-element takes the hit at `--control-xs` (28/24) instead. The drawn box stays on the column, because that column is also the indent step — growing the button would push every name in the tree one column right.
Right-rail actions stay in the tab order, so a row with actions costs extra Tab stops. Keep actions few and reveal them with `reveal-on-hover`, which also shows them on focus and always on touch.
`dimmed` is presentation only. A row switched off must also say so in its actions' aria-pressed or its accessible name; opacity alone is invisible to a screen reader and fails contrast.
Right-rail controls that appear on hover must also appear on focus-visible, or they are unreachable by keyboard.

components.name: Video
components.summary: Styled 16:9 video player frame. Mounts a native <video> when given a src, or shows a poster/placeholder with a centered play overlay.

usage.description: Use Video to embed playable or previewable video media inside a page.

bestPractices.description: Use captions, poster imagery, and controls when the video carries information.
Keep the surrounding layout stable while media loads.
Do not autoplay important audio or make video the only way to access required information.
Do not ship it without captions or a transcript. Captions are what make video usable for deaf users and searchable for everyone; a video with neither is inaccessible content you also cannot index.

props.name: onRequestPlay
props.description: Placeholder only (no src): renders the play mark as a real button labelled "Play video" that calls this — e.g. to load the source. Without it the mark is decorative.

props.name: src
props.description: Video source URL. When omitted, a poster/placeholder with a play overlay renders.

props.name: poster
props.description: Poster image shown before playback (and as the placeholder backdrop).

props.name: controls
props.description: Show native playback controls.

motion.why: The frame arrives with its page. Once there is a source, the poster and controls are the browser's.
With `onRequestPlay`, the play disc firms its scrim on hover, eased, so the mark reads as pressable over any image.
Loading a source can take a moment; the settle on press confirms the tap before the player appears.
Placeholder to player is a swap of elements: the native video mounts where the poster was. Animating the swap would delay the playback the person just asked for.
Buffering belongs to the native controls, which draw their own indicator. A second loader over the frame would compete with the browser's.

a11y: Mounts a native <video> element, preserving built-in keyboard controls when controls is enabled.
Without onRequestPlay the placeholder play mark is decorative (aria-hidden) — nothing on the frame pretends to be pressable. With it, the mark is a native button named "Play video".

components.name: Workspace
components.summary: The shell for a tool: a fixed viewport partitioned into independently scrolling regions, with a compact density scope, a skip link, and a canvas landmark.

usage.description: Use Workspace as the outer frame for a tool — an editor, a console, a canvas app. It owns the viewport, scopes the compact control density, and guarantees a skip link plus a main landmark on the canvas. Reach for AppShell instead for page-register products: it is built around a scrolling document, where a workspace is built around a fixed one. Workspace fills the viewport (h-dvh) by design; to embed one in a page (a docs preview, a modal-sized demo), wrap it in a bounded container and pass className="h-full".

bestPractices.description: Put a PanelGroup in the body and a WorkspaceCanvas inside it, so panels are aside chrome and the work surface is the main landmark.
Let each panel own its scrolling. The shell never scrolls, and the canvas clips rather than scrolls — panning is the viewport's job.
Keep the density scope at compact unless you have a specific reason; the workspace register's measured control ladder is what makes tool chrome read as tool chrome.

Put a WorkspaceBar inside a column when the bar belongs to that column only. An issue tracker's bar (breadcrumb, view tabs, filters) sits above the list, while the sidebar and the inspector beside it run the full height: put the WorkspaceBar first inside the WorkspaceCanvas, not in the `toolbar` slot, which spans every panel. Don't hand-build a fixed-height header for it.

Wrap a reading view inside the workspace (a project overview, an update, a doc, release notes) in <Density value="comfortable">. The compact scope maps body text to the 11–12px UI tiers, which is right for chrome and too small for paragraphs; the comfortable scope gives prose its page size again while the chrome around it stays compact.

Plan the phone layout with the shell rather than around it: pass a BottomNav to `bottomNav`, and give docked Panels `narrow="sheet"` (an inspector, a navigation rail) or `narrow="hidden"`. Don't measure the viewport with a resize listener, render the inspector twice, or subtract the nav's height from 100dvh.
Nest a Region or Page inside it to set a width. Region caps are a page-register idea; a workspace is edge-to-edge and its panels are fixed-width chrome outside the content grid.
Hardcode a control height (h-[32px]). CI rejects it (raw-control-height); read the ladder instead, e.g. h-(--control-sm), so the density scope can size it.
Put a Card in the chrome. Use PanelSection — a card inside a narrow panel spends its border and inset on nothing.
Use it for a dashboard that scrolls. If the primary interaction is reading down a page, that's AppShell plus a Region, not a workspace.

anatomy.name: WorkspaceBar
anatomy.description: Top chrome at --chrome-bar-height with a hairline beneath: toolbar, document tabs, menubar row.

anatomy.name: Body
anatomy.description: The flexible middle row, normally a PanelGroup. Constrained so its children can shrink and scroll.

anatomy.name: WorkspaceCanvas
anatomy.description: The work surface and the main#main-content landmark the skip link targets. Clips rather than scrolls.

anatomy.name: StatusBar
anatomy.description: Bottom chrome for ambient document facts.

anatomy.name: BottomNav
anatomy.description: Phone navigation in the `bottomNav` slot. Its row is reserved below lg and gone above it, so the body ends where the nav begins.

props.name: toolbar
props.description: Top chrome, normally a WorkspaceBar.

props.name: statusBar
props.description: Bottom chrome, normally a StatusBar.

props.name: bottomNav
props.description: Phone navigation, normally a BottomNav. Below lg (BottomNav's own breakpoint) the shell reserves the nav's height as its last row, so the body and the status bar end above the nav instead of under it; above lg the row is gone. Every slot is optional: the body is the shell's one growing row whichever of toolbar, statusBar and bottomNav are present.

props.name: density
props.description: Density scope for everything inside. Sets the --control-* ladder via data-density; compact is the workspace register. Nothing hardcodes a height, so the same size="md" Button is 40px on a page and 32px inside a compact Workspace. A Dialog opened from inside resets to comfortable, because a modal is a page-register surface even when a tool launched it.

props.name: skipLinkLabel
props.description: Text for the skip link that targets the canvas landmark.

subcomponents.name: WorkspaceBar
subcomponents.description: The top chrome strip, sized to --chrome-bar-height with a hairline beneath.

subcomponents.name: WorkspaceCanvas
subcomponents.description: The work surface: renders main#main-content, fills the body, clips its overflow.

subcomponents.name: useMediaQuery
subcomponents.description: True while a media query matches, read through useSyncExternalStore: no resize listener, no setState in an effect, no hydration mismatch (the server reports serverValue, default false). Use it to branch structure a class cannot express; style-only changes stay as lg: classes.

subcomponents.name: useBelowBreakpoint
subcomponents.description: True below a named breakpoint (default lg), flipping at the width where that breakpoint's classes start to apply (Tailwind's sm 40 / md 48 / lg 64 / xl 80 / 2xl 96rem). Panel's `narrow` uses it; reach for it instead of a hand-rolled window.innerWidth check.

a11y: Renders a skip link to #main-content as the first focusable element, even though there is no scrolling document.
WorkspaceCanvas is the <main id="main-content"> landmark; Panels are <aside> chrome with their own names.
Density only changes control sizes, never hit-target rules — an icon button at the 24px floor still needs a padded 44px hit area.

items.name: AuthPage
items.summary: Split sign-in page: a form column (brand mark, heading, email + password, primary sign-in, passkey and email-link alternatives, sign-up switch, terms) beside a brand panel painted from the theme's tones with a customer story card. Below lg the panel drops away and the form is the whole screen.
items.intent: Reach for this for sign-in, sign-up, forgot-password, and any single-purpose one-column form route (invite accept, unsubscribe). Not for multi-section forms (use SettingsPage).
notes: The form column is a `form`-capped Region (480px), so the controls keep the same measure whether the panel is present or not.
No card around the form: the page itself is the surface, and the brand panel carries the identity. A card on a blank page reads as a template.
The heading is `text-heading-1` in an h1 — it is the page outline, so it takes a heading tier, not a card title.
Brand mark, form and terms are a three-part column: mark pinned to the top, form vertically centred in the remaining space, terms pinned to the bottom.
Forgot password sits under the password field, right-aligned, before the submit button — so it comes right after the field in tab order. Field has no label-row action slot yet.
One primary action. Passkey and email link are outline buttons under an `or` Separator; switching to sign-up is a quiet `link-underline` link.

Validation uses Field `validate` for product copy instead of the browser's generic required message. A rejected sign-in comes back through Form `errors` on the password field; the submit Button shows `loading` while the request is in flight.

The brand panel artwork is a mesh of the theme's decorative tones over `--primary`, so it re-paints for every theme and mode. The relative-colour `oklch(from var(--tone-*) …)` lift needs an `inline-color` disable with a reason.
The panel is `hidden lg:flex`: on a phone the form is the whole screen, with no decorative scroll above it.
a11y: The route renders inside <main> with one h1; the brand panel is an <aside> labelled "Customer story".
Field auto-wires labels, describedby, and invalid state onto the inputs; on submit, the first invalid field is focused.
Autocomplete attributes (`email webauthn`, `current-password`) keep password managers and passkey autofill working.
The Forgot password and Create one links use `hit-target` to meet the 44px touch floor without changing layout.
The artwork swatches are aria-hidden decoration; the brand link's accessible name is the wordmark.

items.name: BrandLandingPage
items.summary: High-fidelity brand/product landing page: pill navigation, editorial hero type, a dark product scene, a value section, a how-it-works sequence, a customer story with outcomes, a closing CTA band, and a complete branded footer.
items.intent: Use this for a polished product marketing route that still needs to show a credible app surface. It is warmer and more tactile than the canonical LandingPage, but avoids trend-driven neon and generic hype cues.
notes: The story runs promise → product → value → process → proof → ask: hero, product scene, 'Why Cove' value cards, a three-step how-it-works list, a customer story with outcome figures, then one closing CTA. Each section adds new evidence; no number is repeated from the product scene.
One display headline owns the first viewport; supporting copy stays in body-lg at prose measure. Section headings are heading-1 under a `text-overline` eyebrow.
The nav spends one compact pill surface, with a clear brand signal and two primary paths: sign in and request access.

The product scene and the closing CTA band are dark islands: a `dark` class on the wrapper re-scopes every semantic token, so surfaces, muted ink, Badge tones and Buttons take the theme's own dark values in either page mode. Never fake a dark panel with overlay ink at reduced opacity — status tones tuned for a light page vanish on it.

The scene is a picture of the product: `aria-hidden` + `inert` keep its sample button and figures out of the tab order and the outline. On narrow screens it drops the side column and keeps the signal map, so it scales instead of stacking into a second page.
The chart keeps past weeks on the quiet `secondary` fill and gives the current week the one accent, so the signal reads at a glance.

Value cards are real Cards with a neutral `sable-well` icon tile; the customer story is a Card rendered as a figure, with outcome figures split by Separator. The scene's nested panels take `rounded-concentric-xl/<inset>` from the shell's radius, so the corners stay parallel at any radius preset.
The footer closes the page with brand reassurance, a plain status Badge, a three-column sitemap (three columns at every width), a digest signup, and legal links.
All figures, names and the testimonial are sample content; replace them with real, verifiable claims.
a11y: The brand nav is a labeled nav landmark with real links and visible text.
Each content section is a labelled region (by its h2, or aria-label for the customer story); the decorative product scene is hidden from assistive tech and inert.
The how-it-works steps are an ordered list; the testimonial is a figure with a blockquote and a figcaption naming the speaker.
The footer is a real footer landmark with a labeled footer nav, visible link text, and a labeled email field.
TextReveal preserves the full headline as one accessible label and honors reduced-motion policy; Reveal shows the value cards immediately when motion is off.
Status dots and the status Badge are paired with visible text labels so color is never the only signal.

items.name: ChatPanel
items.summary: A full-height conversation surface: titled header, scrolling transcript, and a composer pinned to the bottom — the assembled shape of an AI assistant, a support thread, or a DM.
items.intent: Reach for this for any conversation that owns its screen — an assistant, a support inbox thread, a DM. Not for a chat docked beside other work (compose the same three parts inside a Sheet or a PanelGroup instead), and not for a comment thread under an article, which is a FeedPage concern.
notes: This is the assembled screen with sample data. To wire it to a real streaming source (a hook such as useChat, or your own transport), read `sable docs building-a-chat`: who owns what, the turn lifecycle mapped to props, and every failure state.

The panel is a fixed-height column, not a growing page. `h-[calc(100dvh_-_--spacing(12))]` on the Card (the viewport minus the Page's py-6, in spacing units so density moves both together — a fixed `3rem` drifts the moment density moves the padding) and `flex-1 min-h-0` on the MessageScroller are what make the transcript scroll instead of the document — the single most common thing to get wrong here, and it fails by pushing the composer off the bottom of the screen.

The panel is a Card, not a hand-built bordered section: CardHeader (title, description, CardAction), the MessageScroller and a CardFooter all inset by the card's own `--card-p`, so the three regions share one edge at any card density.
`dvh` rather than `vh`: on mobile the URL bar collapses, and a `vh`-sized panel puts the composer under it exactly when someone is trying to type.
Region cap is `feed` (640px) — a conversation is a reading column, and the Bubble measure cap is tuned to the same assumption.
The composer sits outside the scroll region, in a bordered CardFooter, so it stays put while the transcript moves.
Grouping is derived from the data (`turns[i - 1].mine === turn.mine`) rather than hand-set, and the tail is dropped on continuations — that pairing is what makes a run read as one block.

What the assistant did before answering — a doc it read, a tool it ran — is a `Marker variant="note"` in that message's `header`, so it reads as part of the turn rather than as an event between turns.

The assistant's long-form answer uses `variant="plain"` and continues the same grouped run. A tinted box around a code block reads as a quote rather than as a turn. A plain Bubble sizes to its content with no measure cap, so it takes `max-w-full` here: bounded by the column, a wide code line scrolls inside the CodeBlock instead of pushing the transcript sideways on a phone.

A settled answer carries its actions (copy, regenerate) in the Message `footer` as a `Toolbar` of icon `ToolbarButton`s with tooltips — one tab stop, arrow keys between them. The answer still streaming has none: there is nothing to copy or regenerate until it settles, and Stop lives in the composer.
One turn, one Message: the reader's question and the file it refers to stack inside a single end-aligned Message rather than being sent as two.
Assistant turns share one Avatar with a glyph fallback and `alt="Assistant"` — initials like "AI" read as a person, and a fallback-only avatar is otherwise unnamed.

The answer in flight is a `StreamingText` in a `plain` Bubble, and ONE `pending` flag drives both it and the composer's `busy`. They are the same wait reported at the two ends of the panel; letting them drift gives you a composer still saying 'sending' under an answer that already finished.

A spinner `Marker` (or `ThinkingOrb`) belongs BEFORE the first token and is replaced once tokens land, not kept alongside. Two indicators for one wait read as two things happening — which is also why `StreamingText` takes `caret={false}` when something adjacent already reports it.

MessageScroller needs no configuring for this: it re-follows on "a message grew" (ResizeObserver) as well as "a message arrived", so the newest token stays pinned while a reader who has scrolled up is left alone.
For a new thread, swap the transcript's children for an `<EmptyState>` inside the same MessageScroller — the panel, header and composer are unchanged, which is the point of keeping them separate.
a11y: The panel header's title is the page's <h1> (an h1 inside CardTitle, which carries the type); the transcript is a scroll region with native overflow, so keyboard scrolling works unchanged.

The answer in flight carries `aria-busy` rather than sitting in a live region. That is deliberate: a live region around streamed text announces every token, which is unusable. Announce once when the turn settles, from whatever owns the turn — the incomplete state is still exposed, just not narrated.

The composer is a real <form> whose Enter handling skips IME composition, and every icon-only control in the panel carries an accessible label — the answer actions also carry a tooltip, and the stop control is named for what it stops (`stopLabel="Stop answering"`).

items.name: DashboardPage
items.summary: App-shell admin dashboard: a branded Sidebar with an account footer (AppHeader + BottomNav below lg), a KPI row, an edge-to-edge accounts table with seat-usage Meters, and supporting payout, top-customer, release and activity cards — the default shape for an operator or analytics home route.
items.intent: Reach for this when a route's job is monitoring or managing many records (sales, orders, accounts, posts) with a few headline numbers. Not for reading-focused routes (use FeedPage) or single-record routes (use ListDetailPage's detail side).
notes: Region cap is `wide` (1280px): dashboards hold tables and multi-column grids, never a reading column.

Hierarchy runs headline → records → context: KPI row, then the primary table beside its two closest companions (payout, top customers), then the lower-priority lists (upcoming, activity). Every row of the grid is filled so the route ends on content, not empty canvas.

Stat cards: CardHeader carries the label (CardDescription) and the value; KPI values are `text-mono-xl` — the metric mono tier, tabular figures — never a heading tier. The trend Badge sits with its comparison note in CardContent, so the value keeps the full card width when the row folds to 2×2 on a phone.
Stat cards use an explicit cols map (2 → 4) — a 4-stat row must fold to 2×2, never strand an orphan the way auto-fit can.

The table runs flush to the card edges with `<CardContent flush>`, which hands the card's padding to the table (`--table-edge-px`), so the first and last columns line up with the CardHeader at any card density — never hand-set pl-6/pr-6. Numeric columns align end in mono; Table scrolls horizontally inside the card on narrow screens.

Seats used / seats is a `Meter` (how full a known range is), not `Progress` (task progress). Status is `Badge appearance="plain" dot`, with the app's own states mapped to tones once at the top of the file.

Lists are Entity rows in CardList, inset to the card padding and divided by hairlines — never CardContent with hand-tuned px. A card that shares a grid row with a taller one becomes `flex flex-col` and pins its CardFooter with `mt-auto`.

Brand and account live in the Sidebar: SidebarHeader holds the mark + wordmark, SidebarFooter holds the signed-in Entity with an OverflowMenu. Sidebar rebinds the page ink tokens to its own, so the Entity and OverflowMenu read correctly even when a theme paints the rail dark on a light page.
The page has exactly one heading-1 (PageHeader); card titles are Title tier, not headings.
Chrome (Sidebar) is outside the content grid; the Page region caps only content.
Sidebar hides below lg, so the shell's header carries an AppHeader (brand + account) and its footer a BottomNav with the same destinations — never strand mobile users without navigation.
a11y: AppShell provides the skip link and <main id="main-content"> landmark.
The active SidebarItem and BottomNavItem carry aria-current via `active`.
DataTable headers are real <th>; sortable columns are announced.
Each seat-usage Meter has an aria-label naming the account and aria-valuetext reading "184 of 250 seats used".
Avatars beside a visible name use an empty alt so the name is not read twice.

items.name: FeedPage
items.summary: Social reading feed with a side rail: a feed-width main column (composer, For you / Following Tabs, one Card per post, an event post with price, capacity Meter and Register, a Skeleton for the next page) beside a sticky rail of who-to-follow and upcoming events that drops away below lg.
items.intent: Reach for this for timelines, activity streams, and any reverse-chronological reading surface where people also act on what they read. Not for record management (DashboardPage) or side-by-side browsing (ListDetailPage).
notes: The main column is capped at `--region-feed` (640px) inside a `wide` page, so posts keep a reading measure while the rail fills the desktop width. The rail is a fixed `w-80` aside, `sticky` at lg and `hidden` below it — its content is supplementary, so nothing is lost on mobile.
Feed scope is `Tabs` (underline, stretched to the column with `flex`): peer views of the same feed. The composer sits above them because posting applies to both.
The composer is a Card holding `Textarea autoResize` plus ghost icon Buttons and a secondary `Post` — not ChatComposer, which submits on Enter and is for conversations.

Each post is a Card: an Entity byline in a CardList (with an OverflowMenu for post actions), body copy, then media in an AspectBox at the asset's own ratio, inset with `rounded-concentric-lg/6` so its corners follow the card's in every theme.

An event post adds a `Badge appearance="overlay"` on the image, title and price, the one primary Button on the page (`Register`), and a `Meter` for capacity — seats taken against a known maximum is a level, not task progress.
Actions are ghost sm Buttons (icon + count) in a Row pulled out by the button's own padding (`-ms-3`) so the first icon sits on the text edge.

Loading the next page shows a Skeleton post in the shape the post will land in, above the explicit load-more Button in its `loading` state — predictable for keyboard and AT users, unlike infinite scroll.
a11y: Each post is an <article>, so AT users can jump between posts; the rail is a labelled <aside> landmark.
Rail card titles render as h2 (CardTitle `render={<h2 />}`) under the page's one h1.
Icon-only buttons and every Follow / Remind button carry aria-labels naming their target; counts stay in the accessible name.
The capacity Meter is role=meter with a getAriaValueText reading ("28 of 40 seats taken").
The Skeleton card is aria-busy; the loading Button keeps its label ("Loading posts").
